abstract: The input/output properties of a 2 compartment model neuron are systematically explored. Taken from the work of MacGregor (MacGregor, 1987), the model neuron compartments contain several active conductances, including a potassium conductance in the dendritic compartment driven by the accumulation of intradendritic calcium. Dynamics of the conductances and potentials are governed by a set of coupled first order differential equations which are integrated numerically. There are a set of 17 internal parameters to this model, specificying conductance rate constants, time constants, thresholds, etc. To study parameter sensitivity, a set of trials were run in which the input driving the neuron is kept fixed while each internal parameter is varied with all others left fixed. To study the input/output relation, the input to the dendrite (a square wave) was varied (in frequency and magnitude) while all internal parameters of the system were left flXed, and the resulting output firing rate and bursting rate was counted. The input/output relation of the model neuron studied turns out to be much more sensitive to modulation of certain dendritic potassium current parameters than to plasticity of synapse efficacy per se (the amount of current influx due to synapse activation). This would in turn suggest, as has been recently observed experimentally, that the potassium current may be as or more important a focus of neural plasticity than synaptic efficacy.

paragraphs: This study investigates how a two-compartment neuron model converts input into firing and bursting. Its compartments contain active electrical conductances, including a dendritic potassium conductance controlled by calcium accumulation. Coupled differential equations describe the changing voltages and conductances, and the authors solve these equations numerically to examine the model's behavior.

The investigation separates two questions. To measure sensitivity to internal properties, the authors hold the input constant and vary each of the model's 17 parameters individually. To measure responses to different inputs, they fix those parameters and vary the frequency and strength of a square-wave signal delivered to the dendrite, counting firing and bursting rates.

Certain parameters governing dendritic potassium current have a stronger effect on the input-output relationship than changes in synaptic efficacy, represented by incoming current during synapse activation. Within this model, changing the neuron's own electrical properties can therefore matter more than changing input strength. The authors suggest potassium currents deserve attention as a possible mechanism of neural plasticity.
summary.tldr: A two-compartment neuron model responds more strongly to certain dendritic potassium parameters than to changes in synaptic efficacy.

title: A Systematic Study of the Input/Output Properties of a 2 Compartment Model Neuron With Active Membranes

paragraphs: A trained network normally maps inputs to outputs. This paper develops a closed-form method for going in the opposite direction: starting with an output and constructing input activity that reproduces it when passed forward through the network. The defining requirement is consistency with the network’s normal forward computation.

Multiple inputs may correspond to the same output, so finding an inverse can involve choosing among alternatives. The authors select a particular inverse with no component in the nullspace of the whole network’s activation flow operator. The nullspace describes directions that the operator maps to zero, making it central to understanding the freedom available when an inverse is not unique.

The calculation also produces an orthogonal basis for a substantial portion of that nullspace. This supplies a structured way to construct alternative inverse mappings and optimize them for a particular application. The contribution therefore includes both a specific inverse solution and mathematical information useful for adapting that solution when several inputs can satisfy the desired output.
summary.tldr: A closed-form network inversion method constructs inputs for desired outputs and exposes ways to optimize alternative solutions.

title: Closed-Form Inversion of Backpropagation Networks: Theory and Optimization Issues

abstract: An important issue in neural computation is the dynamic range of weights in the neural networks. Many experimental results on learning indicate that the weights in the networks can grow prohibitively large with the size of the inputs. Here we address this issue by studying the tradeoffs between the depth and the size of weights in polynomial-size networks of linear threshold elements (LTEs). We show that there is an efficient way of simulating a network of LTEs with large weights by a network of LTEs with small weights. In particular, we prove that every depth-d, polynomial-size network of LTEs with exponentially large integer weights can be simulated by a depth-(2d + 1), polynomial-size network of LTEs with polynomially bounded integer weights. To prove these results, we use tools from harmonic analysis of Boolean functions. Our technique is quite general, it provides insights to some other problems. For example, we are able to improve the best known results on the depth of a network of linear threshold elements that computes the COM PARI SO N, SUM and PRO DU CT of two n-bits numbers, and the MAX 1M U M and the SORTING of n n-bit numbers.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a theoretical tradeoff between network depth and the magnitude of connection weights. Its networks consist of linear threshold elements, which make decisions from weighted inputs. The concern is that weights can become prohibitively large as input size grows, even when the number of network elements remains manageable.

The main theorem shows how to replace large integer weights with smaller ones by increasing depth. Every polynomial-size network of depth d with exponentially large integer weights can be simulated by a polynomial-size network of depth 2d + 1 whose integer weights are polynomially bounded. The replacement preserves the computation while changing the resources used to express it.

The proof uses harmonic analysis of Boolean functions. The same technique also improves known depth results for threshold networks computing comparison, addition, and multiplication of two binary numbers, as well as maximum and sorting over multiple numbers. The contribution shows that large weight magnitudes are not always essential: additional layers can provide an efficient alternative in this formal network setting.
summary.tldr: Threshold networks with exponentially large weights can be simulated using polynomially bounded weights by increasing depth from d to 2d + 1.

title: Neural Computing with Small Weights

abstract: The efficiency of image search can be greatly improved by using a coarse-to-fine search strategy with a multi-resolution image representa(cid:173) tion. However, if the resolution is so low that the objects have few dis(cid:173) tinguishing features, search becomes difficult. We show that the performance of search at such low resolutions can be improved by using context information, i.e., objects visible at low-resolution which are not the objects of interest but are associated with them. The networks can be given explicit context information as inputs, or they can learn to detect the context objects, in which case the user does not have to be aware of their existence. We also use Integrated Feature Pyramids, which repre(cid:173) sent high-frequency information at low resolutions. The use of multi(cid:173) resolution search techniques allows us to combine information about the appearance of the objects on many scales in an efficient way. A natural fOlm of exemplar selection also arises from these techniques. We illus(cid:173) trate these ideas by training hierarchical systems of neural networks to find clusters of buildings in aerial photographs of farmland.

paragraphs: Searching an image at several resolutions can save work: a coarse view guides where to examine finer detail. The difficulty is that small, low-resolution objects may lose the features needed to recognize them. This paper addresses that problem by using contextual objects that remain visible and are associated with the target.

The neural networks can receive context explicitly, or learn to detect useful contextual objects themselves. In the second case, the person configuring the system need not identify those objects in advance. The method also uses Integrated Feature Pyramids, which preserve information about fine image structure within low-resolution representations, allowing coarse searches to use more than blurred appearance.

Hierarchical neural systems demonstrate the approach by finding groups of buildings in aerial photographs of farmland. The stated result is that context improves searching at resolutions where the targets themselves are hard to distinguish. Combining evidence across scales makes search more efficient, and the multiresolution approach also gives rise to a natural way of selecting exemplars.
summary.tldr: Context and multiresolution features help neural networks locate targets even when coarse images hide their distinguishing details.

title: Coarse-to-Fine Image Search Using Neural Networks

abstract: We present a neural model that can perform eye movements to a particular side of an object regardless of the position and orienta(cid:173) tion of the object in space, a generalization of a task which has been recently used by Olson and Gettner [4] to investigate the neu(cid:173) ral structure of object-centered representations. Our model uses an intermediate representation in which units have oculocentric recep(cid:173) tive fields- just like collicular neurons- whose gain is modulated by the side of the object to which the movement is directed, as well as the orientation of the object. We show that these gain modulations are consistent with Olson and Gettner's single cell recordings in the supplementary eye field. This demonstrates that it is possible to perform an object-centered task without a representation involv(cid:173) ing an object-centered map, viz., without neurons whose receptive fields are defined in object-centered coordinates. We also show that the same approach can account for object-centered neglect, a situ(cid:173) ation in which patients with a right parietal lesion neglect the left side of objects regardless of the orientation of the objects. Several authors have argued that tasks such as object recognition [3] and manipula(cid:173) tion [4] are easier to perform if the object is represented in object-centered coordi(cid:173) nates, a representation in which the subparts of the object are encoded with respect to a frame of reference centered on the object. Compelling evidence for the existence of such representations in the cortex comes from experiments on hemineglect- a neurological syndrome resulting from unilateral lesions of the parietal cortex such that a right lesion, for example, leads patients to ignore stimuli located on the left side of their egocentric space. Recently, Driver et al. (1994) showed that the deficit can also be object-centered. Hence, hemineglect patients can detect a gap in the upper edge of a triangle when this gap is associated with the right side of the object Neural Basis of Object-Centered Representations

paragraphs: Acting toward a particular side of an object requires accounting for where the object is and how it is oriented. This paper presents a neural model that can direct eye movements to the requested side despite changes in position and orientation. It asks what kind of internal representation is sufficient for that behavior.

The model's intermediate units have receptive fields defined relative to the eyes. Their response gain is modulated by the intended side of the object and its orientation. This combination allows eye-centered units to support a task defined relative to an object. The authors report that the gain modulations agree with single-cell recordings from the supplementary eye field.

The same approach also accounts for object-centered neglect, in which patients with a right parietal lesion ignore an object's left side regardless of its orientation. Together, these results show that object-centered behavior and deficits can arise without neurons arranged in an object-centered coordinate map. The model establishes a possible mechanism, separating the reference frame of the task from that of individual receptive fields.
summary.tldr: Gain-modulated eye-centered neurons can support object-centered eye movements and account for object-centered neglect.

title: Neural Basis of Object-Centered Representations

abstract: The problem of time series prediction is studied within the uniform convergence framework of Vapnik and Chervonenkis. The dependence inherent in the temporal structure is incorporated into the analysis, thereby generalizing the available theory for memoryless processes. Finite sample bounds are calculated in terms of covering numbers of the approximating class, and the tradeoff between approximation and estimation is discussed. A complexity regularization approach is outlined, based on Vapnik's method of Structural Risk Minimization, and shown to be applicable in the context of mixing stochastic processes.
originalAbstract: The problem of time series prediction is studied within the uniform convergence framework of Vapnik and Chervonenkis. The dependence inherent in the temporal structure is incorporated into the analysis, thereby generalizing the available theory for memoryless processes. Finite sample bounds are calculated in terms of covering numbers of the approximating class, and the tradeoff between approximation and estimation is discussed. A complexity regularization approach is outlined, based on Vapnik's method of Structural Risk Minimization, and shown to be applicable in the context of mixing stochastic processes.

paragraphs: Time-series observations depend on one another, so learning theory for memoryless processes does not directly capture their temporal structure. This paper brings that dependence into a uniform-convergence analysis of prediction. Uniform convergence concerns how reliably performance measured on a finite sample reflects performance across a whole class of candidate predictors.

The authors derive finite-sample bounds expressed through covering numbers of the approximating class. Covering numbers quantify how many representative functions are needed to describe a class at a chosen precision. This connects the richness of the predictor family to the uncertainty involved in estimating its performance from limited, temporally dependent observations.

The analysis addresses the tradeoff between approximation and estimation: richer classes can represent more relationships, but their performance is harder to estimate reliably. The paper outlines complexity regularization based on structural risk minimization and establishes its applicability to mixing stochastic processes. Mixing supplies the relevant dependence setting. The result extends a principled approach to model complexity selection into time-series prediction while explicitly accounting for temporal dependence.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample learning bounds justify structural risk minimization for time-series prediction under mixing dependence.

title: Structural Risk Minimization for Nonparametric Time Series Prediction

abstract: The Vicinal Risk Minimization principle establishes a bridge between generative models and methods derived from the Structural Risk Mini(cid:173) mization Principle such as Support Vector Machines or Statistical Reg(cid:173) ularization. We explain how VRM provides a framework which inte(cid:173) grates a number of existing algorithms, such as Parzen windows, Support Vector Machines, Ridge Regression, Constrained Logistic Classifiers and Tangent-Prop. We then show how the approach implies new algorithm(cid:173) s for solving problems usually associated with generative models. New algorithms are described for dealing with pattern recognition problems with very different pattern distributions and dealing with unlabeled data. Preliminary empirical results are presented.

We explain how VRM provides a framework which inte(cid:173) grates a number of existing algorithms, such as Parzen windows, Support Vector Machines, Ridge Regression, Constrained Logistic Classifiers and Tangent-Prop. We then show how the approach implies new algorithm(cid:173) s for solving problems usually associated with generative models. paragraphs: The paper presents Vicinal Risk Minimization as a framework connecting generative models with methods based on structural risk minimization and statistical regularization. Its aim is to bring approaches usually discussed separately into a shared formulation. Support vector machines are one of the central examples on the regularization side of that connection.

The framework incorporates several existing algorithms, including Parzen windows, support vector machines, ridge regression, constrained logistic classifiers, and Tangent-Prop. Showing how these methods fit together gives the principle a unifying role. It also provides a basis for deriving additional algorithms, extending the contribution beyond a reinterpretation of existing techniques.

The new algorithms address pattern-recognition problems involving very different pattern distributions and problems involving unlabeled data, tasks the abstract associates with generative modeling. The authors present preliminary empirical results. The stated evidence therefore supports an initial investigation of these algorithms, while the broader contribution is a framework that links established methods and generates approaches to additional learning problems.
summary.tldr: Vicinal Risk Minimization unifies several learning methods and yields new algorithms for differing pattern distributions and unlabeled data.

title: Vicinal Risk Minimization

abstract: We describe a model of short-term synaptic depression that is derived from a silicon circuit implementation. The dynamics of this circuit model are similar to the dynamics of some present theoretical models of short- term depression except that the recovery dynamics of the variable de- scribing the depression is nonlinear and it also depends on the presynap- tic frequency. The equations describing the steady-state and transient re- sponses of this synaptic model ﬁt the experimental results obtained from a fabricated silicon network consisting of leaky integrate-and-ﬁre neu- rons and different types of synapses. We also show experimental data demonstrating the possible computational roles of depression. One pos- sible role of a depressing synapse is that the input can quickly bring the neuron up to threshold when the membrane potential is close to the rest- ing potential.

The equations describing the steady-state and transient re- sponses of this synaptic model ﬁt the experimental results obtained from a fabricated silicon network consisting of leaky integrate-and-ﬁre neu- rons and different types of synapses. paragraphs: The paper develops a model of short-term synaptic depression from an implemented silicon circuit. Depression describes a temporary reduction in a synapse's response during activity. Deriving the model from hardware connects its mathematical description to the behavior of a physical system, allowing the equations and circuit measurements to be examined together.

The circuit's dynamics resemble those of some existing theoretical depression models, but its recovery behaves differently. Recovery is nonlinear and depends on the frequency of presynaptic activity. These features make the rate of incoming activity relevant to the evolution of depression, rather than treating recovery as a process independent of that frequency.

The equations fit both steady-state and transient measurements from a fabricated network containing leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and different synapse types. The authors also present experimental data about possible computational roles of depression. One proposed role is that input through a depressing synapse can rapidly bring a neuron toward its firing threshold when its membrane potential starts near rest. This is presented as a possible function, alongside the model's agreement with circuit behavior.
summary.tldr: A silicon-derived synaptic depression model fits circuit measurements and suggests how depressing synapses may help rapidly bring resting neurons to threshold.

title: Circuit Model of Short-Term Synaptic Dynamics

abstract: Approximation structure plays an important role in inference on loopy graphs. As a tractable structure, tree approximations have been utilized in the variational method of Ghahramani & Jordan (1997) and the se- quential projection method of Frey et al. (2000). However, belief propa- gation represents each factor of the graph with a product of single-node messages. In this paper, belief propagation is extended to represent fac- tors with tree approximations, by way of the expectation propagation framework. That is, each factor sends a “message” to all pairs of nodes in a tree structure. The result is more accurate inferences and more fre- quent convergence than ordinary belief propagation, at a lower cost than variational trees or double-loop algorithms.

As a tractable structure, tree approximations have been utilized in the variational method of Ghahramani & Jordan (1997) and the se- quential projection method of Frey et al. (2000). However, belief propa- gation represents each factor of the graph with a product of single-node messages. In this paper, belief propagation is extended to represent fac- tors with tree approximations, by way of the expectation propagation framework. That is, each factor sends a “message” to all pairs of nodes in a tree structure. The result is more accurate inferences and more fre- quent convergence than ordinary belief propagation, at a lower cost than variational trees or double-loop algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies approximate inference in graphical models containing loops, where the structure of the approximation affects the result. Ordinary belief propagation represents a factor through a product of messages concerning individual nodes. The authors investigate a richer representation that retains relationships between pairs of nodes while using a tractable tree structure.

They extend belief propagation through the expectation propagation framework. Each factor is represented with a tree approximation and sends messages concerning node pairs connected by that structure. This changes what the approximation can express: information about selected pairwise relationships is retained within the factor representation, instead of relying only on separate single-node messages.

The authors report more accurate inference and more frequent convergence than ordinary belief propagation. They also report lower cost than variational tree methods or double-loop algorithms. The result presents tree-structured messages as a useful balance between expressive approximations and computation. More frequent convergence is the stated comparison; it does not assert convergence for every loopy graphical model.
summary.tldr: Tree-structured expectation propagation retains pairwise information and reportedly improves accuracy and convergence frequency over ordinary belief propagation.

title: Tree-structured Approximations by Expectation Propagation

abstract: This paper explores the computational consequences of simultaneous in- trinsic and synaptic plasticity in individual model neurons. It proposes a new intrinsic plasticity mechanism for a continuous activation model neuron based on low order moments of the neuron's firing rate distribu- tion. The goal of the intrinsic plasticity mechanism is to enforce a sparse distribution of the neuron's activity level. In conjunction with Hebbian learning at the neuron's synapses, the neuron is shown to discover sparse directions in the input.
originalAbstract: This paper explores the computational consequences of simultaneous in- trinsic and synaptic plasticity in individual model neurons. It proposes a new intrinsic plasticity mechanism for a continuous activation model neuron based on low order moments of the neuron's firing rate distribu- tion. The goal of the intrinsic plasticity mechanism is to enforce a sparse distribution of the neuron's activity level. In conjunction with Hebbian learning at the neuron's synapses, the neuron is shown to discover sparse directions in the input.

paragraphs: This paper asks what a single model neuron can learn when two forms of adaptation operate together. Intrinsic plasticity changes the neuron's own response properties, while synaptic plasticity changes its connections to incoming signals. The study examines their combined computational effect within an individual neuron model.

The authors propose an intrinsic-plasticity mechanism for a neuron with continuous activation. It uses low-order moments, or compact statistical summaries, of the neuron's firing-rate distribution. Its objective is to enforce sparse activity, concentrating the neuron's responses into a distribution in which strong activation is selective. The learning target therefore concerns the pattern of activity across inputs.

When this mechanism is combined with Hebbian learning at the synapses, the neuron is shown to discover sparse directions in its input. The result connects control of the neuron's activity distribution with the input structure learned by its connections. Its significance is the demonstrated cooperation between two adaptive mechanisms in the model, rather than a claim that synaptic learning alone produces the same outcome.
summary.tldr: An intrinsic-plasticity rule that promotes sparse activity works with Hebbian synaptic learning to discover sparse input directions in a model neuron.

title: Synergies between Intrinsic and Synaptic Plasticity in Individual Model Neurons

abstract: Given a set F of classifiers and a probability distribution over their domain, one can define a metric by taking the distance between a pair of classifiers to be the probability that they classify a random item differently. We prove bounds on the sample complexity of PAC learning in terms of the doubling dimension of this metric. These bounds imply known bounds on the sample complexity of learning halfspaces with respect to the uniform distribution that are optimal up to a constant factor. We prove a bound that holds for any algorithm that outputs a classifier with zero error whenever this is possible; this bound is in terms of the maximum of the doubling dimension and the VC-dimension of F , and strengthens the best known bound in terms of the VC-dimension alone. We show that there is no bound on the doubling dimension in terms of the VC-dimension of F (in contrast with the metric dimension).
originalAbstract: Given a set F of classifiers and a probability distribution over their domain, one can define a metric by taking the distance between a pair of classifiers to be the probability that they classify a random item differently. We prove bounds on the sample complexity of PAC learning in terms of the doubling dimension of this metric. These bounds imply known bounds on the sample complexity of learning halfspaces with respect to the uniform distribution that are optimal up to a constant factor. We prove a bound that holds for any algorithm that outputs a classifier with zero error whenever this is possible; this bound is in terms of the maximum of the doubling dimension and the VC-dimension of F , and strengthens the best known bound in terms of the VC-dimension alone. We show that there is no bound on the doubling dimension in terms of the VC-dimension of F (in contrast with the metric dimension).

paragraphs: Two classifiers can be considered close when they rarely disagree on examples drawn from a particular distribution. This paper uses that probability of disagreement as a distance between classifiers. It then relates the number of examples needed for PAC learning to the doubling dimension of the resulting metric space.

This viewpoint brings the distribution of examples into the geometry used to analyze learning. The derived bounds imply known sample complexity results for halfspaces under a uniform distribution that are optimal up to a constant factor. The authors also prove a bound for any learning algorithm that returns a zero-error classifier whenever such a classifier is available.

That latter bound depends on the larger of the doubling dimension and the classifier family’s VC dimension, and strengthens the previous bound expressed using VC dimension alone. However, the two dimensions are not interchangeable: the paper shows that VC dimension cannot by itself bound doubling dimension. The results therefore establish both the usefulness and the distinct role of this geometric measure.
summary.tldr: The geometry of classifier disagreement yields PAC sample complexity bounds through doubling dimension, which VC dimension alone cannot bound.

title: Learnability and the doubling dimension

abstract: We present a novel method for inducing synchronous context free grammars (SCFGs) from a corpus of parallel string pairs. SCFGs can model equivalence between strings in terms of substitutions, insertions and deletions, and the reordering of sub-strings. We develop a non-parametric Bayesian model and apply it to a machine translation task, using priors to replace the various heuristics commonly used in this field. Using a variational Bayes training procedure, we learn the latent structure of translation equivalence through the induction of synchronous grammar categories for phrasal translations, showing improvements in translation performance over previously proposed maximum likelihood models.
originalAbstract: We present a novel method for inducing synchronous context free grammars (SCFGs) from a corpus of parallel string pairs. SCFGs can model equivalence between strings in terms of substitutions, insertions and deletions, and the reordering of sub-strings. We develop a non-parametric Bayesian model and apply it to a machine translation task, using priors to replace the various heuristics commonly used in this field. Using a variational Bayes training procedure, we learn the latent structure of translation equivalence through the induction of synchronous grammar categories for phrasal translations, showing improvements in translation performance over previously proposed maximum likelihood models.

paragraphs: The paper learns synchronous context-free grammars from paired strings, using machine translation as its application. These grammars describe how two strings correspond through substitutions, insertions, deletions, and rearrangements of substrings. This makes the learning problem about discovering structured relationships between paired expressions, including cases where their parts appear in different orders.

The authors develop a nonparametric Bayesian model that uses prior distributions in place of various heuristics commonly used in translation modeling. Training proceeds through variational Bayes. The model induces categories for phrase translations, learning hidden grammatical structure that expresses how the two sides of a translation pair are related.

The reported translation results improve over previously proposed maximum likelihood models. The contribution is therefore both a way to learn translation grammars and evidence that the Bayesian formulation helps in the studied translation task. Its significance lies in learning the underlying categories of translation equivalence while expressing modeling preferences through priors, rather than relying on the replaced heuristics.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric Bayesian model learns synchronous translation grammars and improves translation performance over earlier maximum likelihood models.

title: Bayesian Synchronous Grammar Induction

abstract: In recent years, deep learning approaches have gained significant interest as a way of building hierarchical representations from unlabeled data. However, to our knowledge, these deep learning approaches have not been extensively studied for auditory data. In this paper, we apply convolutional deep belief networks to audio data and empirically evaluate them on various audio classification tasks. For the case of speech data, we show that the learned features correspond to phones/phonemes. In addition, our feature representations trained from unlabeled audio data show very good performance for multiple audio classification tasks. We hope that this paper will inspire more research on deep learning approaches applied to a wide range of audio recognition tasks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether hierarchical representations learned from unlabeled data are useful for audio recognition. It applies convolutional deep belief networks to audio and evaluates the resulting representations on several classification tasks. The focus is on learning useful features from the recordings before assessing them through classification.

For speech, the authors find that learned features correspond to phones or phonemes, units associated with speech sounds. This gives the representation a meaningful connection to the structure of the input. It shows that learning from unlabeled audio can produce features aligned with recognizable speech units in the studied setting.

The learned representations also achieve very good performance across multiple audio classification tasks. Together, the feature correspondence and classification results provide empirical support for applying this kind of deep learning to auditory data. The contribution is both a demonstration of useful learned audio structure and an evaluation of its predictive value, motivating broader investigation of hierarchical feature learning for audio recognition.
summary.tldr: Convolutional deep belief networks learn useful features from unlabeled audio, including speech-sound representations, and perform well across multiple classification tasks.

title: Unsupervised feature learning for audio classification using convolutional deep belief networks

abstract: We develop a method for discovering the parts of an articulated object from aligned meshes capturing various three-dimensional (3D) poses. We adapt the distance dependent Chinese restaurant process (ddCRP) to allow nonparametric discovery of a potentially unbounded number of parts, while simultaneously guaranteeing a spatially connected segmentation. To allow analysis of datasets in which object instances have varying shapes, we model part variability across poses via affine transformations. By placing a matrix normal-inverse-Wishart prior on these affine transformations, we develop a ddCRP Gibbs sampler which tractably marginalizes over transformation uncertainty. Analyzing a dataset of humans captured in dozens of poses, we infer parts which provide quantitatively better motion predictions than conventional clustering methods.

paragraphs: The paper discovers parts of articulated objects from aligned three-dimensional meshes showing different poses. Its input therefore supplies corresponding geometry across poses, and the task is to infer a meaningful segmentation from how that geometry changes. The method allows the number of discovered parts to remain flexible.

The authors adapt the distance-dependent Chinese restaurant process to support a potentially unbounded number of parts while guaranteeing that each segment is spatially connected. They represent changes in each part through affine transformations, allowing analysis when object instances also differ in shape. A matrix normal-inverse-Wishart prior makes it possible for a Gibbs sampler to marginalize tractably over uncertainty in those transformations.

On a dataset of humans captured in dozens of poses, the inferred parts produce quantitatively better motion predictions than conventional clustering methods. This ties the segmentation to predictive usefulness: the discovered groups help describe movement across poses. The contribution combines flexible part counts, connected segments, and explicit treatment of transformation uncertainty within one probabilistic method.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian method discovers spatially connected parts from aligned 3D poses and improves motion prediction in the reported human-mesh study.

title: From Deformations to Parts: Motion-based Segmentation of 3D Objects

abstract: Even though heterogeneous databases can be found in a broad variety of applications, there exists a lack of tools for estimating missing data in such databases. In this paper, we provide an efficient and robust table completion tool, based on a Bayesian nonparametric latent feature model. In particular, we propose a general observation model for the Indian buffet process (IBP) adapted to mixed continuous (real-valued and positive real-valued) and discrete (categorical, ordinal and count) observations. Then, we propose an inference algorithm that scales linearly with the number of observations. Finally, our experiments over five real databases show that the proposed approach provides more robust and accurate estimates than the standard IBP and the Bayesian probabilistic matrix factorization with Gaussian observations.

paragraphs: Missing-data estimation becomes more complicated when a table mixes different kinds of values. Real-valued measurements, positive quantities, categories, ordered categories, and counts do not all have the same observation structure. This paper develops a table-completion method designed to accommodate that heterogeneity within a single model.

The method builds on a Bayesian nonparametric latent feature model using the Indian buffet process. Its main modeling contribution is a general observation model adapted to the different continuous and discrete data types. This allows the latent feature approach to represent mixed tables while accounting for the kind of value each observation contains.

The authors also propose an inference algorithm whose cost scales linearly with the number of observations, addressing the computational side of completion. Experiments on five real databases find more accurate and robust estimates than standard IBP and Bayesian probabilistic matrix factorization with Gaussian observations. The results support the value of combining shared latent structure with observation models suited to heterogeneous data, alongside an inference procedure designed to scale with the observed table.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian latent-feature model completes mixed-type tables using suitable observation models and inference that scales linearly with observations.

title: General Table Completion using a Bayesian Nonparametric Model

abstract: We develop a scoring and classification procedure based on the PAC-Bayesian approach and the AUC (Area Under Curve) criterion. We focus initially on the class of linear score functions. We derive PAC-Bayesian non-asymptotic bounds for two types of prior for the score parameters: a Gaussian prior, and a spike-and-slab prior; the latter makes it possible to perform feature selection. One important advantage of our approach is that it is amenable to powerful Bayesian computational tools. We derive in particular a Sequential Monte Carlo algorithm, as an efficient method which may be used as a gold standard, and an Expectation-Propagation algorithm, as a much faster but approximate method. We also extend our method to a class of non-linear score functions, essentially leading to a nonparametric procedure, by considering a Gaussian process prior.

paragraphs: This paper develops a scoring and classification procedure around the area-under-the-curve criterion, or AUC, using PAC-Bayesian theory. It starts with linear score functions, which combine input features into a numerical score. The framework connects the choice of scoring parameters with statistical bounds and Bayesian approaches to computation.

The authors derive non-asymptotic bounds for Gaussian and spike-and-slab priors on the score parameters. Non-asymptotic bounds describe finite-sample behavior rather than only a limiting regime. The spike-and-slab choice additionally supports feature selection, allowing the procedure to identify which inputs contribute to the score within the same general framework.

Sequential Monte Carlo is presented as an efficient approach that may serve as a reference standard, while Expectation Propagation supplies a much faster approximate alternative. The paper also moves beyond linear scoring by introducing a Gaussian process prior, leading to an essentially nonparametric procedure. Together, these contributions combine AUC-focused learning, finite-sample analysis, feature selection, and several routes for carrying out the inference.
summary.tldr: A PAC-Bayesian AUC framework combines finite-sample guarantees, optional feature selection, and Bayesian computation for linear and nonlinear scoring.

title: PAC-Bayesian AUC classification and scoring

abstract: Random walk kernels measure graph similarity by counting matching walks in two graphs. In their most popular form of geometric random walk kernels, longer walks of length $k$ are downweighted by a factor of $\lambda^k$ ($\lambda < 1$) to ensure convergence of the corresponding geometric series. We know from the field of link prediction that this downweighting often leads to a phenomenon referred to as halting: Longer walks are downweighted so much that the similarity score is completely dominated by the comparison of walks of length 1. This is a naive kernel between edges and vertices. We theoretically show that halting may occur in geometric random walk kernels. We also empirically quantify its impact in simulated datasets and popular graph classification benchmark datasets. Our findings promise to be instrumental in future graph kernel development and applications of random walk kernels.

paragraphs: Random walk kernels compare graphs by counting walks that match between them. In geometric versions, a walk of length k receives a weight proportional to λ raised to k, with λ below one. This downweighting is used to make the corresponding infinite series converge, but it also determines how much longer walks contribute to the comparison.

The paper studies a phenomenon called halting: longer walks can receive so little weight that walks of length one dominate the similarity score. In that situation, a method expressed in terms of walks of many lengths effectively behaves like a simple comparison of edges and vertices. The authors theoretically show that this can occur in geometric random walk kernels.

They also quantify the effect empirically using simulated datasets and graph classification benchmarks. The contribution is a diagnosis of what these kernels may actually measure under their weighting scheme. It gives graph-kernel development and application a concrete issue to examine: whether longer structural patterns meaningfully affect similarity, rather than merely appearing in the mathematical definition.
summary.tldr: Geometric random walk kernels can downweight longer walks so strongly that graph similarity becomes dominated by single-edge comparisons.

title: Halting in Random Walk Kernels

abstract: In this paper, we introduce the public-private framework of data summarization motivated by privacy concerns in personalized recommender systems and online social services. Such systems have usually access to massive data generated by a large pool of users. A major fraction of the data is public and is visible to (and can be used for) all users. However, each user can also contribute some private data that should not be shared with other users to ensure her privacy. The goal is to provide a succinct summary of massive dataset, ideally as small as possible, from which customized summaries can be built for each user, i.e. it can contain elements from the public data (for diversity) and users' private data (for personalization). To formalize the above challenge, we assume that the scoring function according to which a user evaluates the utility of her summary satisfies submodularity, a widely used notion in data summarization applications. Thus, we model the data summarization targeted to each user as an instance of a submodular cover problem. However, when the data is massive it is infeasible to use the centralized greedy algorithm to find a customized summary even for a single user. Moreover, for a large pool of users, it is too time consuming to find such summaries separately. Instead, we develop a fast distributed algorithm for submodular cover, FASTCOVER, that provides a succinct summary in one shot and for all users. We show that the solution provided by FASTCOVER is competitive with that of the centralized algorithm with the number of rounds that is exponentially smaller than state of the art results. Moreover, we have implemented FASTCOVER with Spark to demonstrate its practical performance on a number of concrete applications, including personalized location recommendation, personalized movie recommendation, and dominating set on tens of millions of data points and varying number of users.

paragraphs: The paper considers personalized summaries built from two kinds of information: public data available to everyone and private data belonging to an individual user. A compact shared summary should support diverse public content, while each user's private contributions enable personalization without being shared with other users.

Running a centralized greedy procedure separately for every user is too costly at the scale considered. FASTCOVER instead uses a distributed algorithm to produce a compact summary for all users in one operation.

A Spark implementation demonstrates practical performance for personalized location and movie recommendations, as well as dominating-set problems, on tens of millions of data points. The contribution makes the shared computation reusable across users under the stated utility assumption.
summary.tldr: FASTCOVER efficiently builds shared summaries for public-private personalization, with competitive submodular-cover solutions and substantially fewer distributed rounds.

title: Fast Distributed Submodular Cover: Public-Private Data Summarization

abstract: We study the problem of 3D object generation. We propose a novel framework, namely 3D Generative Adversarial Network (3D-GAN), which generates 3D objects from a probabilistic space by leveraging recent advances in volumetric convolutional networks and generative adversarial nets. The benefits of our model are three-fold: first, the use of an adversarial criterion, instead of traditional heuristic criteria, enables the generator to capture object structure implicitly and to synthesize high-quality 3D objects; second, the generator establishes a mapping from a low-dimensional probabilistic space to the space of 3D objects, so that we can sample objects without a reference image or CAD models, and explore the 3D object manifold; third, the adversarial discriminator provides a powerful 3D shape descriptor which, learned without supervision, has wide applications in 3D object recognition. Experiments demonstrate that our method generates high-quality 3D objects, and our unsupervisedly learned features achieve impressive performance on 3D object recognition, comparable with those of supervised learning methods.

paragraphs: This paper introduces 3D-GAN, a framework for generating three-dimensional objects from a probabilistic latent space. It combines volumetric convolutional networks with adversarial learning. The generator learns object structure through the adversarial criterion, providing an alternative to prescribing traditional heuristic criteria for what a generated shape should look like.

The generator maps a low-dimensional probabilistic representation into three-dimensional objects. Once that mapping is learned, objects can be sampled without supplying a reference image or CAD model for each generation. The latent space also provides a way to explore the learned space of object shapes. A second benefit comes from the discriminator, whose learned representation serves as a shape descriptor.

Experiments report high-quality generated objects and strong object-recognition performance using these descriptors. Although the features are learned without supervision, their recognition performance is reported as comparable to features from supervised methods. The findings connect generation and recognition: adversarial training can support both the synthesis of shapes and the learning of representations useful for identifying three-dimensional objects.
summary.tldr: 3D-GAN generates object shapes from a low-dimensional probabilistic space and learns unsupervised shape features with competitive recognition performance.

title: Learning a Probabilistic Latent Space of Object Shapes via 3D Generative-Adversarial Modeling

abstract: Probabilistic techniques are central to data analysis, but different approaches can be challenging to apply, combine, and compare. This paper introduces composable generative population models (CGPMs), a computational abstraction that extends directed graphical models and can be used to describe and compose a broad class of probabilistic data analysis techniques. Examples include discriminative machine learning, hierarchical Bayesian models, multivariate kernel methods, clustering algorithms, and arbitrary probabilistic programs. We demonstrate the integration of CGPMs into BayesDB, a probabilistic programming platform that can express data analysis tasks using a modeling definition language and structured query language. The practical value is illustrated in two ways. First, the paper describes an analysis on a database of Earth satellites, which identifies records that probably violate Kepler’s Third Law by composing causal probabilistic programs with non-parametric Bayes in 50 lines of probabilistic code. Second, it reports the lines of code and accuracy of CGPMs compared with baseline solutions from standard machine learning libraries.

paragraphs: Probabilistic data analysis offers many useful techniques, but combining them can require substantial effort because they are expressed and implemented differently. This paper introduces composable generative population models, or CGPMs, as a common computational abstraction. The aim is to make diverse probabilistic methods easier to describe, combine, and compare within one framework.

CGPMs extend directed graphical models and accommodate approaches including discriminative learning, hierarchical Bayesian modeling, kernel methods, clustering, and probabilistic programs. The authors integrate this abstraction into BayesDB, where a modeling language specifies models and a structured query language expresses analysis tasks. This connects model composition with a practical interface for asking questions about data.

The satellite example illustrates why composition matters: causal probabilistic programs and nonparametric Bayesian methods work together to flag records that probably violate Kepler’s Third Law, using 50 lines of probabilistic code. The paper also compares code length and accuracy against standard machine learning library solutions. These demonstrations address both analytical usefulness and implementation effort, without establishing that every combination is automatically superior.
summary.tldr: CGPMs provide a shared abstraction for combining diverse probabilistic analysis methods within BayesDB.

title: A Probabilistic Programming Approach To Probabilistic Data Analysis

abstract: The restricted isometry property (RIP) for design matrices gives guarantees for optimal recovery in sparse linear models. It is of high interest in compressed sensing and statistical learning. This property is particularly important for computationally efficient recovery methods. As a consequence, even though it is in general NP-hard to check that RIP holds, there have been substantial efforts to find tractable proxies for it. These would allow the construction of RIP matrices and the polynomial-time verification of RIP given an arbitrary matrix. We consider the framework of average-case certifiers, that never wrongly declare that a matrix is RIP, while being often correct for random instances. While there are such functions which are tractable in a suboptimal parameter regime, we show that this is a computationally hard task in any better regime. Our results are based on a new, weaker assumption on the problem of detecting dense subgraphs.

paragraphs: The restricted isometry property, or RIP, gives guarantees for recovering sparse signals from linear measurements. It is especially valuable for computationally efficient recovery methods. Checking RIP is generally NP-hard, motivating attempts to develop tractable certificates that can establish when a matrix has the property.

This paper examines average-case certifiers. Such a certifier must never incorrectly declare that a matrix satisfies RIP, while succeeding often on random instances. This separates the demand for trustworthy positive answers from the demand to handle every possible input. Tractable certifiers already exist in a parameter regime that the abstract describes as suboptimal.

The authors show that improving on that regime is computationally hard under a new, weaker assumption concerning dense-subgraph detection. The conclusion is conditional on this hardness assumption. Its significance is that random inputs do not automatically make reliable RIP certification easy: requiring certificates to avoid false positive declarations can preserve a computational barrier even in an average-case setting.
summary.tldr: Under a dense-subgraph detection assumption, reliable average-case RIP certification is computationally hard beyond a known suboptimal regime.

title: Average-case hardness of RIP certification

abstract: Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) is a deterministic sampling algorithm that iteratively transports a set of particles to approximate given distributions, based on a gradient-based update constructed to optimally decrease the KL divergence within a function space. This paper develops the first theoretical analysis on SVGD. We establish that the empirical measures of the SVGD samples weakly converge to the target distribution, and show that the asymptotic behavior of SVGD is characterized by a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation known as Vlasov equation in physics. We develop a geometric perspective that views SVGD as a gradient flow of the KL divergence functional under a new metric structure on the space of distributions induced by Stein operator.

This paper develops the first theoretical analysis on SVGD. We establish that the empirical measures of the SVGD samples weakly converge to the target distribution, and show that the asymptotic behavior of SVGD is characterized by a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation known as Vlasov equation in physics. We develop a geometric perspective that views SVGD as a gradient flow of the KL divergence functional under a new metric structure on the space of distributions induced by Stein operator.

paragraphs: Stein variational gradient descent approximates a target distribution by deterministically moving a collection of particles. Its update is chosen to decrease KL divergence optimally within a function space. This paper develops a theoretical account of that particle transport, connecting the algorithm’s updates with the evolution of probability distributions.

The authors establish weak convergence of the empirical distributions represented by the particles to the target distribution. They also characterize SVGD’s asymptotic behavior through a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation known as the Vlasov equation. This connects the discrete collection of moving particles with a continuous description of how their distribution changes.

A geometric interpretation ties these results together: SVGD is a gradient flow of KL divergence under a new metric on the space of distributions, induced by the Stein operator. The contribution gives a mathematical interpretation of the algorithm’s direction of movement and its limiting behavior. It explains particle-based approximation through distributional geometry, with convergence expressed in the weak sense established by the analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes SVGD convergence and interprets its particle dynamics as a KL-divergence gradient flow under a Stein-induced metric.

title: Stein Variational Gradient Descent as Gradient Flow

abstract: Low-dimensional embeddings of nodes in large graphs have proved extremely useful in a variety of prediction tasks, from content recommendation to identifying protein functions. However, most existing approaches require that all nodes in the graph are present during training of the embeddings; these previous approaches are inherently transductive and do not naturally generalize to unseen nodes. Here we present GraphSAGE, a general, inductive framework that leverages node feature information (e.g., text attributes) to efficiently generate node embeddings. Instead of training individual embeddings for each node, we learn a function that generates embeddings by sampling and aggregating features from a node's local neighborhood. Our algorithm outperforms strong baselines on three inductive node-classification benchmarks: we classify the category of unseen nodes in evolving information graphs based on citation and Reddit post data, and we show that our algorithm generalizes to completely unseen graphs using a multi-graph dataset of protein-protein interactions.

Here we present GraphSAGE, a general, inductive framework that leverages node feature information (e.g., text attributes) to efficiently generate node embeddings. paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes into compact numerical representations useful for prediction. Many existing methods require all nodes to be present during training, which makes unseen nodes difficult to handle naturally. This paper introduces GraphSAGE, a framework that learns how to generate embeddings from node features and local graph neighborhoods.

GraphSAGE samples a node's neighborhood and aggregates features from the sampled nodes. Training therefore produces a function that can be applied to new nodes, rather than only a collection of embeddings tied to the training graph. Feature information, such as text attributes, supplies inputs that the learned function can use when a previously unseen node appears.

The authors evaluate GraphSAGE on three inductive node-classification benchmarks and report improvements over strong baselines. Citation and Reddit data test classification of unseen nodes in evolving information graphs. A protein-interaction dataset tests transfer to entirely unseen graphs. These findings demonstrate both forms of generalization in the studied datasets: handling new nodes and generating useful representations in new graphs.
summary.tldr: GraphSAGE learns to generate node embeddings by sampling and aggregating neighborhood features, enabling prediction on unseen nodes and graphs.

title: Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs

abstract: Uncertainty sampling, a popular active learning algorithm, is used to reduce the amount of data required to learn a classifier, but it has been observed in practice to converge to different parameters depending on the initialization and sometimes to even better parameters than standard training on all the data. In this work, we give a theoretical explanation of this phenomenon, showing that uncertainty sampling on a convex (e.g., logistic) loss can be interpreted as performing a preconditioned stochastic gradient step on the population zero-one loss. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support this connection.
originalAbstract: Uncertainty sampling, a popular active learning algorithm, is used to reduce the amount of data required to learn a classifier, but it has been observed in practice to converge to different parameters depending on the initialization and sometimes to even better parameters than standard training on all the data. In this work, we give a theoretical explanation of this phenomenon, showing that uncertainty sampling on a convex (e.g., logistic) loss can be interpreted as performing a preconditioned stochastic gradient step on the population zero-one loss. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support this connection.

paragraphs: Uncertainty sampling reduces the data needed to train a classifier by focusing learning on examples about which the model is uncertain. In practice, its final parameters can depend on initialization, and it sometimes produces better parameters than training on all available data. This paper provides a theoretical explanation for that behavior.

The central result connects uncertainty sampling with a different optimization perspective. Even when training uses a convex loss such as logistic loss, the sampling procedure can be interpreted as taking a preconditioned stochastic gradient step on population zero-one loss. That loss measures classification mistakes across the underlying data distribution, while preconditioning changes how the gradient step is scaled or directed.

This connection helps explain why the apparent simplicity of the training loss does not fully describe the behavior of the overall learning procedure. Selecting examples based on uncertainty changes the effective optimization process. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the proposed relationship. The result explains the observed possibility of initialization sensitivity and improved parameters without claiming that uncertainty sampling always outperforms training on all data.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty sampling with a convex training loss can behave like preconditioned stochastic gradient descent on population classification error.

title: Uncertainty Sampling is Preconditioned Stochastic Gradient Descent on Zero-One Loss

abstract: We present a framework to train a structured prediction model by performing smoothing on the inference algorithm it builds upon. Smoothing overcomes the non-smoothness inherent to the maximum margin structured prediction objective, and paves the way for the use of fast primal gradient-based optimization algorithms. We illustrate the proposed framework by developing a novel primal incremental optimization algorithm for the structural support vector machine. The proposed algorithm blends an extrapolation scheme for acceleration and an adaptive smoothing scheme and builds upon the stochastic variance-reduced gradient algorithm. We establish its worst-case global complexity bound and study several practical variants. We present experimental results on two real-world problems, namely named entity recognition and visual object localization. The experimental results show that the proposed framework allows us to build upon efficient inference algorithms to develop large-scale optimization algorithms for structured prediction which can achieve competitive performance on the two real-world problems.
originalAbstract: We present a framework to train a structured prediction model by performing smoothing on the inference algorithm it builds upon. Smoothing overcomes the non-smoothness inherent to the maximum margin structured prediction objective, and paves the way for the use of fast primal gradient-based optimization algorithms. We illustrate the proposed framework by developing a novel primal incremental optimization algorithm for the structural support vector machine. The proposed algorithm blends an extrapolation scheme for acceleration and an adaptive smoothing scheme and builds upon the stochastic variance-reduced gradient algorithm. We establish its worst-case global complexity bound and study several practical variants. We present experimental results on two real-world problems, namely named entity recognition and visual object localization. The experimental results show that the proposed framework allows us to build upon efficient inference algorithms to develop large-scale optimization algorithms for structured prediction which can achieve competitive performance on the two real-world problems.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves outputs with multiple related parts, making the procedure that selects an output central to training. Maximum-margin training objectives in this setting have sharp, nonsmooth points that complicate gradient-based optimization. This paper proposes smoothing the underlying inference algorithm to make faster optimization methods applicable.

The authors demonstrate the framework with a training algorithm for structural support vector machines. It combines stochastic variance-reduced gradients with an extrapolation mechanism for acceleration and a smoothing scheme that adapts during optimization. The algorithm works in the primal formulation, directly optimizing the model's training objective. The paper establishes a worst-case global complexity bound and also examines practical variants.

Experiments cover named entity recognition and visual object localization. The reported results show competitive performance on both tasks, supporting the usefulness of building large-scale training procedures around efficient inference algorithms. The broader contribution is the connection between smoothing inference and improving optimization: an inference procedure becomes a foundation for a faster training method, rather than merely a component used to produce predictions.
summary.tldr: Smoothing structured inference enables accelerated gradient-based training with theoretical guarantees and competitive results on two prediction tasks.

title: A Smoother Way to Train Structured Prediction Models

abstract: Expectation Maximization (EM) is among the most popular algorithms for maximum likelihood estimation, but it is generally only guaranteed to find its stationary points of the log-likelihood objective. The goal of this article is to present theoretical and empirical evidence that over-parameterization can help EM avoid spurious local optima in the log-likelihood. We consider the problem of estimating the mean vectors of a Gaussian mixture model in a scenario where the mixing weights are known. Our study shows that the global behavior of EM, when one uses an over-parameterized model in which the mixing weights are treated as unknown, is better than that when one uses the (correct) model with the mixing weights fixed to the known values. For symmetric Gaussians mixtures with two components, we prove that introducing the (statistically redundant) weight parameters enables EM to find the global maximizer of the log-likelihood starting from almost any initial mean parameters, whereas EM without this over-parameterization may very often fail. For other Gaussian mixtures, we provide empirical evidence that shows similar behavior. Our results corroborate the value of over-parameterization in solving non-convex optimization problems, previously observed in other domains.

paragraphs: Expectation Maximization is widely used to fit statistical models, but its usual guarantees do not ensure finding the best likelihood value. It can instead stop at an undesirable stationary point. This paper investigates whether adding parameters that are unnecessary for describing the data can nevertheless make that optimization problem easier.

The setting is mean estimation in Gaussian mixture models whose mixing weights are already known. The authors compare fixing those weights to their correct values with allowing EM to estimate them. This deliberately over-parameterized formulation gives the optimization procedure additional freedom, even though the extra parameters are statistically redundant.

For symmetric mixtures with two Gaussian components, the authors prove that estimating the weights allows EM to reach the global likelihood maximizer from almost any initialization of the means. Keeping the known weights fixed can fail frequently. Experiments on other Gaussian mixtures show similar behavior, extending the evidence beyond the proved case without making that broader observation a theorem. The result illustrates how additional parameters can improve optimization even when they provide no needed expansion of the statistical description.
summary.tldr: Allowing EM to estimate already-known mixture weights can help it avoid bad optima, with a global guarantee for symmetric two-component Gaussian mixtures.

title: Benefits of over-parameterization with EM

abstract: Comparing different neural network representations and determining how representations evolve over time remain challenging open questions in our understanding of the function of neural networks. Comparing representations in neural networks is fundamentally difficult as the structure of representations varies greatly, even across groups of networks trained on identical tasks, and over the course of training. Here, we develop projection weighted CCA (Canonical Correlation Analysis) as a tool for understanding neural networks, building off of SVCCA, a recently proposed method (Raghu et al, 2017). We first improve the core method, showing how to differentiate between signal and noise, and then apply this technique to compare across a group of CNNs, demonstrating that networks which generalize converge to more similar representations than networks which memorize, that wider networks converge to more similar solutions than narrow networks, and that trained networks with identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters with diverse representations. We also investigate the representational dynamics of RNNs, across both training and sequential timesteps, finding that RNNs converge in a bottom-up pattern over the course of training and that the hidden state is highly variable over the course of a sequence, even when accounting for linear transforms. Together, these results provide new insights into the function of CNNs and RNNs, and demonstrate the utility of using CCA to understand representations.

paragraphs: Networks trained on the same task can develop representations with very different structures, making direct comparisons difficult. This paper develops projection-weighted canonical correlation analysis, building on SVCCA, to study those representations. The improved method distinguishes signal from noise and provides a tool for comparing networks and tracking changes during training.

Applied to convolutional networks, the method reveals that networks which generalize converge to more similar representations than networks which memorize. Wider networks also converge to more similar solutions than narrower ones. Networks with identical topology but different learning rates form distinct clusters of representations, showing that the training configuration can correspond to substantial representational differences.

The authors additionally examine recurrent networks across training and across positions in a sequence. They find bottom-up convergence during training and substantial hidden-state variation along a sequence, even after accounting for linear transformations. Together, these findings show how representation comparisons can expose differences associated with generalization, width, learning rate, and temporal processing, extending analysis beyond a network's final predictions.
summary.tldr: Projection-weighted CCA reveals how neural representations differ with generalization, width, learning rate, training progress, and sequence position.

title: Insights on representational similarity in neural networks with canonical correlation

abstract: The goal of this paper is to design image classification systems that, after an initial multi-task training phase, can automatically adapt to new tasks encountered at test time. We introduce a conditional neural process based approach to the multi-task classification setting for this purpose, and establish connections to the meta- and few-shot learning literature. The resulting approach, called CNAPs, comprises a classifier whose parameters are modulated by an adaptation network that takes the current task's dataset as input. We demonstrate that CNAPs achieves state-of-the-art results on the challenging Meta-Dataset benchmark indicating high-quality transfer-learning. We show that the approach is robust, avoiding both over-fitting in low-shot regimes and under-fitting in high-shot regimes. Timing experiments reveal that CNAPs is computationally efficient at test-time as it does not involve gradient based adaptation. Finally, we show that trained models are immediately deployable to continual learning and active learning where they can outperform existing approaches that do not leverage transfer learning.

paragraphs: CNAPs tackles image classification when a system must adapt to new tasks after an initial period of training across multiple tasks. The challenge is to transfer what it has learned while accommodating the particular examples available for the current task. Those examples may be scarce or comparatively plentiful.

The system pairs a classifier with an adaptation network. Given the current task's dataset, the adaptation network modulates the classifier's parameters. This conditional neural process approach connects task adaptation with meta-learning and few-shot learning. Because adaptation does not require gradient-based updates at test time, the model can produce a task-specific classifier without an additional gradient optimization procedure.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on Meta-Dataset and robustness across both low-shot and high-shot settings, avoiding the respective problems of overfitting and underfitting in their evaluations. Timing experiments support test-time efficiency. They also demonstrate that trained models can be used directly for continual and active learning, where they can outperform approaches that do not use transfer learning. These findings connect adaptable representations with practical deployment across several learning settings.
summary.tldr: CNAPs adapts image classifiers to new tasks through a dataset-conditioned network, avoiding gradient-based adaptation at test time.

title: Fast and Flexible Multi-Task Classification using Conditional Neural Adaptive Processes

abstract: We present a study of generalization for data-dependent hypothesis sets. We give a general learning guarantee for data-dependent hypothesis sets based on a notion of transductive Rademacher complexity. Our main result is a generalization bound for data-dependent hypothesis sets expressed in terms of a notion of hypothesis set stability and a notion of Rademacher complexity for data-dependent hypothesis sets that we introduce. This bound admits as special cases both standard Rademacher complexity bounds and algorithm-dependent uniform stability bounds. We also illustrate the use of these learning bounds in the analysis of several scenarios.
originalAbstract: We present a study of generalization for data-dependent hypothesis sets. We give a general learning guarantee for data-dependent hypothesis sets based on a notion of transductive Rademacher complexity. Our main result is a generalization bound for data-dependent hypothesis sets expressed in terms of a notion of hypothesis set stability and a notion of Rademacher complexity for data-dependent hypothesis sets that we introduce. This bound admits as special cases both standard Rademacher complexity bounds and algorithm-dependent uniform stability bounds. We also illustrate the use of these learning bounds in the analysis of several scenarios.

paragraphs: Generalization theory studies how learning from observed data translates into performance beyond those observations. This paper focuses on a setting where the collection of candidate predictors, called the hypothesis set, itself depends on the data. That dependence becomes part of the analysis, rather than treating the candidate set as something fixed before learning begins.

The authors first provide a general learning guarantee using a notion of transductive Rademacher complexity. Their main result introduces a generalization bound combining hypothesis set stability with a Rademacher complexity notion designed for data-dependent hypothesis sets. These quantities give the analysis two complementary perspectives: stability of the candidate collection and complexity of the predictors it makes available.

The resulting bound includes both standard Rademacher complexity bounds and algorithm-dependent uniform stability bounds as special cases. This is a unifying theoretical contribution: two established ways of controlling generalization fit within one framework. The authors also illustrate how the learning bounds can be used to analyze several scenarios involving data-dependent hypothesis sets.
summary.tldr: A generalization framework for data-dependent hypothesis sets unifies complexity-based and algorithmic stability bounds.

title: Hypothesis Set Stability and Generalization

abstract: Object segmentation is a crucial problem that is usually solved by using supervised learning approaches over very large datasets composed of both images and corresponding object masks. Since the masks have to be provided at pixel level, building such a dataset for any new domain can be very costly. We present ReDO, a new model able to extract objects from images without any annotation in an unsupervised way. It relies on the idea that it should be possible to change the textures or colors of the objects without changing the overall distribution of the dataset. Following this assumption, our approach is based on an adversarial architecture where the generator is guided by an input sample: given an image, it extracts the object mask, then redraws a new object at the same location. The generator is controlled by a discriminator that ensures that the distribution of generated images is aligned to the original one. We experiment with this method on different datasets and demonstrate the good quality of extracted masks.
