We present ReDO, a new model able to extract objects from images without any annotation in an unsupervised way. It relies on the idea that it should be possible to change the textures or colors of the objects without changing the overall distribution of the dataset. Following this assumption, our approach is based on an adversarial architecture where the generator is guided by an input sample: given an image, it extracts the object mask, then redraws a new object at the same location. The generator is controlled by a discriminator that ensures that the distribution of generated images is aligned to the original one. We experiment with this method on different datasets and demonstrate the good quality of extracted masks.

paragraphs: Object segmentation identifies the pixels belonging to an object, but collecting pixel-level training masks is expensive. ReDO learns to extract objects without annotations by connecting segmentation to image generation. Its guiding assumption is that changing an object’s colors or textures should be possible without changing the overall distribution of images in the dataset.

Given an image, the generator first extracts an object mask and then redraws an object at that location. A discriminator evaluates the generated images, pushing their distribution to align with that of the original data. The mask is therefore learned as part of a process that must produce plausible image variations, rather than through direct comparisons with manually labeled masks.

This setup makes the ability to redraw a region useful as a learning signal for discovering object boundaries. The assumption about allowable appearance changes is central: it supplies the connection between plausible generated images and segmentation. Experiments on different datasets show good-quality extracted masks, supporting the feasibility of learning object segmentation through the redrawing task without annotation.
summary.tldr: ReDO learns object masks without annotations by extracting and redrawing objects while training generated images to match the original data distribution.

title: Unsupervised Object Segmentation by Redrawing

abstract: Recent learning-to-plan methods have shown promising results on planning directly from observation space. Yet, their ability to plan for long-horizon tasks is limited by the accuracy of the prediction model. On the other hand, classical symbolic planners show remarkable capabilities in solving long-horizon tasks, but they require predefined symbolic rules and symbolic states, restricting their real-world applicability. In this work, we combine the benefits of these two paradigms and propose a learning-to-plan method that can directly generate a long-term symbolic plan conditioned on high-dimensional observations. We borrow the idea of regression (backward) planning from classical planning literature and introduce Regression Planning Networks (RPN), a neural network architecture that plans backward starting at a task goal and generates a sequence of intermediate goals that reaches the current observation. We show that our model not only inherits many favorable traits from symbolic planning --including the ability to solve previously unseen tasks-- but also can learn from visual inputs in an end-to-end manner. We evaluate the capabilities of RPN in a grid world environment and a simulated 3D kitchen environment featuring complex visual scenes and long task horizon, and show that it achieves near-optimal performance in completely new task instances.

paragraphs: Learning to plan directly from observations is promising, but long-horizon performance can be limited by prediction-model accuracy. Classical symbolic planners handle long tasks well, yet require predefined symbolic rules and states. Regression Planning Networks, or RPN, combine elements of both approaches to produce long-term symbolic plans conditioned on high-dimensional observations.

RPN uses regression planning, meaning that it reasons backward from the desired task goal. The network generates a sequence of intermediate goals that works back toward the current observation. This gives the learned planner a goal-directed structure drawn from classical planning while allowing it to learn from visual inputs end to end.

The authors show that the model retains useful symbolic-planning traits, including solving tasks not encountered during training. Evaluations use a grid world and a simulated three-dimensional kitchen with complex visual scenes and long task horizons. RPN achieves near-optimal performance on completely new task instances in those settings. The findings support backward intermediate-goal generation as a way to connect visual learning with longer-term planning and task generalization.
summary.tldr: RPN learns to plan backward through intermediate goals, producing long-term symbolic plans from visual observations and generalizing to unseen tasks.

title: Regression Planning Networks

abstract: Neural architecture search methods are able to find high performance deep learning architectures with minimal effort from an expert. However, current systems focus on specific use-cases (e.g. convolutional image classifiers and recurrent language models), making them unsuitable for general use-cases that an expert might wish to write. Hyperparameter optimization systems are general-purpose but lack the constructs needed for easy application to architecture search. In this work, we propose a formal language for encoding search spaces over general computational graphs. The language constructs allow us to write modular, composable, and reusable search space encodings and to reason about search space design. We use our language to encode search spaces from the architecture search literature. The language allows us to decouple the implementations of the search space and the search algorithm, allowing us to expose search spaces to search algorithms through a consistent interface. Our experiments show the ease with which we can experiment with different combinations of search spaces and search algorithms without having to implement each combination from scratch. We release an implementation of our language with this paper.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can discover strong network designs, but many systems are built around particular applications. General hyperparameter-optimization tools offer broader coverage while lacking convenient constructs for describing architecture choices. This paper addresses that gap with a formal language for search spaces over general computational graphs.

The language supports modular, composable, reusable descriptions of candidate architectures. It also separates the implementation of a search space from the algorithm that explores it. A consistent interface exposes the same space to different search algorithms, making the description of possible architectures an independent component that can be reused.

The authors encode search spaces from the architecture-search literature and demonstrate experiments combining different spaces and search algorithms. These combinations can be explored without implementing every pairing from scratch. The contribution is a programming foundation for architecture search: it makes search-space design easier to express and reason about while reducing repeated implementation work. The paper also releases an implementation of the language.
summary.tldr: A formal language makes architecture-search spaces modular and reusable through a consistent interface to different search algorithms.

title: Towards modular and programmable architecture search

abstract: The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is one of the most widely used first-order optimisation methods in the literature owing to its simplicity, flexibility and efficiency. Over the years, numerous efforts are made to improve the performance of the method, such as the inertial technique. By studying the geometric properties of ADMM, we discuss the limitations of current inertial accelerated ADMM and then present and analyze an adaptive acceleration scheme for the method. Numerical experiments on problems arising from image processing, statistics and machine learning demonstrate the advantages of the proposed acceleration approach.

paragraphs: The alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, is widely used because it combines simplicity, flexibility, and efficiency. Even so, improving its optimization performance remains an important problem. This paper examines acceleration through the geometry of ADMM's trajectory: the path formed by its successive optimization iterates.

The authors use that geometric perspective to discuss limitations of existing inertial acceleration methods. Their approach makes the behavior of the underlying iteration central to understanding acceleration. They then present and analyze an adaptive acceleration scheme for ADMM, connecting the proposed improvement to the trajectory properties investigated in the paper.

Numerical experiments cover problems from image processing, statistics, and machine learning, and demonstrate advantages for the proposed scheme. The evidence therefore combines analysis of the method's behavior with evaluations across several application areas. The main contribution is a geometry-informed approach to improving an established optimizer, together with an account of why current inertial acceleration has limitations and a proposed adaptive alternative.
summary.tldr: The paper studies ADMM’s trajectory geometry to analyze inertial acceleration limits and develop an adaptive acceleration scheme with demonstrated numerical advantages.

title: Trajectory of Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers and Adaptive Acceleration

abstract: We propose a novel reinforcement learning algorithm, AlphaNPI, that incorpo- rates the strengths of Neural Programmer-Interpreters (NPI) and AlphaZero. NPI contributes structural biases in the form of modularity, hierarchy and recursion, which are helpful to reduce sample complexity, improve generalization and in- crease interpretability. AlphaZero contributes powerful neural network guided search algorithms, which we augment with recursion. AlphaNPI only assumes a hierarchical program specification with sparse rewards: 1 when the program execution satisfies the specification, and 0 otherwise. This specification enables us to overcome the need for strong supervision in the form of execution traces and consequently train NPI models effectively with reinforcement learning. The experiments show that AlphaNPI can sort as well as previous strongly supervised NPI variants. The AlphaNPI agent is also trained on a Tower of Hanoi puzzle with two disks and is shown to generalize to puzzles with an arbitrary number of disks. The experiments also show that when deploying our neural network policies, it is advantageous to do planning with guided Monte Carlo tree search.

paragraphs: AlphaNPI combines Neural Programmer-Interpreters with AlphaZero-style search to learn compositional programs through reinforcement learning. The interpreter contributes modularity, hierarchy, and recursion, providing structure for assembling programs from reusable parts. Neural-network-guided search contributes a way to explore possible executions, and the authors extend that search to support recursion.

Training assumes a hierarchical program specification and a sparse success signal: an execution receives one if it satisfies the specification and zero otherwise. This removes the need for execution traces that demonstrate the full sequence of correct steps. The method therefore retains an explicit program structure while learning behavior from success or failure.

Experiments show sorting performance comparable to earlier strongly supervised interpreter variants. An agent trained on the two-disk Tower of Hanoi is also shown to generalize to puzzles with an arbitrary number of disks. The authors additionally find that guided Monte Carlo tree search helps when deploying learned policies. These results illustrate the benefits of recursive structure and planning in the tested program-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: AlphaNPI learns structured recursive programs from sparse success rewards by combining neural interpreters with guided tree search.

title: Learning Compositional Neural Programs with Recursive Tree Search and Planning

abstract: In vision-and-language grounding problems, fine-grained representations of the image are considered to be of paramount importance. Most of the current systems incorporate visual features and textual concepts as a sketch of an image. However, plainly inferred representations are usually undesirable in that they are composed of separate components, the relations of which are elusive. In this work, we aim at representing an image with a set of integrated visual regions and corresponding textual concepts, reflecting certain semantics. To this end, we build the Mutual Iterative Attention (MIA) module, which integrates correlated visual features and textual concepts, respectively, by aligning the two modalities. We evaluate the proposed approach on two representative vision-and-language grounding tasks, i.e., image captioning and visual question answering. In both tasks, the semantic-grounded image representations consistently boost the performance of the baseline models under all metrics across the board. The results demonstrate that our approach is effective and generalizes well to a wide range of models for image-related applications. (The code is available at \url{https://github.com/fenglinliu98/MIA)

paragraphs: Systems that connect images with language often represent an image using visual features alongside textual concepts. Having both kinds of information does not by itself make their relationships clear. This paper seeks an image representation in which visual regions and the concepts associated with them form an integrated description of the image's meaning.

The proposed Mutual Iterative Attention module aligns the two modalities and integrates correlated information within them. Its role is to connect what the visual representation captures with what the textual concepts describe. The resulting representation therefore contains more than two separate collections of features: it makes their semantic correspondence part of the information supplied to subsequent models.

The authors evaluate these representations in image captioning and visual question answering. Across the reported evaluations, adding them improves baseline models under every measured metric. The results support the usefulness of explicit visual–textual alignment in both tasks and across the models examined, suggesting that the representation can serve as a broadly useful component for image-and-language applications.
summary.tldr: Mutual Iterative Attention aligns image regions with textual concepts to improve representations for captioning and visual question answering.

title: Aligning Visual Regions and Textual Concepts for Semantic-Grounded Image Representations

abstract: We revisit the classic randomized sketch of a tensor product of $q$ vectors $x_i\in\mathbb{R}^n$. The $i$-th coordinate $(Sx)_i$ of the sketch is equal to $\prod_{j = 1}^q \langle u^{i, j}, x^j \rangle / \sqrt{m}$, where $u^{i,j}$ are independent random sign vectors. Kar and Karnick (JMLR, 2012) show that if the sketching dimension $m = \Omega(\epsilon^{-2} C_{\Omega}^2 \log (1/\delta))$, where $C_{\Omega}$ is a certain property of the point set $\Omega$ one wants to sketch, then with probability $1-\delta$, $\|Sx\|_2 = (1\pm \epsilon)\|x\|_2$ for all $x\in\Omega$. However, in their analysis $C_{\Omega}^2$ can be as large as $\Theta(n^{2q})$, even for a set $\Omega$ of $O(1)$ vectors $x$. We give a new analysis of this sketch, providing nearly optimal bounds. Namely, we show an upper bound of $m = \Theta \left (\epsilon^{-2} \log(n/\delta) + \epsilon^{-1} \log^q(n/\delta) \right ),$ which by composing with CountSketch, can be improved to $\Theta(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/(\delta \epsilon)) + \epsilon^{-1} \log^q (1/(\delta \epsilon))$. For the important case of $q = 2$ and $\delta = 1/\poly(n)$, this shows that $m = \Theta(\epsilon^{-2} \log(n) + \epsilon^{-1} \log^2(n))$, demonstrating that the $\epsilon^{-2}$ and $\log^2(n)$ terms do not multiply each other. We also show a nearly matching lower bound of $m = \Omega(\eps^{-2} \log(1/(\delta)) + \eps^{-1} \log^q(1/(\delta)))$. In a number of applications, one has $|\Omega| = \poly(n)$ and in this case our bounds are optimal up to a constant factor. This is the first high probability sketch for tensor products that has optimal sketch size and can be implemented in $m \cdot \sum_{i=1}^q \textrm{nnz}(x_i)$ time, where $\textrm{nnz}(x_i)$ is the number of non-zero entries of $x_i$. Lastly, we empirically compare our sketch to other sketches for tensor products, and give a novel application to compressing neural networks.
originalAbstract: We revisit the classic randomized sketch of a tensor product of $q$ vectors $x_i\in\mathbb{R}^n$. The $i$-th coordinate $(Sx)_i$ of the sketch is equal to $\prod_{j = 1}^q \langle u^{i, j}, x^j \rangle / \sqrt{m}$, where $u^{i,j}$ are independent random sign vectors. Kar and Karnick (JMLR, 2012) show that if the sketching dimension $m = \Omega(\epsilon^{-2} C_{\Omega}^2 \log (1/\delta))$, where $C_{\Omega}$ is a certain property of the point set $\Omega$ one wants to sketch, then with probability $1-\delta$, $\|Sx\|_2 = (1\pm \epsilon)\|x\|_2$ for all $x\in\Omega$. However, in their analysis $C_{\Omega}^2$ can be as large as $\Theta(n^{2q})$, even for a set $\Omega$ of $O(1)$ vectors $x$. We give a new analysis of this sketch, providing nearly optimal bounds. Namely, we show an upper bound of $m = \Theta \left (\epsilon^{-2} \log(n/\delta) + \epsilon^{-1} \log^q(n/\delta) \right ),$ which by composing with CountSketch, can be improved to $\Theta(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/(\delta \epsilon)) + \epsilon^{-1} \log^q (1/(\delta \epsilon))$. For the important case of $q = 2$ and $\delta = 1/\poly(n)$, this shows that $m = \Theta(\epsilon^{-2} \log(n) + \epsilon^{-1} \log^2(n))$, demonstrating that the $\epsilon^{-2}$ and $\log^2(n)$ terms do not multiply each other. We also show a nearly matching lower bound of $m = \Omega(\eps^{-2} \log(1/(\delta)) + \eps^{-1} \log^q(1/(\delta)))$. paragraphs: Tensor products can create very large representations even when their constituent vectors are manageable. Earlier analysis could demand a sketch dimension growing extremely quickly with the original dimension and tensor order, even for a small collection of vectors.

For second-order products at the stated high-probability setting, the bound separates a squared inverse-error term times a logarithm from an inverse-error term times a squared logarithm. The squared inverse-error and squared-logarithm factors therefore need not multiply.

A nearly matching lower bound establishes how close these guarantees are to the best possible ones. For polynomial-size point collections, the bounds are optimal up to constants. The sketch can also be computed in time proportional to its dimension times the total number of nonzero input entries. The paper includes empirical comparisons with other tensor-product sketches and an application to neural-network compression.
summary.tldr: A sharper analysis gives nearly optimal dimensions for a fast randomized tensor-product sketch, with optimal bounds for polynomial-size point collections.

title: Tight Dimensionality Reduction for Sketching Low Degree Polynomial Kernels

abstract: We propose a novel active learning (AL) model that integrates Bayesian and discriminative kernel machines for fast and accurate multi-class data sampling. By joining a sparse Bayesian model and a maximum margin machine under a unified kernel machine committee (KMC), the proposed model is able to identify a small number of data samples that best represent the overall data space while accurately capturing the decision boundaries. The integration is conducted using the maximum entropy discrimination framework, resulting in a joint objective function that contains generalized entropy as a regularizer. Such a property allows the proposed AL model to choose data samples that more effectively handle non-separable classification problems. Parameter learning is achieved through a principled optimization framework that leverages convex duality and sparse structure of KMC to efficiently optimize the joint objective function. Key model parameters are used to design a novel sampling function to choose data samples that can simultaneously improve multiple decision boundaries, making it an effective sampler for problems with a large number of classes. Experiments conducted over both synthetic and real data and comparison with competitive AL methods demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which data samples to label, so the selection rule influences how effectively a model learns. This paper develops a method for multiclass problems that combines two goals: representing the overall data space and capturing the boundaries between classes. It integrates a sparse Bayesian model with a maximum-margin machine in a shared kernel machine committee.

The integration uses maximum entropy discrimination to produce one joint objective with a generalized entropy regularizer. According to the authors, this helps the sampling method address classification problems whose classes are not separable. Parameter learning uses convex duality and the committee's sparse structure to make optimization efficient.

The learned parameters also define a sampling function that can select examples useful for improving multiple decision boundaries at once. That feature is especially relevant when there are many classes and hence many boundaries to refine. Experiments on synthetic and real data, including comparisons with competitive active-learning methods, demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution links a unified modeling objective to a sample-selection rule serving both representation and discrimination.
summary.tldr: A unified Bayesian and maximum-margin kernel committee selects multiclass training examples that represent the data and improve multiple decision boundaries.

title: Integrating Bayesian and Discriminative Sparse Kernel Machines for Multi-class Active Learning

abstract: Boosting is one of the most successful ideas in machine learning. The most well-accepted explanations for the low generalization error of boosting algorithms such as AdaBoost stem from margin theory. The study of margins in the context of boosting algorithms was initiated by Schapire, Freund, Bartlett and Lee (1998), and has inspired numerous boosting algorithms and generalization bounds. To date, the strongest known generalization (upper bound) is the $k$th margin bound of Gao and Zhou (2013). Despite the numerous generalization upper bounds that have been proved over the last two decades, nothing is known about the tightness of these bounds. In this paper, we give the first margin-based lower bounds on the generalization error of boosted classifiers. Our lower bounds nearly match the $k$th margin bound and thus almost settle the generalization performance of boosted classifiers in terms of margins.

paragraphs: Margin theory is a leading explanation for why boosting methods such as AdaBoost can generalize well. Much of that theory consists of upper bounds on generalization error, which describe how large the error can be given margin information. This paper asks how close those guarantees are to the best guarantees that margins can support.

The authors derive the first margin-based lower bounds on the generalization error of boosted classifiers. Lower bounds complement upper bounds by showing that error at certain levels can occur. Together, the two kinds of result reveal whether an existing guarantee leaves substantial room for improvement or already captures the essential behavior.

The new lower bounds nearly match the strongest known upper bound identified in the abstract, the kth margin bound. This almost resolves the generalization performance of boosted classifiers as characterized through margins. The contribution is a theoretical clarification of the explanatory power of margin analysis, showing that its strongest existing guarantee is close to tight.
summary.tldr: New lower bounds nearly match the strongest margin-based upper bound, showing that margin theory almost tightly characterizes boosted classifiers' generalization.

title: Margin-Based Generalization Lower Bounds for Boosted Classifiers

abstract: Applications such as weather forecasting and personalized medicine demand models that output calibrated probability estimates---those representative of the true likelihood of a prediction. Most models are not calibrated out of the box but are recalibrated by post-processing model outputs. We find in this work that popular recalibration methods like Platt scaling and temperature scaling are (i) less calibrated than reported, and (ii) current techniques cannot estimate how miscalibrated they are. An alternative method, histogram binning, has measurable calibration error but is sample inefficient---it requires $O(B/\epsilon^2)$ samples, compared to $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ for scaling methods, where $B$ is the number of distinct probabilities the model can output. To get the best of both worlds, we introduce the scaling-binning calibrator, which first fits a parametric function that acts like a baseline for variance reduction and then bins the function values to actually ensure calibration. This requires only $O(1/\epsilon^2 + B)$ samples. We then show that methods used to estimate calibration error are suboptimal---we prove that an alternative estimator introduced in the meteorological community requires fewer samples ($O(\sqrt{B})$ instead of $O(B)$). We validate our approach with multiclass calibration experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, where we obtain a 35\% lower calibration error than histogram binning and, unlike scaling methods, guarantees on true calibration.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet report 35% lower calibration error than histogram binning, together with guarantees on true calibration unavailable from the scaling methods considered. The paper therefore improves both recalibration and the ability to assess it.
summary.tldr: Scaling-binning combines sample-efficient recalibration with verifiable guarantees, while an improved estimator reduces the data needed to assess calibration error.

title: Verified Uncertainty Calibration

abstract: Supervised classification techniques use training samples to find classification rules with small expected 0-1 loss. Conventional methods achieve efficient learning and out-of-sample generalization by minimizing surrogate losses over specific families of rules. This paper presents minimax risk classifiers (MRCs) that do not rely on a choice of surrogate loss and family of rules. MRCs achieve efficient learning and out-of-sample generalization by minimizing worst-case expected 0-1 loss w.r.t. uncertainty sets that are defined by linear constraints and include the true underlying distribution. In addition, MRCs' learning stage provides performance guarantees as lower and upper tight bounds for expected 0-1 loss. We also present MRCs' finite-sample generalization bounds in terms of training size and smallest minimax risk, and show their competitive classification performance w.r.t. state-of-the-art techniques using benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Classification ultimately seeks a low probability of making an incorrect prediction, expressed by expected zero-one loss. Conventional learning methods typically optimize a surrogate loss within a selected family of classification rules. This paper introduces minimax risk classifiers that avoid relying on those choices and directly address worst-case expected zero-one loss.

The method considers uncertainty sets of distributions defined through linear constraints. These sets include the true underlying distribution, and learning minimizes the worst expected classification loss over the set. The uncertainty set therefore plays a central role: it specifies which distributions the classifier must account for when choosing a rule.

Training also provides tight lower and upper bounds on expected zero-one loss, giving performance guarantees alongside the learned classifier. The authors derive finite-sample generalization bounds involving training-set size and the smallest minimax risk. On benchmark datasets, the classifiers perform competitively with leading techniques. The contribution combines direct treatment of classification error, distributional uncertainty, and explicit performance bounds.
summary.tldr: Minimax risk classifiers optimize worst-case zero-one loss over distributional uncertainty sets and provide tight performance bounds during learning.

title: Minimax Classification with 0-1 Loss and Performance Guarantees

abstract: Recent work suggests improving the performance of Bloom filter by incorporating a machine learning model as a binary classifier. However, such learned Bloom filter does not take full advantage of the predicted probability scores. We propose new algorithms that generalize the learned Bloom filter by using the complete spectrum of the score regions. We prove our algorithms have lower false positive rate (FPR) and memory usage compared with the existing approaches to learned Bloom filter. We also demonstrate the improved performance of our algorithms on real-world information filtering tasks over the web.
originalAbstract: Recent work suggests improving the performance of Bloom filter by incorporating a machine learning model as a binary classifier. However, such learned Bloom filter does not take full advantage of the predicted probability scores. We propose new algorithms that generalize the learned Bloom filter by using the complete spectrum of the score regions. We prove our algorithms have lower false positive rate (FPR) and memory usage compared with the existing approaches to learned Bloom filter. We also demonstrate the improved performance of our algorithms on real-world information filtering tasks over the web.

paragraphs: Learned Bloom filters incorporate a machine learning classifier into a filtering system, with the aim of improving its performance. This paper focuses on information that existing learned filters leave underused: the classifier’s predicted probability scores. Treating the classifier mainly as a binary decision maker does not make full use of the distinctions present across those scores.

The proposed algorithms generalize learned Bloom filtering by using the complete range of score regions. The central idea is to let more of the classifier’s output inform the filtering procedure. This matters because the learning component supplies more information than a final yes-or-no prediction, and that additional information can affect how efficiently the filter operates.

The authors prove improvements in both false positive rate and memory usage relative to existing learned Bloom filter approaches. They also demonstrate better performance on real-world web information filtering tasks. Together, these results connect a change in how classifier scores are used to two practical objectives: reducing mistaken positive responses and reducing the storage needed for filtering.
summary.tldr: Ada-BF uses the full range of classifier scores to improve learned Bloom filters’ false positive rates and memory usage.

title: Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ada-BF): Efficient Utilization of the Classifier with Application to Real-Time Information Filtering on the Web

abstract: Recently, Transformer networks have redefined the state of the art in many NLP tasks. However, these models suffer from quadratic computational cost in the input sequence length $n$ to compute pairwise attention in each layer. This has prompted recent research into sparse Transformers that sparsify the connections in the attention layers. While empirically promising for long sequences, fundamental questions remain unanswered: Can sparse Transformers approximate any arbitrary sequence-to-sequence function, similar to their dense counterparts? How does the sparsity pattern and the sparsity level affect their performance? In this paper, we address these questions and provide a unifying framework that captures existing sparse attention models. We propose sufficient conditions under which we prove that a sparse attention model can universally approximate any sequence-to-sequence function. Surprisingly, our results show that sparse Transformers with only $O(n)$ connections per attention layer can approximate the same function class as the dense model with $n^2$ connections. Lastly, we present experiments comparing different patterns/levels of sparsity on standard NLP tasks.

paragraphs: Dense Transformer attention connects every position in a sequence to every other position, producing a quadratic number of connections per layer. Sparse attention reduces those connections, making it attractive for long sequences. The paper asks whether this reduction also removes the ability to represent functions that dense Transformers can approximate.

The authors develop a unifying framework covering existing sparse attention models and identify sufficient conditions for universal approximation of sequence-to-sequence functions. Under those conditions, a sparse Transformer with only a linear number of attention connections per layer can approximate the same function class as a dense model with quadratically many connections.

This is a statement about representational capacity for qualifying sparse patterns. It does not assert that every way of removing attention connections preserves that capacity. The paper also compares sparsity patterns and levels in experiments on standard language tasks. Together, the theory and experiments address complementary questions: which sparse structures retain broad approximation power, and how choices of sparsity behave in evaluated tasks. The main theoretical finding shows that quadratic connectivity is not required for the stated approximation capability.
summary.tldr: Under sufficient structural conditions, sparse Transformers with linear attention connections per layer retain the universal approximation capacity of dense models.

title: O(n) Connections are Expressive Enough: Universal Approximability of Sparse Transformers

abstract: Sparse sequences of neural spikes are posited to underlie aspects of working memory, motor production, and learning. Discovering these sequences in an unsupervised manner is a longstanding problem in statistical neuroscience. Promising recent work utilized a convolutive nonnegative matrix factorization model to tackle this challenge. However, this model requires spike times to be discretized, utilizes a sub-optimal least-squares criterion, and does not provide uncertainty estimates for model predictions or estimated parameters. We address each of these shortcomings by developing a point process model that characterizes fine-scale sequences at the level of individual spikes and represents sequence occurrences as a small number of marked events in continuous time. This ultra-sparse representation of sequence events opens new possibilities for spike train modeling. For example, we introduce learnable time warping parameters to model sequences of varying duration, which have been experimentally observed in neural circuits. We demonstrate these advantages on recordings from songbird higher vocal center and rodent hippocampus.

paragraphs: Sequences of neural spikes are hypothesized to support functions such as working memory, movement, and learning. Discovering those sequences without labels is difficult. This paper develops a point process model that describes sequences at the level of individual spikes and represents their occurrences as a small number of marked events in continuous time.

The model addresses three shortcomings of a preceding convolutive nonnegative matrix factorization approach: discretizing spike times, using a suboptimal least-squares criterion, and lacking uncertainty estimates for predictions or parameters. The authors also introduce learnable time-warping parameters so a sequence can occur over different durations. This accommodates duration variability that has been observed experimentally in neural circuits. Demonstrations on songbird higher vocal center and rodent hippocampus recordings illustrate the model’s advantages. The contribution links precise event timing, uncertainty estimation, and flexible sequence duration within one framework for unsupervised discovery.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time point process model detects neural spike sequences while representing uncertainty and accommodating sequences with varying durations.

title: Point process models for sequence detection in high-dimensional neural spike trains

abstract: We propose a novel method for gradient-based optimization of black-box simulators using differentiable local surrogate models. In fields such as physics and engineering, many processes are modeled with non-differentiable simulators with intractable likelihoods. Optimization of these forward models is particularly challenging, especially when the simulator is stochastic. To address such cases, we introduce the use of deep generative models to iteratively approximate the simulator in local neighborhoods of the parameter space. We demonstrate that these local surrogates can be used to approximate the gradient of the simulator, and thus enable gradient-based optimization of simulator parameters. In cases where the dependence of the simulator on the parameter space is constrained to a low dimensional submanifold, we observe that our method attains minima faster than baseline methods, including Bayesian optimization, numerical optimization and approaches using score function gradient estimators.

paragraphs: Many physics and engineering simulators can produce outcomes for chosen parameters without supplying derivatives that reveal how to improve those parameters. Optimization becomes especially difficult when outputs are stochastic and their likelihoods are intractable. This paper proposes using differentiable learned models to make gradient-based optimization possible for such black-box simulators.

The method repeatedly trains deep generative models to approximate the simulator within local neighborhoods of parameter space. These local surrogates supply approximate gradients, which guide changes to the simulator's parameters. Local approximation is central to the approach: the learned model is used to describe behavior around the region currently relevant to optimization.

The authors demonstrate that the surrogate gradients can support optimization. They observe faster attainment of minima than Bayesian optimization, numerical optimization, and score-function gradient approaches in cases where simulator dependence lies on a low-dimensional submanifold. That condition is part of the reported finding. The result supports local generative approximation as a useful route when the effective parameter dependence has this structure.
summary.tldr: Differentiable local generative models provide approximate gradients for optimizing stochastic black-box simulators.

title: Black-Box Optimization with Local Generative Surrogates

abstract: Recently, different machine learning methods have been introduced to tackle the challenging few-shot learning scenario that is, learning from a small labeled dataset related to a specific task. Common approaches have taken the form of meta-learning: learning to learn on the new problem given the old. Following the recognition that meta-learning is implementing learning in a multi-level model, we present a Bayesian treatment for the meta-learning inner loop through the use of deep kernels. As a result we can learn a kernel that transfers to new tasks; we call this Deep Kernel Transfer (DKT). This approach has many advantages: is straightforward to implement as a single optimizer, provides uncertainty quantification, and does not require estimation of task-specific parameters. We empirically demonstrate that DKT outperforms several state-of-the-art algorithms in few-shot classification, and is the state of the art for cross-domain adaptation and regression. We conclude that complex meta-learning routines can be replaced by a simpler Bayesian model without loss of accuracy.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning requires solving a new task from very few labeled examples. Meta-learning approaches use experience with previous tasks to make this possible. This paper treats that process as a multilevel model and gives the task-specific inner learning step a Bayesian formulation through deep kernels.

The resulting method, Deep Kernel Transfer, learns a kernel that can carry useful information across tasks. The kernel supplies a learned way to relate examples, while the Bayesian treatment provides uncertainty estimates. The approach uses a single optimizer and avoids estimating task-specific parameters, simplifying the machinery required to learn from a small new dataset.

In the reported experiments, DKT beats several leading few-shot classification algorithms and achieves leading results for cross-domain adaptation and regression. These findings support the authors' conclusion that a simpler Bayesian model can replace complex meta-learning routines without losing accuracy in the evaluated settings. The contribution therefore combines predictive performance with a simpler learning procedure and an explicit treatment of uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Deep Kernel Transfer uses a simpler Bayesian meta-learning model to achieve strong few-shot results while quantifying uncertainty.

title: Bayesian Meta-Learning for the Few-Shot Setting via Deep Kernels

abstract: High dimensional black-box optimization has broad applications but remains a challenging problem to solve. Given a set of samples x_i, y_i, building a global model (like Bayesian Optimization (BO)) suffers from the curse of dimensionality in the high-dimensional search space, while a greedy search may lead to sub-optimality. By recursively splitting the search space into regions with high/low function values, recent works like LaNAS shows good performance in Neural Architecture Search (NAS), reducing the sample complexity empirically. In this paper, we coin LA-MCTS that extends LaNAS to other domains. Unlike previous approaches, LA-MCTS learns the partition of the search space using a few samples and their function values in an online fashion. While LaNAS uses linear partition and performs uniform sampling in each region, our LA-MCTS adopts a nonlinear decision boundary and learns a local model to pick good candidates. If the nonlinear partition function and the local model fits well with ground-truth black-box function, then good partitions and candidates can be reached with much fewer samples. LA-MCTS serves as a meta-algorithm by using existing black-box optimizers (e.g., BO, TuRBO as its local models, achieving strong performance in general black-box optimization and reinforcement learning benchmarks, in particular for high-dimensional problems.

paragraphs: High-dimensional black-box optimization must find good inputs using observed function values. A global model can struggle with dimensionality, while greedy search can settle for inferior solutions. This paper develops LA-MCTS, extending the search-space partitioning approach of LaNAS beyond neural architecture search to more general optimization problems.

LA-MCTS learns partitions online from sampled inputs and their values, recursively separating regions associated with higher and lower function values. It uses nonlinear boundaries rather than the linear partitions of LaNAS. Within each region, a learned local model selects promising candidates instead of sampling uniformly. The method therefore learns both where to search and how to search within a region.

The anticipated sample savings are conditional: substantially fewer samples may suffice when the partition function and local model fit the underlying black-box function well. LA-MCTS acts as a meta-algorithm that can incorporate existing optimizers, including Bayesian optimization and TuRBO, as local models. The authors report strong results on general black-box optimization and reinforcement learning benchmarks, especially in high dimensions.
summary.tldr: LA-MCTS learns nonlinear search regions and uses local optimizers to find promising candidates, with strong reported performance on high-dimensional problems.

title: Learning Search Space Partition for Black-box Optimization using Monte Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Large width limits have been a recent focus of deep learning research: modulo computational practicalities, do wider networks outperform narrower ones? Answering this question has been challenging, as conventional networks gain representational power with width, potentially masking any negative effects. Our analysis in this paper decouples capacity and width via the generalization of neural networks to Deep Gaussian Processes (Deep GP), a class of nonparametric hierarchical models that subsume neural nets. In doing so, we aim to understand how width affects (standard) neural networks once they have sufficient capacity for a given modeling task. Our theoretical and empirical results on Deep GP suggest that large width can be detrimental to hierarchical models. Surprisingly, we prove that even nonparametric Deep GP converge to Gaussian processes, effectively becoming shallower without any increase in representational power. The posterior, which corresponds to a mixture of data-adaptable basis functions, becomes less data-dependent with width. Our tail analysis demonstrates that width and depth have opposite effects: depth accentuates a model’s non-Gaussianity, while width makes models increasingly Gaussian. We find there is a “sweet spot” that maximizes test performance before the limiting GP behavior prevents adaptability, occurring at width = 1 or width = 2 for nonparametric Deep GP. These results make strong predictions about the same phenomenon in conventional neural networks trained with L2 regularization (analogous to a Gaussian prior on parameters): we show that such neural networks may need up to 500 − 1000 hidden units for sufficient capacity - depending on the dataset - but further width degrades performance.

summary.tldr: Deep Gaussian process analysis shows how increasing width can reduce data adaptability and hurt performance after capacity is sufficient.

title: The Limitations of Large Width in Neural Networks: A Deep Gaussian Process Perspective

abstract: Learning representations from sets has become increasingly important with many applications in point cloud processing, graph learning, image/video recognition, and object detection. We introduce a geometrically-interpretable and generic pooling mechanism for aggregating a set of features into a fixed-dimensional representation. In particular, we treat elements of a set as samples from a probability distribution and propose an end-to-end trainable Euclidean embedding for sliced-Wasserstein distance to learn from set-structured data effectively. We evaluate our proposed pooling method on a wide variety of set-structured data, including point-cloud, graph, and image classification tasks, and demonstrate that our proposed method provides superior performance over existing set representation learning approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/navid-naderi/PSWE.

paragraphs: Many learning problems describe an object through a set of features, such as those arising from point clouds, graphs, or images. A model needs to aggregate that set into a fixed-dimensional representation. This paper proposes a pooling mechanism that gives the aggregation a geometric interpretation by treating set elements as samples from a probability distribution.

The method builds an end-to-end trainable Euclidean embedding for sliced-Wasserstein distance. Its central move is to represent a collection through the distribution suggested by its elements, using that distributional viewpoint to construct the pooled vector. Because the embedding is trainable, pooling can be learned together with the surrounding model for the task being solved.

The authors evaluate the method on point-cloud, graph, and image classification, reporting better performance than existing set-representation approaches in those evaluations. The range of tasks supports its intended use as a generic pooling component. Its contribution joins a fixed-size output suitable for learning systems with an explicit geometric basis for representing the input set.
summary.tldr: A trainable sliced-Wasserstein embedding pools feature sets into fixed-size vectors and improves the reported classification results.

title: Pooling by Sliced-Wasserstein Embedding

abstract: Inspired by human intelligence, the research on online continual learning aims to push the limits of the machine learning models to constantly learn from sequentially encountered tasks, with the data from each task being observed in an online fashion. Though recent studies have achieved remarkable progress in improving the online continual learning performance empowered by the deep neural networks-based models, many of today's approaches still suffer a lot from catastrophic forgetting, a persistent challenge for continual learning. In this paper, we present a novel method which attempts to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in online continual learning from a new perspective, i.e., neuron calibration. In particular, we model the neurons in the deep neural networks-based models as calibrated units under a general formulation. Then we formalize a learning framework to effectively train the calibrated model, where neuron calibration could give ubiquitous benefit to balance the stability and plasticity of online continual learning algorithms through influencing both their forward inference path and backward optimization path. Our proposed formulation for neuron calibration is lightweight and applicable to general feed-forward neural networks-based models. We perform extensive experiments to evaluate our method on four benchmark continual learning datasets. The results show that neuron calibration plays a vital role in improving online continual learning performance and our method could substantially improve the state-of-the-art performance on all~the~evaluated~datasets.

paragraphs: Online continual learning asks a model to keep learning as tasks arrive sequentially and their data are observed online. A central difficulty is catastrophic forgetting: learning new tasks can erode previously acquired abilities. This paper approaches that problem through neuron calibration, changing how the network's individual units participate in learning and prediction.

The authors formulate neurons as calibrated units and provide a framework for training the resulting model. Calibration influences both the forward path used to produce outputs and the backward path used for optimization. That gives it a role in balancing stability, which supports retaining earlier learning, with plasticity, which supports adapting to new tasks.

The formulation is lightweight and applicable to general feed-forward neural network models. Experiments across four continual learning benchmark datasets show improved online learning performance, with substantial gains over the reported state of the art on all evaluated datasets. These results support calibration as a useful intervention at the neuron level, affecting both what the model computes and how subsequent training changes it.
summary.tldr: Lightweight neuron calibration improves online continual learning by influencing both prediction and optimization to balance retention and adaptation.

title: Mitigating Forgetting in Online Continual Learning with Neuron Calibration

abstract: Deep learning systems typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting of past knowledge when acquiring new skills continually. In this paper, we emphasize two dilemmas, representation bias and classifier bias in class-incremental learning, and present a simple and novel approach that employs explicit class augmentation (classAug) and implicit semantic augmentation (semanAug) to address the two biases, respectively. On the one hand, we propose to address the representation bias by learning transferable and diverse representations. Specifically, we investigate the feature representations in incremental learning based on spectral analysis and present a simple technique called classAug, to let the model see more classes during training for learning representations transferable across classes. On the other hand, to overcome the classifier bias, semanAug implicitly involves the simultaneous generating of an infinite number of instances of old classes in the deep feature space, which poses tighter constraints to maintain the decision boundary of previously learned classes. Without storing any old samples, our method can perform comparably with representative data replay based approaches.

paragraphs: When a model learns new classes over time, it can lose the ability to recognize earlier ones. This paper separates that problem into two biases: one in the representations the model learns, and another in the classifier that uses those representations. It introduces a different augmentation mechanism for each source of forgetting.

The first mechanism, classAug, exposes the model to more classes during training to encourage diverse representations that transfer across classes. Its development is informed by spectral analysis of incremental-learning features. The second, semanAug, implicitly represents an infinite collection of old-class instances in deep feature space, imposing tighter constraints that help preserve earlier decision boundaries.

The method does not store old training samples. The authors report that it can nevertheless perform comparably to representative approaches that replay past data. This finding supports treating representation quality and classifier stability as complementary targets, and shows how implicit feature-space augmentation can help retain old knowledge without retaining the original examples.
summary.tldr: Two complementary augmentations address representation and classifier bias, enabling competitive class-incremental learning without storing old samples.

title: Class-Incremental Learning via Dual Augmentation

abstract: Recently, many researchers have made successful progress in building the AI systems for MOBA-game-playing with deep reinforcement learning, such as on Dota 2 and Honor of Kings. Even though these AI systems have achieved or even exceeded human-level performance, they still suffer from the lack of policy diversity. In this paper, we propose a novel Macro-Goals Guided framework, called MGG, to learn diverse policies in MOBA games. MGG abstracts strategies as macro-goals from human demonstrations and trains a Meta-Controller to predict these macro-goals. To enhance policy diversity, MGG samples macro-goals from the Meta-Controller prediction and guides the training process towards these goals. Experimental results on the typical MOBA game Honor of Kings demonstrate that MGG can execute diverse policies in different matches and lineups, and also outperform the state-of-the-art methods over 102 heroes.

paragraphs: An AI can play a multiplayer online battle arena game extremely well while still using a limited range of strategies. This paper treats strategic diversity as a distinct learning objective. Its Macro-Goals Guided framework, MGG, uses high-level goals to encourage different policies rather than relying on strong game performance alone to produce variety.

MGG extracts macro-goals from human demonstrations and trains a Meta-Controller to predict them. During training, it samples goals from the Meta-Controller's predictions and guides learning toward the selected goals. Human demonstrations thus supply strategic abstractions, while sampling creates opportunities to train behavior directed at different strategies.

Experiments in Honor of Kings show that MGG executes diverse policies across matches and team lineups. The authors also report outperforming state-of-the-art methods over 102 heroes. These results matter because the framework pursues variation in play while also delivering strong measured performance. The evidence supports macro-goal guidance as a way to broaden the policies learned in the evaluated game, rather than treating diversity as an automatic consequence of competitive strength.
summary.tldr: MGG samples high-level goals learned from human demonstrations to train diverse, strong policies in Honor of Kings.

title: Learning Diverse Policies in MOBA Games via Macro-Goals

abstract: Federated learning methods typically learn a model by iteratively sampling updates from a population of clients. In this work, we explore how the number of clients sampled at each round (the cohort size) impacts the quality of the learned model and the training dynamics of federated learning algorithms. Our work poses three fundamental questions. First, what challenges arise when trying to scale federated learning to larger cohorts? Second, what parallels exist between cohort sizes in federated learning, and batch sizes in centralized learning? Last, how can we design federated learning methods that effectively utilize larger cohort sizes? We give partial answers to these questions based on extensive empirical evaluation. Our work highlights a number of challenges stemming from the use of larger cohorts. While some of these (such as generalization issues and diminishing returns) are analogs of large-batch training challenges, others (including catastrophic training failures and fairness concerns) are unique to federated learning.

paragraphs: Federated learning repeatedly gathers updates from selected clients to train a shared model. This paper examines cohort size: the number of clients selected in each round. It asks how increasing that number affects both the quality of the resulting model and the behavior of training, rather than treating greater participation as an automatically beneficial scaling choice.

The study connects this question to large-batch training in centralized learning. Its empirical evaluation identifies parallels, including generalization problems and diminishing returns. These findings indicate that increasing the amount of participation per round can bring familiar optimization and performance tradeoffs even though the updates come from separate clients.

The authors also identify challenges they distinguish as specific to federated learning, including catastrophic training failures and fairness concerns. They investigate how methods might use larger cohorts effectively, while describing their answers as partial. The work frames cohort size as an algorithmic design choice with consequences beyond aggregate training progress, including whether benefits are distributed fairly.
summary.tldr: An empirical study finds that larger federated-learning cohorts introduce generalization, diminishing-return, training-failure, and fairness challenges.

title: On Large-Cohort Training for Federated Learning

abstract: We propose a novel neural representation for videos (NeRV) which encodes videos in neural networks. Unlike conventional representations that treat videos as frame sequences, we represent videos as neural networks taking frame index as input. Given a frame index, NeRV outputs the corresponding RGB image. Video encoding in NeRV is simply fitting a neural network to video frames and decoding process is a simple feedforward operation. As an image-wise implicit representation, NeRV output the whole image and shows great efficiency compared to pixel-wise implicit representation, improving the encoding speed by $\textbf{25}\times$ to $\textbf{70}\times$, the decoding speed by $\textbf{38}\times$ to $\textbf{132}\times$, while achieving better video quality. With such a representation, we can treat videos as neural networks, simplifying several video-related tasks. For example, conventional video compression methods are restricted by a long and complex pipeline, specifically designed for the task. In contrast, with NeRV, we can use any neural network compression method as a proxy for video compression, and achieve comparable performance to traditional frame-based video compression approaches (H.264, HEVC \etc). Besides compression, we demonstrate the generalization of NeRV for video denoising. The source code and pre-trained model can be found at https://github.com/haochen-rye/NeRV.git.

paragraphs: NeRV represents a video through a neural network that maps a frame index to a complete RGB image. Encoding means fitting the network to the video’s frames, and decoding means evaluating that network at the requested index. The video is therefore represented by a learned function that can reconstruct its frames.

Producing an entire image at once is central to the approach. Compared with pixel-wise implicit representations, the paper reports encoding speed improvements of 25 to 70 times and decoding improvements of 38 to 132 times, alongside better video quality. These comparisons support the efficiency of using an image-wise representation for the tested videos.

Treating a video as a network also makes network compression a way to compress the video itself. The authors report performance comparable to traditional frame-based approaches such as H.264 and HEVC. They additionally demonstrate video denoising, showing that the representation can support more than compression. The common mechanism is to perform video-related operations through the network representing its frames.
summary.tldr: NeRV encodes a video as a neural network that generates whole frames from their indices, enabling efficient reconstruction, compression, and denoising.

title: NeRV: Neural Representations for Videos

abstract: Optical Processing Units (OPUs) -- low-power photonic chips dedicated to large scale random projections -- have been used in previous work to train deep neural networks using Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), an effective alternative to backpropagation. Here, we demonstrate how to leverage the intrinsic noise of optical random projections to build a differentially private DFA mechanism, making OPUs a solution of choice to provide a \emph{private-by-design} training. We provide a theoretical analysis of our adaptive privacy mechanism, carefully measuring how the noise of optical random projections propagates in the process and gives rise to provable Differential Privacy. Finally, we conduct experiments demonstrating the ability of our learning procedure to achieve solid end-task performance.

paragraphs: Optical Processing Units are low-power photonic chips built for large-scale random projections. Earlier work used them to train deep networks through Direct Feedback Alignment, an alternative to backpropagation. This paper investigates how the intrinsic noise in those optical projections can also support a differentially private training mechanism.

The authors construct a private DFA mechanism around that noise and provide a theoretical analysis of its adaptive privacy behavior. The analysis tracks how optical projection noise propagates through the learning process and establishes a differential privacy guarantee. This connects a physical property of the computation to a formal property of the resulting training procedure.

Experiments demonstrate solid end-task performance for the proposed learning method. The stated outcome is therefore a combination of provable privacy and useful empirical learning behavior. The privacy claim comes from the analyzed mechanism and the way it handles noise; the contribution is the deliberate incorporation of hardware noise into private training. It gives optical random projections an additional function beyond their existing role in implementing DFA.
summary.tldr: An analyzed Direct Feedback Alignment mechanism uses optical projection noise to provide differential privacy while retaining solid task performance.

title: Photonic Differential Privacy with Direct Feedback Alignment

abstract: The generalization ability of most meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) methods is largely limited to test tasks that are sampled from the same distribution used to sample training tasks. To overcome the limitation, we propose Latent Dynamics Mixture (LDM) that trains a reinforcement learning agent with imaginary tasks generated from mixtures of learned latent dynamics. By training a policy on mixture tasks along with original training tasks, LDM allows the agent to prepare for unseen test tasks during training and prevents the agent from overfitting the training tasks. LDM significantly outperforms standard meta-RL methods in test returns on the gridworld navigation and MuJoCo tasks where we strictly separate the training task distribution and the test task distribution.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to prepare an agent for new tasks, but its generalization is often largely confined to tasks drawn from the training distribution. This paper targets the harder situation where test tasks come from a different distribution. Its approach expands training with imaginary tasks built from what the agent has learned about environment dynamics.

Latent Dynamics Mixture, or LDM, constructs these tasks by mixing learned latent dynamics. The policy trains on both the original tasks and the generated mixture tasks. This exposes the agent to additional task variation during training, helping it prepare for unfamiliar tasks and reducing overfitting to the original training collection.

The experiments use gridworld navigation and MuJoCo tasks with strictly separated training and test task distributions. LDM achieves significantly higher test returns than standard meta-RL methods in these evaluations. The result supports generated task variation as a way to improve transfer beyond the training distribution, with the reported evidence tied to those evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: LDM improves meta-RL transfer to different task distributions by training on imaginary tasks formed from mixtures of learned latent dynamics.

title: Improving Generalization in Meta-RL with Imaginary Tasks from Latent Dynamics Mixture

abstract: One of the primary purposes of video is to capture people and their unique activities. It is often the case that the experience of watching the video can be enhanced by adding a musical soundtrack that is in-sync with the rhythmic features of these activities. How would this soundtrack sound? Such a problem is challenging since little is known about capturing the rhythmic nature of free body movements. In this work, we explore this problem and propose a novel system, called `RhythmicNet', which takes as an input a video which includes human movements and generates a soundtrack for it. RhythmicNet works directly with human movements by extracting skeleton keypoints and implements a sequence of models which translate the keypoints to rhythmic sounds.RhythmicNet follows the natural process of music improvisation which includes the prescription of streams of the beat, the rhythm and the melody. In particular, RhythmicNet first infers the music beat and the style pattern from body keypoints per each frame to produce rhythm. Next, it implements a transformer-based model to generate the hits of drum instruments and implements a U-net based model to generate the velocity and the offsets of the instruments. Additional types of instruments are added to the soundtrack by further conditioning on the generated drum sounds. We evaluate RhythmicNet on large scale datasets of videos that include body movements with inherit sound association, such as dance, as well as 'in the wild' internet videos of various movements and actions. We show that the method can generate plausible music that aligns well with different types of human movements.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to generate music that follows the rhythm of human movement in a video. This requires identifying rhythmic structure in free body motion, including actions that do not already come with an obvious musical accompaniment. The proposed system, RhythmicNet, starts from skeleton keypoints extracted from the people moving in the video.

Its sequence of models builds a soundtrack in stages. First, frame-level body keypoints inform estimates of the musical beat and style pattern. A Transformer then generates drum instrument hits, while a U-net predicts their velocities and timing offsets. Further instruments are added by conditioning on the generated drum sounds, linking later musical content to the established rhythmic foundation.

The authors evaluate the system on large-scale video datasets containing movements with inherent sound associations, such as dance, and on internet videos showing varied movements and actions. They report plausible music that aligns well with different types of motion. The finding supports using explicit body movement as a basis for rhythmic soundtrack generation.
summary.tldr: RhythmicNet turns human body movements in video into musical soundtracks whose rhythms align with the motion.

title: How Does it Sound?

abstract: We study the problem of learning generalized linear models under adversarial corruptions.We analyze a classical heuristic called the \textit{iterative trimmed maximum likelihood estimator} which is known to be effective against \textit{label corruptions} in practice. Under label corruptions, we prove that this simple estimator achieves minimax near-optimal risk on a wide range of generalized linear models, including Gaussian regression, Poisson regression and Binomial regression. Finally, we extend the estimator to the much more challenging setting of \textit{label and covariate corruptions} and demonstrate its robustness and optimality in that setting as well.

Under label corruptions, we prove that this simple estimator achieves minimax near-optimal risk on a wide range of generalized linear models, including Gaussian regression, Poisson regression and Binomial regression. Finally, we extend the estimator to the much more challenging setting of \textit{label and covariate corruptions} and demonstrate its robustness and optimality in that setting as well.

paragraphs: This paper examines learning generalized linear models when an adversary corrupts training data. Its starting point is iterative trimmed maximum likelihood estimation, a classical heuristic already known to work well against corrupted labels in practice. The authors investigate whether that practical behavior can be supported by statistical guarantees.

For label corruption, they prove that the estimator achieves nearly minimax-optimal risk across a broad collection of generalized linear models, including Gaussian, Poisson, and Binomial regression. A minimax comparison asks how the estimator performs against the best achievable worst-case risk. Near-optimality therefore gives a stronger justification than showing that the heuristic merely tolerates some damaged labels.

The authors then extend the estimator to corruption affecting both labels and covariates, meaning that both responses and input variables may be altered. They demonstrate robustness and optimality in this more challenging setting as well. The contribution is a theoretical foundation for a simple established estimator, together with an extension that addresses a broader form of adversarial data corruption.
summary.tldr: Iterative trimmed maximum likelihood achieves near-optimal risk under label corruption and extends robustly to corrupted inputs and labels.

title: Trimmed Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Robust Generalized Linear Model

abstract: Large-scale vision-language pre-training has shown impressive advances in a wide range of downstream tasks. Existing methods mainly model the cross-modal alignment by the similarity of the global representations of images and text, or advanced cross-modal attention upon image and text features. However, they fail to explicitly learn the fine-grained semantic alignment between visual regions and textual phrases, as only global image-text alignment information is available. In this paper, we introduce LOUPE, a fine-grained semantically aLigned visiOn-langUage PrE-training framework, which learns fine-grained semantic alignment from the novel perspective of game-theoretic interactions. To efficiently estimate the game-theoretic interactions, we further propose an uncertainty-aware neural Shapley interaction learning module. Experiments show that LOUPE achieves state-of-the-art performance on a variety of vision-language tasks. Without any object-level human annotations and fine-tuning, LOUPE achieves competitive performance on object detection and visual grounding. More importantly, LOUPE opens a new promising direction of learning fine-grained semantics from large-scale raw image-text pairs.

In this paper, we introduce LOUPE, a fine-grained semantically aLigned visiOn-langUage PrE-training framework, which learns fine-grained semantic alignment from the novel perspective of game-theoretic interactions. To efficiently estimate the game-theoretic interactions, we further propose an uncertainty-aware neural Shapley interaction learning module. Without any object-level human annotations and fine-tuning, LOUPE achieves competitive performance on object detection and visual grounding. title: Fine-Grained Semantically Aligned Vision-Language Pre-Training

abstract: Recently, transformer-based networks have shown impressive results in semantic segmentation. Yet for real-time semantic segmentation, pure CNN-based approaches still dominate in this field, due to the time-consuming computation mechanism of transformer. We propose RTFormer, an efficient dual-resolution transformer for real-time semantic segmenation, which achieves better trade-off between performance and efficiency than CNN-based models. To achieve high inference efficiency on GPU-like devices, our RTFormer leverages GPU-Friendly Attention with linear complexity and discards the multi-head mechanism. Besides, we find that cross-resolution attention is more efficient to gather global context information for high-resolution branch by spreading the high level knowledge learned from low-resolution branch. Extensive experiments on mainstream benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed RTFormer, it achieves state-of-the-art on Cityscapes, CamVid and COCOStuff, and shows promising results on ADE20K.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image location, making inference speed important when predictions must arrive in real time. Transformers have achieved strong segmentation results, but their computation can be costly. RTFormer redesigns transformer components to improve the balance between segmentation performance and efficiency on GPU-like devices.

The model uses two resolutions and a GPU-friendly attention mechanism with linear complexity. It also removes the multi-head mechanism. Cross-resolution attention transfers high-level information from the low-resolution branch to the high-resolution branch. This lets the finer representation receive global context through information already learned at a coarser resolution, which the authors find more efficient for gathering that context.

Experiments show a better performance-efficiency tradeoff than CNN-based models in the evaluated comparisons. RTFormer reports state-of-the-art results on Cityscapes, CamVid, and COCOStuff, with promising results on ADE20K. The contribution is an architecture whose attention and information exchange are designed around efficient inference, showing that transformers can be competitive for real-time segmentation when those computational choices are addressed directly.
summary.tldr: RTFormer combines efficient attention and cross-resolution context sharing to improve the speed-accuracy tradeoff in real-time semantic segmentation.

title: RTFormer: Efficient Design for Real-Time Semantic Segmentation with Transformer

abstract: As an important framework for safe Reinforcement Learning, the Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) has been extensively studied in the recent literature. However, despite the rich results under various on-policy learning settings, there still lacks some essential understanding of the offline CMDP problems, in terms of both the algorithm design and the information theoretic sample complexity lower bound. In this paper, we focus on solving the CMDP problems where only offline data are available. By adopting the concept of the single-policy concentrability coefficient $C^*$, we establish an $\Omega\left(\frac{\min\left\{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|,|\mathcal{S}|+I\right\} C^*}{(1-\gamma)^3\epsilon^2}\right)$ sample complexity lower bound for the offline CMDP problem, where $I$ stands for the number of constraints. By introducing a simple but novel deviation control mechanism, we propose a near-optimal primal-dual learning algorithm called DPDL. This algorithm provably guarantees zero constraint violation and its sample complexity matches the above lower bound except for an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}((1-\gamma)^{-1})$ factor. Comprehensive discussion on how to deal with the unknown constant $C^*$ and the potential asynchronous structure on the offline dataset are also included.
