paragraphs: A constrained Markov decision process describes learning to make decisions while respecting specified constraints. This paper studies the offline version, where learning must rely entirely on an existing dataset. Its central questions are how much data this requires and whether an algorithm can learn an effective policy without violating the constraints.

The authors establish a lower bound on the required number of samples using a single-policy concentrability coefficient, C*. The bound accounts for the numbers of states, actions, and constraints, as well as the discount factor and desired accuracy. This gives a theoretical reference for judging how close an algorithm comes to the best possible sample requirements in the studied setting.

They then introduce DPDL, a primal-dual algorithm with a deviation-control mechanism. It provably achieves zero constraint violation and matches the lower bound apart from an additional factor involving the discount factor, up to logarithmic terms. The paper also discusses handling unknown C* and possible asynchronous structure in the offline data.
summary.tldr: DPDL learns constrained policies from offline data with zero constraint violation and sample requirements close to a proved lower bound.

title: A Near-Optimal Primal-Dual Method for Off-Policy Learning in CMDP

abstract: Adaptive algorithms like AdaGrad and AMSGrad are successful in nonconvex optimization owing to their parameter-agnostic ability – requiring no a priori knowledge about problem-specific parameters nor tuning of learning rates. However, when it comes to nonconvex minimax optimization, direct extensions of such adaptive optimizers without proper time-scale separation may fail to work in practice. We provide such an example proving that the simple combination of Gradient Descent Ascent (GDA) with adaptive stepsizes can diverge if the primal-dual stepsize ratio is not carefully chosen; hence, a fortiori, such adaptive extensions are not parameter-agnostic. To address the issue, we formally introduce a Nested Adaptive framework, NeAda for short, that carries an inner loop for adaptively maximizing the dual variable with controllable stopping criteria and an outer loop for adaptively minimizing the primal variable. Such mechanism can be equipped with off-the-shelf adaptive optimizers and automatically balance the progress in the primal and dual variables. Theoretically, for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems, we show that NeAda with AdaGrad stepsizes can achieve the near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ and $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ gradient complexities respectively in the deterministic and stochastic settings, without prior information on the problem's smoothness and strong concavity parameters. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that simultaneously achieves near-optimal convergence rates and parameter-agnostic adaptation in the nonconvex minimax setting. Numerically, we further illustrate the robustness of the NeAda family with experiments on simple test functions and a real-world application.

paragraphs: Adaptive step sizes can reduce the need for problem-specific tuning in ordinary optimization, but minimax problems involve coordinating minimization and maximization. This paper shows that simply adding adaptive steps to gradient descent-ascent can diverge when the ratio between the two step sizes is poorly chosen. Adaptivity alone therefore does not provide the desired freedom from parameter tuning.

NeAda addresses this coordination problem with nested loops. An inner loop adaptively maximizes over the dual variable until a controllable stopping criterion is met. An outer loop adaptively minimizes over the primal variable. The framework accepts existing adaptive optimizers and uses this structure to balance progress between the two variables.

These guarantees do not require advance knowledge of smoothness or strong-concavity parameters. Experiments on test functions and a real-world application further illustrate robustness, connecting the theoretical coordination mechanism to practical optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: NeAda nests adaptive maximization inside minimization to obtain parameter-agnostic, near-optimal guarantees for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems.

title: Nest Your Adaptive Algorithm for Parameter-Agnostic Nonconvex Minimax Optimization

abstract: Infinite visual synthesis aims to generate high-resolution images, long-duration videos, and even visual generation of infinite size. Some recent work tried to solve this task by first dividing data into processable patches and then training the models on them without considering the dependencies between patches. However, since they fail to model global dependencies between patches, the quality and consistency of the generation can be limited. To address this issue, we propose NUWA-Infinity, a patch-level \emph{``render-and-optimize''} strategy for infinite visual synthesis. Given a large image or a long video, NUWA-Infinity first splits it into non-overlapping patches and uses the ordered patch chain as a complete training instance, a rendering model autoregressively predicts each patch based on its contexts. Once a patch is predicted, it is optimized immediately and its hidden states are saved as contexts for the next \emph{``render-and-optimize''} process. This brings two advantages: ($i$) The autoregressive rendering process with information transfer between contexts provides an implicit global probabilistic distribution modeling; ($ii$) The timely optimization process alleviates the optimization stress of the model and helps convergence. Based on the above designs, NUWA-Infinity shows a strong synthesis ability on high-resolution images and long-duration videos. The homepage link is \url{https://nuwa-infinity.microsoft.com}.

paragraphs: NUWA-Infinity addresses visual synthesis at scales such as high-resolution images and long videos. Dividing these outputs into manageable patches makes processing possible, but independently modeling patches can lose relationships across the full image or video. The paper focuses on retaining those relationships while working one patch at a time.

Its training strategy treats an ordered sequence of non-overlapping patches as a complete instance. A rendering model predicts each patch using its available context. After a patch is predicted, optimization happens immediately, and the model saves hidden states to provide context for the next patch. This repeats as a render-and-optimize sequence.

Passing context forward provides implicit modeling of a global probability distribution, while immediate optimization is intended to reduce optimization pressure and help convergence. The authors report strong synthesis ability for high-resolution images and long-duration videos. The central contribution is a way to connect local generation steps across a larger visual output while structuring optimization around those same steps.
summary.tldr: NUWA-Infinity generates and optimizes patches sequentially while carrying context forward to support coherent large images and long videos.

title: NUWA-Infinity: Autoregressive over Autoregressive Generation for Infinite Visual Synthesis

abstract: We propose a generalization of constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) that we call the \emph{semi-infinitely constrained Markov decision process} (SICMDP).Particularly, in a SICMDP model, we impose a continuum of constraints instead of a finite number of constraints as in the case of ordinary CMDPs.We also devise a reinforcement learning algorithm for SICMDPs that we call SI-CRL.We first transform the reinforcement learning problem into a linear semi-infinitely programming (LSIP) problem and then use the dual exchange method in the LSIP literature to solve it.To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to apply tools from semi-infinitely programming (SIP) to solve reinforcement learning problems.We present theoretical analysis for SI-CRL, identifying its sample complexity and iteration complexity.We also conduct extensive numerical examples to illustrate the SICMDP model and validate the SI-CRL algorithm.

paragraphs: A constrained Markov decision process combines sequential decision making with requirements that a policy must satisfy. Ordinary formulations impose a finite collection of constraints. This paper expands the model to allow a continuum of constraints, calling the result a semi-infinitely constrained Markov decision process, or SICMDP.

The authors develop SI-CRL, a reinforcement learning algorithm for this broader formulation. They first express the learning problem as a linear semi-infinite program, then use a dual exchange method from that optimization literature to solve it. The approach creates a bridge between reinforcement learning and mathematical tools designed to handle infinitely many constraints within an optimization problem.

The theoretical analysis characterizes both sample complexity and iteration complexity, addressing the data and computational steps required by the algorithm. Numerical examples illustrate the new model and validate the proposed solution method. The contribution is therefore both a more expressive way to specify constrained decision problems and an analyzed algorithm for learning within that formulation.
summary.tldr: SICMDPs extend constrained decision making to a continuum of constraints, with a learning algorithm based on semi-infinite programming.

title: Semi-infinitely Constrained Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Recent advances in differentiable rendering have enabled high-quality reconstruction of 3D scenes from multi-view images. Most methods rely on simple rendering algorithms: pre-filtered direct lighting or learned representations of irradiance. We show that a more realistic shading model, incorporating ray tracing and Monte Carlo integration, substantially improves decomposition into shape, materials & lighting. Unfortunately, Monte Carlo integration provides estimates with significant noise, even at large sample counts, which makes gradient-based inverse rendering very challenging. To address this, we incorporate multiple importance sampling and denoising in a novel inverse rendering pipeline. This improves convergence and enables gradient-based optimization at low sample counts. We present an efficient method to jointly reconstruct geometry (explicit triangle meshes), materials, and lighting, which substantially improves material and light separation compared to previous work. We argue that denoising can become an integral part of high quality inverse rendering pipelines.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a scene from multiple images involves separating geometry, materials, and illumination, all of which influence appearance. The paper shows that a more realistic shading model using ray tracing and Monte Carlo integration substantially improves this decomposition. The challenge is making that model usable inside gradient-based reconstruction.

Monte Carlo integration produces noisy estimates, even with many samples, and this noise makes optimization difficult. The authors incorporate multiple importance sampling and denoising into an inverse rendering pipeline. These additions improve convergence and allow optimization with low sample counts, addressing the computational and numerical difficulty introduced by the more realistic renderer.

The resulting method jointly reconstructs explicit triangle-mesh geometry, materials, and lighting. It substantially improves separation of material properties from illumination compared with previous work. This matters because a reconstructed scene should account for which aspects of appearance come from the surface and which come from the light. The results support the authors' argument that denoising can be a useful integral component of high-quality inverse rendering.
summary.tldr: Combining realistic Monte Carlo rendering with sampling and denoising improves joint reconstruction of scene geometry, materials, and lighting.

title: Shape, Light, and Material Decomposition from Images using Monte Carlo Rendering and Denoising

abstract: We propose an online training procedure for a transformer-based automated theorem prover. Our approach leverages a new search algorithm, HyperTree Proof Search (HTPS), that learns from previous proof searches through online training, allowing it to generalize to domains far from the training distribution. We report detailed ablations of our pipeline’s main components by studying performance on three environments of increasing complexity. In particular, we show that with HTPS alone, a model trained on annotated proofs manages to prove 65.4% of a held-out set of Metamath theorems, significantly outperforming the previous state of the art of 56.5% by GPT-f. Online training on these unproved theorems increases accuracy to 82.6%. With a similar computational budget, we improve the state of the art on the Lean-based miniF2F-curriculum dataset from 31% to 42% proving accuracy.

It combines a transformer-based model with HyperTree Proof Search, or HTPS, and an online training procedure. This creates a way for the prover to keep improving as it encounters the theorems it is trying to solve.

The authors separate the benefits of search from those of online learning. The results support both the search algorithm and the online training procedure, including the approach’s ability to generalize to domains far from its training distribution.
summary.tldr: HyperTree Proof Search combines stronger proof search with online learning from previous searches to improve automated theorem proving.

title: HyperTree Proof Search for Neural Theorem Proving

abstract: We investigate the problem of testing whether a discrete probability distribution over an ordered domain is a histogram on a specified number of bins. One of the most common tools for the succinct approximation of data, $k$-histograms over $[n]$, are probability distributions that are piecewise constant over a set of $k$ intervals. Given samples from an unknown distribution $\mathbf p$ on $[n]$, we want to distinguish between the cases that $\mathbf p$ is a $k$-histogram versus far from any $k$-histogram, in total variation distance. Our main result is a sample near-optimal and computationally efficient algorithm for this testing problem, and a nearly-matching (within logarithmic factors) sample complexity lower bound, showing that the testing problem has sample complexity $\widetilde \Theta (\sqrt{nk} / \epsilon + k / \epsilon^2 + \sqrt{n} / \epsilon^2)$.

paragraphs: A histogram distribution assigns constant probability within each of several intervals of an ordered domain. This paper studies whether samples alone can reveal if an unknown distribution has that structure. Specifically, the task is to distinguish a distribution representable with k intervals from one that is far from every such distribution in total variation distance.

The authors provide a computationally efficient testing algorithm whose sample requirements are nearly optimal. They also establish a lower bound showing that any tester needs nearly as many samples, with the upper and lower results differing only by logarithmic factors. This pairs an achievable procedure with evidence about the fundamental difficulty of the problem.

For a domain of size n and distance threshold epsilon, the sample complexity scales, up to logarithmic factors, as sqrt(nk)/epsilon + k/epsilon² + sqrt(n)/epsilon². The expression makes the roles of domain size, histogram complexity, and testing resolution explicit. The result characterizes the resources needed to test histogram structure, rather than requiring a full reconstruction of the unknown distribution.
summary.tldr: An efficient histogram-distribution tester and a nearly matching lower bound characterize the required sample count up to logarithmic factors.

title: Nearly-Tight Bounds for Testing Histogram Distributions

abstract: Although a vast body of literature relates to image segmentation methods that use deep neural networks (DNNs), less attention has been paid to assessing the statistical reliability of segmentation results. In this study, we interpret the segmentation results as hypotheses driven by DNN (called DNN-driven hypotheses) and propose a method to quantify the reliability of these hypotheses within a statistical hypothesis testing framework. To this end, we introduce a conditional selective inference (SI) framework---a new statistical inference framework for data-driven hypotheses that has recently received considerable attention---to compute exact (non-asymptotic) valid p-values for the segmentation results. To use the conditional SI framework for DNN-based segmentation, we develop a new SI algorithm based on the homotopy method, which enables us to derive the exact (non-asymptotic) sampling distribution of DNN-driven hypothesis. We conduct several experiments to demonstrate the performance of the proposed method.

paragraphs: A neural network can divide an image into regions, but producing a segmentation does not by itself quantify its statistical reliability. This paper treats the segmentation result as a hypothesis selected by the network. It then asks how to assess that hypothesis within a formal statistical testing framework.

The authors use conditional selective inference, which addresses hypotheses chosen using data. This is relevant because the network's output determines which segmentation hypothesis is evaluated. The method computes valid, exact p-values without relying on a large-sample approximation. The resulting significance assessment is attached to the network-driven hypothesis.

To make selective inference work for neural-network segmentation, the paper develops a homotopy-based algorithm that derives the hypothesis's exact sampling distribution. Several experiments demonstrate the proposed method's performance. The contribution adds a statistical assessment layer to segmentation: it evaluates the significance of a selected result rather than only producing the regions. Its central technical advance is making non-asymptotic inference available for these data-driven hypotheses.
summary.tldr: A homotopy-based selective inference method computes exact valid p-values for hypotheses derived from neural-network image segmentations.

title: Quantifying Statistical Significance of Neural Network-based Image Segmentation by Selective Inference

abstract: Rehearsal approaches enjoy immense popularity with Continual Learning (CL) practitioners. These methods collect samples from previously encountered data distributions in a small memory buffer; subsequently, they repeatedly optimize on the latter to prevent catastrophic forgetting. This work draws attention to a hidden pitfall of this widespread practice: repeated optimization on a small pool of data inevitably leads to tight and unstable decision boundaries, which are a major hindrance to generalization. To address this issue, we propose Lipschitz-DrivEn Rehearsal (LiDER), a surrogate objective that induces smoothness in the backbone network by constraining its layer-wise Lipschitz constants w.r.t. replay examples. By means of extensive experiments, we show that applying LiDER delivers a stable performance gain to several state-of-the-art rehearsal CL methods across multiple datasets, both in the presence and absence of pre-training. Through additional ablative experiments, we highlight peculiar aspects of buffer overfitting in CL and better characterize the effect produced by LiDER. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/LiDER.

paragraphs: Continual learning systems often retain a small buffer of past examples and replay them during later training to reduce forgetting. This paper identifies a problem with that practice: repeatedly optimizing on a small memory can create tight, unstable decision boundaries. Remembering the stored examples can therefore come at the expense of generalization beyond that buffer.

The proposed method, Lipschitz-Driven Rehearsal, adds a surrogate objective that encourages smoother behavior in the network backbone. It constrains layer-wise Lipschitz constants with respect to replay examples, controlling how strongly layers can respond to changes around those examples. The approach targets the network's sensitivity during rehearsal.

Across multiple datasets, adding LiDER produces stable performance gains for several leading rehearsal methods, both with and without pretraining. Additional ablation experiments examine buffer overfitting and help characterize the regularizer's effect. These findings support smoothness control as a useful complement to retaining past data: the way a model learns from its memory matters alongside the presence of the memory itself.
summary.tldr: LiDER constrains network sensitivity around replay examples to reduce buffer overfitting and improve rehearsal-based continual learning.

title: On the Effectiveness of Lipschitz-Driven Rehearsal in Continual Learning

abstract: Neural network-based Combinatorial Optimization (CO) methods have shown promising results in solving various NP-complete (NPC) problems without relying on hand-crafted domain knowledge. This paper broadens the current scope of neural solvers for NPC problems by introducing a new graph-based diffusion framework, namely DIFUSCO. It formulates NPC problems into a discrete {0, 1}-vector space and uses graph-based denoising diffusion models to generate high-quality solutions. Specifically, we explore diffusion models with Gaussian and Bernoulli noise, respectively, and also introduce an effective inference schedule to improve the generation quality. We evaluate our methods on two well-studied combinatorial optimization problems: Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and Maximal Independent Set (MIS). Experimental results show that DIFUSCO strongly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art neural solvers, improving the performance gap between ground-truth and neural solvers from 1.76% to 0.46% on TSP-500, from 2.46% to 1.17% on TSP-1000, and from 3.19% to 2.58% on TSP-10000. For the MIS problem, DIFUSCO outperforms the previous state-of-the-art neural solver on the challenging SATLIB benchmark. Our code is available at [this url](https://github.com/Edward-Sun/DIFUSCO).

title: DIFUSCO: Graph-based Diffusion Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: The applications of direct policy search in reinforcement learning and continuous control have received increasing attention.In this work, we present novel theoretical results on the complexity of derivative-free policy optimization on an important class of robust control tasks, namely the structured $H_\infty$ synthesis with static output feedback. Optimal $H_\infty$ synthesis under structural constraints leads to a constrained nonconvex nonsmooth problem and is typicallyaddressed using subgradient-based policy search techniques that are built upon the concept of Goldstein subdifferential or other notions of enlarged subdifferential. In this paper, we study the complexity of finding $(\delta,\epsilon)$-stationary points for such nonsmooth robust control design tasks using policy optimization methods which can only access the zeroth-order oracle (i.e. the $H_\infty$ norm of the closed-loop system). First, we study the exact oracle setting and identify the coerciveness of the cost function to prove high-probability feasibility/complexity bounds for derivative-free policy optimization on this problem. Next, we derive a sample complexity result for the multi-input multi-output (MIMO) $H_\infty$-norm estimation. We combine this with our analysis to obtain the first sample complexity of model-free, trajectory-based, zeroth-order policy optimization on finding $(\delta,\epsilon)$-stationary points for structured $H_\infty$ control. Numerical results are also provided to demonstrate our theory.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes direct policy search for structured H-infinity control with static output feedback. Structural constraints make the optimization problem constrained, nonconvex, and nonsmooth. The authors ask how much computation or trajectory data is needed when the optimizer can evaluate control performance but cannot access its derivatives.

They first study an exact oracle that returns the closed-loop system's H-infinity norm. Using a property of the cost function called coerciveness, they establish high-probability bounds on feasibility and optimization complexity. The target is a specified form of approximate stationarity, expressed through delta and epsilon, rather than a guarantee of finding the globally best controller.

The authors next derive a sample complexity result for estimating the H-infinity norm of systems with multiple inputs and outputs. Combining this estimator with the optimization analysis yields their stated first sample complexity guarantee for model-free, trajectory-based, zeroth-order optimization in this structured control setting. Numerical results illustrate the theory. The combined analysis connects idealized access to exact performance values with the more practical task of estimating those values from system trajectories.
summary.tldr: The paper gives complexity guarantees for derivative-free structured H-infinity control, including a trajectory-based route to approximate stationary points.

title: Complexity of Derivative-Free Policy Optimization for Structured $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Control

abstract: Wasserstein distributionally robust estimators have emerged as powerful models for prediction and decision-making under uncertainty. These estimators provide attractive generalization guarantees: the robust objective obtained from the training distribution is an exact upper bound on the true risk with high probability. However, existing guarantees either suffer from the curse of dimensionality, are restricted to specific settings, or lead to spurious error terms. In this paper, we show that these generalization guarantees actually hold on general classes of models, do not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, and can even cover distribution shifts at testing. We also prove that these results carry over to the newly-introduced regularized versions of Wasserstein distributionally robust problems.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust prediction addresses uncertainty about the distribution on which a model will be used. For Wasserstein robust estimators, an especially useful guarantee links the training objective to true risk: with high probability, the robust objective itself is an upper bound. That makes the objective meaningful as a bound on performance beyond the training distribution.

Existing results supporting this relationship have faced several obstacles. Some deteriorate with dimension, some apply only in narrow settings, and others introduce additional error terms. This paper proves that exact upper-bound guarantees hold for general classes of models without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. The results can also cover distribution shifts at test time.

The authors further extend the guarantees to regularized Wasserstein robust problems. This matters because the theoretical relationship between the objective and true risk survives that change in formulation. The result remains a high-probability statement for the model classes and shifts covered by the theory; exactness describes the upper bound, rather than an assertion that the objective equals the true risk.
summary.tldr: The paper proves exact high-probability risk bounds for broad classes of Wasserstein robust models, including regularized versions, without dimensionality-driven deterioration.

title: Exact Generalization Guarantees for (Regularized) Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Models

abstract: The neural network structures of generative models and their corresponding inference models paired in variational autoencoders (VAEs) play a critical role in the models' generative performance. However, powerful VAE network structures are hand-crafted and fixed prior to training, resulting in a one-size-fits-all approach that requires heavy computation to tune for given data. Moreover, existing VAE regularization methods largely overlook the importance of network structures and fail to prevent overfitting in deep VAE models with cascades of hidden layers. To address these issues, we propose a Bayesian inference framework that automatically adapts VAE network structures to data and prevent overfitting as they grow deeper. We model the number of hidden layers with a beta process to infer the most plausible encoding/decoding network depths warranted by data and perform layer-wise dropout regularization with a conjugate Bernoulli process. We develop a scalable estimator that performs joint inference on both VAE network structures and latent variables. Our experiments show that the inference framework effectively prevents overfitting in both shallow and deep VAE models, yielding state-of-the-art performance. We demonstrate that our framework is compatible with different types of VAE backbone networks and can be applied to various VAE variants, further improving their performance.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder pairs a network that generates data with one that infers latent representations. The structures of both networks affect performance, yet their depths are usually chosen before training. Finding a suitable fixed structure can require substantial tuning, and the abstract argues that existing regularization methods do not adequately address overfitting in deeper networks.

AdaVAE makes network structure part of Bayesian inference. It uses a beta process to model how many hidden layers the data justify in the encoding and decoding networks. A paired Bernoulli process supplies layer-wise dropout regularization. These findings suggest that adapting depth to data can be a useful part of VAE training, rather than leaving structural decisions entirely to advance manual tuning.
summary.tldr: AdaVAE jointly learns VAE depth and latent variables through Bayesian inference, with experiments showing reduced overfitting and improved performance.

title: AdaVAE: Bayesian Structural Adaptation for Variational Autoencoders

abstract: We consider the problem of identifying the best arm in stochastic Multi-Armed Bandits (MABs) using a fixed sampling budget. Characterizing the minimal instance-specific error probability for this problem constitutes one of the important remaining open problems in MABs. When arms are selected using a static sampling strategy, the error probability decays exponentially with the number of samples at a rate that can be explicitly derived via Large Deviation techniques. Analyzing the performance of algorithms with adaptive sampling strategies is however much more challenging. In this paper, we establish a connection between the Large Deviation Principle (LDP) satisfied by the empirical proportions of arm draws and that satisfied by the empirical arm rewards. This connection holds for any adaptive algorithm, and is leveraged (i) to improve error probability upper bounds of some existing algorithms, such as the celebrated SR (Successive Rejects) algorithm \cite{audibert2010best}, and (ii) to devise and analyze new algorithms. In particular, we present CR (Continuous Rejects), a truly adaptive algorithm that can reject arms in {\it any} round based on the observed empirical gaps between the rewards of various arms. Applying our Large Deviation results, we prove that CR enjoys better performance guarantees than existing algorithms, including SR. Extensive numerical experiments confirm this observation.

paragraphs: With a fixed sampling budget, best-arm identification asks which uncertain option has the highest expected reward. The challenge is distributing observations so that the final choice is unlikely to be wrong. Error rates are easier to analyze when the sampling plan is fixed in advance; adaptive sampling makes that analysis substantially harder.

The paper connects large-deviation behavior of the observed sampling proportions to that of the observed arm rewards. Large-deviation analysis describes how probabilities of unusual outcomes shrink as more samples are collected. The connection applies to any adaptive algorithm and gives the authors a way to sharpen error upper bounds for existing methods, including Successive Rejects.

The same framework motivates Continuous Rejects, which can eliminate an arm in any round using observed reward gaps. This gives the algorithm flexibility to react as evidence accumulates. The authors prove stronger performance guarantees than those of existing algorithms, including Successive Rejects, and report supporting numerical experiments. The work advances adaptive error analysis without claiming to fully characterize the minimum instance-specific error probability.
summary.tldr: A large-deviation framework sharpens adaptive best-arm error guarantees and supports Continuous Rejects, an algorithm that can eliminate arms at any round.

title: Best Arm Identification with Fixed Budget: A Large Deviation Perspective

abstract: Large-scale pre-trained models have achieved remarkable success in many applications, but how to leverage them to improve the prediction reliability of downstream models is undesirably under-explored. Moreover, modern neural networks have been found to be poorly calibrated and make overconfident predictions regardless of inherent sample difficulty and data uncertainty. To address this issue, we propose to utilize large-scale pre-trained models to guide downstream model training with sample difficulty-aware entropy regularization. Pre-trained models that have been exposed to large-scale datasets and do not overfit the downstream training classes enable us to measure each training sample’s difficulty via feature-space Gaussian modeling and relative Mahalanobis distance computation. Importantly, by adaptively penalizing overconfident prediction based on the sample difficulty, we simultaneously improve accuracy and uncertainty calibration across challenging benchmarks (e.g., +0.55% ACC and −3.7% ECE on ImageNet1k using ResNet34), consistently surpassing competitive baselines for reliable prediction. The improved uncertainty estimate further improves selective classification (abstaining from erroneous predictions) and out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: This paper uses large pretrained models to help downstream classifiers express more reliable confidence. The problem is that neural networks can make overconfident predictions without adequately reflecting sample difficulty or uncertainty. The proposed approach makes the training penalty for overconfidence depend on how difficult each example appears to be.

Difficulty is estimated from pretrained feature representations using Gaussian modeling and relative Mahalanobis distance. The approach relies on pretrained models that have seen large datasets and do not overfit the downstream training classes. These estimates guide sample-dependent entropy regularization, adapting the pressure against overconfident predictions during downstream training.

The authors report simultaneous improvements in accuracy and uncertainty calibration across challenging benchmarks, consistently exceeding competitive baselines. For ResNet34 on ImageNet1k, they report a 0.55% increase in accuracy and a 3.7% reduction in expected calibration error. Improved uncertainty estimates also benefit selective classification, where a model can abstain, and out-of-distribution detection. The findings connect information in pretrained features to more dependable downstream confidence.
summary.tldr: Pretrained feature-based difficulty estimates guide an adaptive overconfidence penalty that improves downstream accuracy and calibration.

title: Learning Sample Difficulty from Pre-trained Models for Reliable Prediction

abstract: Homophily principle, i.e., nodes with the same labels are more likely to be connected, has been believed to be the main reason for the performance superiority of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) over Neural Networks on node classification tasks. Recent research suggests that, even in the absence of homophily, the advantage of GNNs still exists as long as nodes from the same class share similar neighborhood patterns. However, this argument only considers intra-class Node Distinguishability (ND) but neglects inter-class ND, which provides incomplete understanding of homophily on GNNs. In this paper, we first demonstrate such deficiency with examples and argue that an ideal situation for ND is to have smaller intra-class ND than inter-class ND. To formulate this idea and study ND deeply, we propose Contextual Stochastic Block Model for Homophily (CSBM-H) and define two metrics, Probabilistic Bayes Error (PBE) and negative generalized Jeffreys divergence, to quantify ND. With the metrics, we visualize and analyze how graph filters, node degree distributions and class variances influence ND, and investigate the combined effect of intra- and inter-class ND. Besides, we discovered the mid-homophily pitfall, which occurs widely in graph datasets. Furthermore, we verified that, in real-work tasks, the superiority of GNNs is indeed closely related to both intra- and inter-class ND regardless of homophily levels. Grounded in this observation, we propose a new hypothesis-testing based performance metric beyond homophily, which is non-linear, feature-based and can provide statistical threshold value for GNNs' the superiority. Experiments indicate that it is significantly more effective than the existing homophily metrics on revealing the advantage and disadvantage of graph-aware modes on both synthetic and benchmark real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A common explanation for graph neural network performance is homophily: connected nodes tend to share labels. Another explanation emphasizes similar neighborhood patterns among nodes of the same class. This paper argues that either account is incomplete unless it also considers how different those nodes are from nodes in other classes.

The authors propose that a favorable representation has less variation within classes than separation between classes. They develop a contextual stochastic block model and two measures of node distinguishability to investigate this relationship. The analysis examines graph filters, node-degree distributions, and class variances, and identifies a mid-homophily pitfall that occurs widely in graph datasets.

Experiments on real tasks link the advantage of graph neural networks to both within-class and between-class distinguishability across homophily levels. Building on this observation, the authors introduce a nonlinear, feature-based metric using hypothesis testing and a statistical threshold. In synthetic and real-world benchmark experiments, it reveals advantages and disadvantages of graph-aware models more effectively than existing homophily measures.
summary.tldr: The paper explains GNN usefulness through both within-class similarity and between-class separation, producing a metric that outperforms homophily measures in reported experiments.

title: When Do Graph Neural Networks Help with Node Classification? Investigating the Homophily Principle on Node Distinguishability

abstract: Cooperatively utilizing both ego-vehicle and infrastructure sensor data can significantly enhance autonomous driving perception abilities. However, the uncertain temporal asynchrony and limited communication conditions that are present in traffic environments can lead to fusion misalignment and constrain the exploitation of infrastructure data. To address these issues in vehicle-infrastructure cooperative 3D (VIC3D) object detection, we propose the Feature Flow Net (FFNet), a novel cooperative detection framework. FFNet is a flow-based feature fusion framework that uses a feature flow prediction module to predict future features and compensate for asynchrony. Instead of transmitting feature maps extracted from still-images, FFNet transmits feature flow, leveraging the temporal coherence of sequential infrastructure frames. Furthermore, we introduce a self-supervised training approach that enables FFNet to generate feature flow with feature prediction ability from raw infrastructure sequences. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing cooperative detection methods while only requiring about 1/100 of the transmission cost of raw data and covers all latency in one model on the DAIR-V2X dataset. The code is available https://github.com/haibao-yu/FFNet-VIC3D.

paragraphs: Combining vehicle sensors with infrastructure sensors can improve perception, but information may arrive at different times and communication capacity is limited. Misaligned observations can weaken the benefit of cooperation. Feature Flow Net addresses both problems in cooperative 3D object detection by modeling how infrastructure features change over time.

Its prediction module uses feature flow to estimate future features and compensate for temporal mismatch. The system transmits this flow instead of feature maps extracted from individual still images, drawing on continuity across successive infrastructure frames. The result connects communication efficiency with temporal prediction: information about feature evolution can help synchronize shared perception while limiting the amount of data that must be transmitted.
summary.tldr: FFNet shares predictive feature flow to compensate for sensor asynchrony and improve cooperative 3D detection with reduced transmission cost.

title: Flow-Based Feature Fusion for Vehicle-Infrastructure Cooperative 3D Object Detection

abstract: Modern recording techniques now allow us to record from distinct neuronal populations in different brain networks. However, especially as we consider multiple (more than two) populations, new conceptual and statistical frameworks are needed to characterize the multi-dimensional, concurrent flow of signals among these populations. Here, we develop a dimensionality reduction framework that determines (1) the subset of populations described by each latent dimension, (2) the direction of signal flow among those populations, and (3) how those signals evolve over time within and across experimental trials. We illustrate these features in simulation, and further validate the method by applying it to previously studied recordings from neuronal populations in macaque visual areas V1 and V2. Then we study interactions across select laminar compartments of areas V1, V2, and V3d, recorded simultaneously with multiple Neuropixels probes. Our approach uncovered signatures of selective communication across these three areas that related to their retinotopic alignment. This work advances the study of concurrent signaling across multiple neuronal populations.

paragraphs: Recording several neuronal populations at once creates a challenge beyond describing interactions between pairs. Signals may involve different subsets of populations and evolve concurrently over time. This paper develops a dimensionality-reduction framework that summarizes this activity while retaining information about which populations participate and the direction of signal flow.

Each latent dimension describes a subset of populations, the flow among them, and how its signal evolves within and across experimental trials. The authors illustrate these capabilities in simulations and validate the method using previously studied recordings from macaque visual areas V1 and V2. This connects the framework's intended behavior to both controlled examples and neural recordings.

They then analyze simultaneous Neuropixels recordings from selected layers of V1, V2, and V3d. The method uncovers signatures of selective communication related to retinotopic alignment, the correspondence of represented visual locations across areas. These findings demonstrate how a shared framework can describe concurrent signaling patterns across more than two populations while preserving their selective structure.
summary.tldr: A dimensionality-reduction framework identifies participating populations, signal-flow direction, and temporal patterns in concurrent neural activity.

title: Uncovering motifs of concurrent signaling across multiple neuronal populations

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are often used for tasks involving the 3D geometry of a given graph, such as molecular dynamics simulation. While incorporating Euclidean distance into Message Passing Neural Networks (referred to as Vanilla DisGNN) is a straightforward way to learn the geometry, it has been demonstrated that Vanilla DisGNN is geometrically incomplete. In this work, we first construct families of novel and symmetric geometric graphs that Vanilla DisGNN cannot distinguish even when considering all-pair distances, which greatly expands the existing counterexample families. Our counterexamples show the inherent limitation of Vanilla DisGNN to capture symmetric geometric structures. We then propose $k$-DisGNNs, which can effectively exploit the rich geometry contained in the distance matrix. We demonstrate the high expressive power of $k$-DisGNNs from three perspectives: 1. They can learn high-order geometric information that cannot be captured by Vanilla DisGNN. 2. They can unify some existing well-designed geometric models. 3. They are universal function approximators from geometric graphs to scalars (when $k\geq 2$) and vectors (when $k\geq 3$). Most importantly, we establish a connection between geometric deep learning (GDL) and traditional graph representation learning (GRL), showing that those highly expressive GNN models originally designed for GRL can also be applied to GDL with impressive performance, and that existing complicated, equivariant models are not the only solution. Experiments verify our theory. Our $k$-DisGNNs achieve many new state-of-the-art results on MD17.

They are universal function approximators from geometric graphs to scalars (when $k\geq 2$) and vectors (when $k\geq 3$). Most importantly, we establish a connection between geometric deep learning (GDL) and traditional graph representation learning (GRL), showing that those highly expressive GNN models originally designed for GRL can also be applied to GDL with impressive performance, and that existing complicated, equivariant models are not the only solution. Experiments verify our theory. Our $k$-DisGNNs achieve many new state-of-the-art results on MD17.

paragraphs: Providing a graph neural network with distances does not ensure it can distinguish different geometric structures. The authors construct families of symmetric geometric graphs that ordinary distance-based message passing cannot tell apart, even when every pairwise distance is available. These examples expose limitations in how the network processes geometry.

The proposed k-DisGNN models extract richer geometric information from the distance matrix. The authors show that these models can learn higher-order information missed by the ordinary approach and encompass some existing geometric architectures. They also establish universal approximation results for scalar outputs when k is at least two and vector outputs when k is at least three.

These results connect geometric learning with expressive graph representation methods originally developed for other graph tasks. They show that complicated equivariant architectures are not the only available route to strong geometric models. Experiments support the theoretical analysis, and k-DisGNNs obtain multiple state-of-the-art results on MD17. The central lesson is that the architecture's use of distances matters alongside the distances themselves.
summary.tldr: Higher-order k-DisGNNs exploit distance matrices more expressively than ordinary message passing, with approximation guarantees and strong MD17 results.

title: Is Distance Matrix Enough for Geometric Deep Learning?

abstract: Classic network clustering tackles the problem of identifying sets of nodes (communities) that have similar connection patterns. However, in many scenarios nodes also have attributes that are correlated and can also be used to identify node clusters. Thus, network information (edges) and node information (attributes) can be jointly leveraged to design high-performance clustering algorithms. Under a general model for the network and node attributes, this work establishes an information-theoretic criteria for the exact recovery of community labels and characterizes a phase transition determined by the Chernoff-Hellinger divergence of the model. The criteria shows how network and attribute information can be exchanged in order to have exact recovery (e.g., more reliable network information requires less reliable attribute information). This work also presents an iterative clustering algorithm that maximizes the joint likelihood, assuming that the probability distribution of network interactions and node attributes belong to exponential families. This covers a broad range of possible interactions (e.g., edges with weights) and attributes (e.g., non-Gaussian models) while also exploring the connection between exponential families and Bregman divergences. Extensive numerical experiments using synthetic and real data indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms algorithms that leverage only network or only attribute information as well as recently proposed algorithms that perform clustering using both sources of information. The contributions of this work provide insights into the fundamental limits and practical techniques for inferring community labels on node-attributed networks.

The paper thus connects a theoretical account of when recovery is possible with a practical approach for combining network structure and node information.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes exact community recovery from edges and node attributes and develops a joint-likelihood clustering algorithm.

title: Exact recovery and Bregman hard clustering of node-attributed Stochastic Block Model

abstract: We explore the matrix sensing problem from near-isotropic linear measurements, distributed across a network of agents modeled as an undirected graph, with no centralized node. We provide the first study of statistical, computational/communication guarantees for a decentralized gradient algorithm that solves the (nonconvex) Burer-Monteiro type decomposition associated to the low-rank matrix estimation. With small random initialization, the algorithm displays an approximate two-phase convergence: (i) a spectral phase that aligns the iterates' column space with the underlying low-rank matrix, mimicking centralized spectral initialization (not directly implementable over networks); and (ii) a local refinement phase that diverts the iterates from certain degenerate saddle points, while ensuring swift convergence to the underlying low-rank matrix. Central to our analysis is a novel "in-network" Restricted Isometry Property which accommodates for the decentralized nature of the optimization, revealing an intriguing interplay between sample complexity and network connectivity, topology, and communication complexity.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a network of agents can recover a low-rank matrix from linear measurements without a central coordinator. The proposed analysis covers a decentralized gradient algorithm that works with a nonconvex factorization of the unknown matrix.

This resembles centralized spectral initialization, which is not directly implementable over the network. A subsequent refinement stage moves iterates away from certain degenerate saddle points while supporting fast convergence toward the target.

The authors provide statistical, computational, and communication guarantees for this procedure. Their key analytical tool is an in-network Restricted Isometry Property that incorporates decentralized optimization into the measurement analysis. It exposes connections between the number of measurements needed, network connectivity and topology, and communication requirements. Recovery quality and efficiency are therefore analyzed together with the structure of the cooperating network.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes recovery and convergence guarantees for decentralized low-rank matrix sensing, linking measurement requirements to network structure and communication.

title: Decentralized Matrix Sensing: Statistical Guarantees and Fast Convergence

abstract: Large language models of code (Code-LLMs) have recently brought tremendous advances to code completion, a fundamental feature of programming assistance and code intelligence. However, most existing works ignore the possible presence of bugs in the code context for generation, which are inevitable in software development. Therefore, we introduce and study the buggy-code completion problem, inspired by the realistic scenario of real-time code suggestion where the code context contains potential bugs – anti-patterns that can become bugs in the completed program. To systematically study the task, we introduce two datasets: one with synthetic bugs derived from semantics-altering operator changes (buggy-HumanEval) and one with realistic bugs derived from user submissions to coding problems (buggy-FixEval). We find that the presence of potential bugs significantly degrades the generation performance of the high-performing Code-LLMs. For instance, the passing rates of CODEGEN-2B-MONO on test cases of buggy-HumanEval drop more than 50% given a single potential bug in the context. Finally, we investigate several post-hoc methods for mitigating the adverse effect of potential bugs and find that there remains a large gap in post-mitigation performance.

paragraphs: Code-completion models are often evaluated with clean input code, but real programmers may provide unfinished context containing potential bugs. This paper defines buggy-code completion to study whether models can produce correct programs when that context already contains a harmful pattern.

The authors introduce buggy-HumanEval with synthetic bugs created by meaning-changing operator edits and buggy-FixEval with realistic bugs from user submissions. These datasets separate the effects of controlled changes from problems observed in actual programming attempts.

Potential bugs substantially degrade strong code models. For CODEGEN-2B-MONO, one potential bug in buggy-HumanEval context reduces test-passing rates by more than 50%. Several post-hoc mitigation methods leave a large remaining performance gap. The abstract does not imply every context bug causes failure, but demonstrates that clean-context benchmarks can miss a consequential weakness in practical completion behavior.
summary.tldr: Potential bugs in code context sharply reduce completion quality and remain difficult to mitigate.

title: Large Language Models of Code Fail at Completing Code with Potential Bugs

abstract: We present a simple but effective method to measure and mitigate model biases caused by reliance on spurious cues. Instead of requiring costly changes to one's data or model training, our method better utilizes the data one already has by sorting them. Specifically, we rank images within their classes based on spuriosity (the degree to which common spurious cues are present), proxied via deep neural features of an interpretable network. With spuriosity rankings, it is easy to identify minority subpopulations (i.e. low spuriosity images) and assess model bias as the gap in accuracy between high and low spuriosity images. One can even efficiently remove a model's bias at little cost to accuracy by finetuning its classification head on low spuriosity images, resulting in fairer treatment of samples regardless of spuriosity. We demonstrate our method on ImageNet, annotating $5000$ class-feature dependencies ($630$ of which we find to be spurious) and generating a dataset of $325k$ soft segmentations for these features along the way. Having computed spuriosity rankings via the identified spurious neural features, we assess biases for $89$ diverse models and find that class-wise biases are highly correlated across models. Our results suggest that model bias due to spurious feature reliance is influenced far more by what the model is trained on than how it is trained.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can depend on cues that frequently accompany a class without being reliable evidence of it. This paper measures that reliance by sorting images within each class according to how strongly such cues appear. An interpretable network’s deep features provide a proxy for this degree of spuriosity.

The rankings identify low-spuriosity minority groups and allow bias to be measured as the accuracy difference between high- and low-spuriosity images. They also guide a mitigation procedure: finetuning the classification head on low-spuriosity examples. The authors report that this can remove the measured bias with little loss of accuracy, using images already available in the dataset.

On ImageNet, the work annotates 5,000 class-feature dependencies, identifies 630 as spurious, and produces 325,000 soft feature segmentations. Evaluating 89 models reveals that class-specific biases are highly correlated across models. This pattern suggests that training data influence spurious-feature reliance much more strongly than the training approach does. The interpretation remains a conclusion suggested by those comparisons, while the rankings provide a concrete method for inspecting and addressing the measured dependence.
summary.tldr: Ranking images by spurious-cue strength reveals classifier biases and enables inexpensive mitigation through classification-head finetuning.

title: Spuriosity Rankings: Sorting Data to Measure and Mitigate Biases

abstract: Assessing factuality of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is an emerging yet crucial research area, aimed at alerting users to potential errors and guiding the development of more reliable LLMs. Nonetheless, the evaluators assessing factuality necessitate suitable evaluation themselves to gauge progress and foster advancements. This direction remains under-explored, resulting in substantial impediments to the progress of factuality evaluators. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a benchmark for Factuality Evaluation of large Language Models, referred to as FELM. In this benchmark, we collect responses generated from LLMs and annotate factuality labels in a fine-grained manner. Contrary to previous studies that primarily concentrate on the factuality of world knowledge (e.g. information from Wikipedia), FELM focuses on factuality across diverse domains, spanning from world knowledge to math and reasoning. Our annotation is based on text segments, which can help pinpoint specific factual errors. The factuality annotations are further supplemented by predefined error types and reference links that either support or contradict the statement. In our experiments, we investigate the performance of several LLM-based factuality evaluators on FELM, including both vanilla LLMs and those augmented with retrieval mechanisms and chain-of-thought processes. Our findings reveal that while retrieval aids factuality evaluation, current LLMs are far from satisfactory to faithfully detect factual errors.

paragraphs: Systems that check language-model outputs for factual errors also need to be evaluated. FELM supplies a benchmark for this purpose, making the quality of factuality evaluators the object of study. It covers several domains, including world knowledge, mathematics, and reasoning, so evaluation extends beyond checking familiar factual information.

The authors collect language-model responses and annotate factuality at the level of text segments. This makes it possible to identify particular errors within a response instead of assigning only a broad judgment to the whole answer. The annotations also include predefined error categories and reference links that support or contradict statements, giving additional structure to the assessment.

Retrieval helps factuality evaluation, but the tested models remain far from satisfactory at reliably detecting factual errors. The benchmark therefore provides both a way to measure evaluator progress and evidence that useful assistance from retrieval does not resolve the evaluated detection problem.
summary.tldr: FELM benchmarks factuality evaluators across domains and finds that retrieval helps, but tested language models still struggle to detect errors reliably.

title: FELM: Benchmarking Factuality Evaluation of Large Language Models

abstract: Meta-learning enables quick adaptation of machine learning models to new tasks with limited data. While tasks could come from varying distributions in reality, most of the existing meta-learning methods consider both training and testing tasks as from the same uni-component distribution, overlooking two critical needs of a practical solution: (1) the various sources of tasks may compose a multi-component mixture distribution, and (2) novel tasks may come from a distribution that is unseen during meta-training. In this paper, we demonstrate these two challenges can be solved jointly by modeling the density of task instances. We develop a meta-training framework underlain by a novel Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture based Task Generative Model (HTGM). HTGM extends the widely used empirical process of sampling tasks to a theoretical model, which learns task embeddings, fits the mixture distribution of tasks, and enables density-based scoring of novel tasks. The framework is agnostic to the encoder and scales well with large backbone networks. The model parameters are learned end-to-end by maximum likelihood estimation via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets indicate the effectiveness of our method for both sample classification and novel task detection.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to help models adapt quickly to new tasks using little data. A practical complication is that tasks may come from several distinct sources, and a new task may come from a source absent during training. Treating all tasks as samples from one shared component overlooks both possibilities.

The proposed Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture based Task Generative Model represents task instances probabilistically. It learns task embeddings, fits a mixture distribution over tasks, and assigns density-based scores to new tasks. This provides one framework for modeling multiple task populations and detecting tasks that are unfamiliar relative to the learned distribution.

Training uses maximum likelihood estimation through an Expectation-Maximization algorithm, with the parameters learned end to end. The framework can work with different encoders and scales to large backbone networks. Benchmark experiments support its effectiveness for both classifying samples and detecting novel tasks, linking rapid adaptation with an explicit model of where tasks come from.
summary.tldr: HTGM models multiple task populations with a hierarchical Gaussian mixture to support classification and detection of unfamiliar tasks.

title: Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture based Task Generative Model for Robust Meta-Learning

abstract: Robustness to distribution shift has become a growing concern for text and image models as they transition from research subjects to deployment in the real world. However, high-quality benchmarks for distribution shift in tabular machine learning tasks are still lacking despite the widespread real-world use of tabular data and differences in the models used for tabular data in comparison to text and images. As a consequence, the robustness of tabular models to distribution shift is poorly understood. To address this issue, we introduce TableShift, a distribution shift benchmark for tabular data. TableShift contains 15 binary classification tasks in total, each with an associated shift, and includes a diverse set of data sources, prediction targets, and distribution shifts. The benchmark covers domains including finance, education, public policy, healthcare, and civic participation, and is accessible using only a few lines of Python code via the TableShift API. We conduct a large-scale study comparing several state-of-the-art tabular data models alongside robust learning and domain generalization methods on the benchmark tasks. Our study demonstrates (1) a linear trend between in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) accuracy; (2) domain robustness methods can reduce shift gaps but at the cost of reduced ID accuracy; (3) a strong relationship between shift gap (difference between ID and OOD performance) and shifts in the label distribution. The benchmark data, Python package, model implementations, and more information about TableShift are available at https://github.com/mlfoundations/tableshift and https://tableshift.org .

paragraphs: Models trained on tables often encounter deployment data that differ from their training data. Despite the widespread use of tabular prediction, its robustness under such changes has been less well characterized than robustness for images and text. TableShift supplies a common benchmark for studying this problem across 15 binary classification tasks, each paired with a distribution shift.

The tasks span finance, education, public policy, healthcare, and civic participation. The authors compare leading tabular models with robust learning and domain generalization methods. Across this study, accuracy on familiar data and accuracy on shifted data follow a linear trend. Methods designed for domain robustness can narrow the performance gap, but the observed improvement comes with reduced accuracy on familiar data.

The study also finds a strong relationship between performance gaps and changes in the label distribution. These findings make a smaller shift gap something to interpret alongside both underlying accuracies. The released benchmark and Python interface provide a shared basis for examining these tradeoffs across different prediction problems.
summary.tldr: TableShift benchmarks 15 tabular classification tasks and reveals empirical relationships among distribution shifts, accuracy gaps, and robustness tradeoffs.

title: Benchmarking Distribution Shift in Tabular Data with TableShift

abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithms such as AlphaGo and MuZero have achieved superhuman performance in many challenging tasks. However, the computational complexity of MCTS-based algorithms is influenced by the size of the search space. To address this issue, we propose a novel probability tree state abstraction (PTSA) algorithm to improve the search efficiency of MCTS. A general tree state abstraction with path transitivity is defined. In addition, the probability tree state abstraction is proposed for fewer mistakes during the aggregation step. Furthermore, the theoretical guarantees of the transitivity and aggregation error bound are justified. To evaluate the effectiveness of the PTSA algorithm, we integrate it with state-of-the-art MCTS-based algorithms, such as Sampled MuZero and Gumbel MuZero. Experimental results on different tasks demonstrate that our method can accelerate the training process of state-of-the-art algorithms with 10%-45% search space reduction.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo Tree Search explores possible future decisions through a search tree, and its computational demands depend on the size of that search space. This paper proposes probability tree state abstraction, or PTSA, to make that exploration more efficient. The central idea is to aggregate states in the tree, reducing the space that the search algorithm must handle.

Aggregation introduces a correctness question: simplifying the tree can combine states in ways that create errors. The authors first define a general tree abstraction with a property called path transitivity. They then introduce a probability-based abstraction intended to make fewer aggregation mistakes, and provide theoretical guarantees for transitivity and a bound on aggregation error.

The method is integrated with Sampled MuZero and Gumbel MuZero to test its usefulness within existing search systems. Across the evaluated tasks, the authors report faster training alongside search-space reductions of 10% to 45%. These results support abstraction as a practical way to reduce search demands, while the analysis explicitly addresses errors introduced by the simplification.
summary.tldr: PTSA aggregates search-tree states with theoretical error guarantees and reduces search space by 10%–45% in the reported experiments.

title: Accelerating Monte Carlo Tree Search with Probability Tree State Abstraction

abstract: In this paper, we propose the Masked Space-Time Hash encoding (MSTH), a novel method for efficiently reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from multi-view or monocular videos. Based on the observation that dynamic scenes often contain substantial static areas that result in redundancy in storage and computations, MSTH represents a dynamic scene as a weighted combination of a 3D hash encoding and a 4D hash encoding. The weights for the two components are represented by a learnable mask which is guided by an uncertainty-based objective to reflect the spatial and temporal importance of each 3D position. With this design, our method can reduce the hash collision rate by avoiding redundant queries and modifications on static areas, making it feasible to represent a large number of space-time voxels by hash tables with small size.Besides, without the requirements to fit the large numbers of temporally redundant features independently, our method is easier to optimize and converge rapidly with only twenty minutes of training for a 300-frame dynamic scene. We evaluate our method on extensive dynamic scenes. As a result, MSTH obtains consistently better results than previous state-of-the-art methods with only 20 minutes of training time and 130 MB of memory storage.

paragraphs: A dynamic video scene often contains large regions that do not move. Representing those regions independently across time wastes storage and computation. Masked Space-Time Hash encoding, or MSTH, uses this observation to reconstruct dynamic 3D scenes efficiently from either multiple viewpoints or a single-camera video.

The scene representation combines a three-dimensional spatial hash encoding with a four-dimensional space-time encoding. A learned mask controls their relative contributions at each location. An uncertainty-based objective guides that mask to reflect how important spatial and temporal information is there. Avoiding redundant operations in static regions reduces hash collisions and allows many space-time voxels to share compact hash tables more effectively.

The design also removes the need to fit many temporally redundant features independently, making optimization easier. The authors report convergence after twenty minutes for a 300-frame scene. Across their dynamic-scene evaluations, MSTH delivers consistently better results than previous state-of-the-art methods with twenty minutes of training and 130 MB of storage. These findings connect representation efficiency directly to reconstruction quality and training speed.
summary.tldr: MSTH learns where temporal encoding is needed, reducing redundant storage and computation in dynamic 3D reconstruction.

title: Masked Space-Time Hash Encoding for Efficient Dynamic Scene Reconstruction

abstract: In clustering algorithms, the choice of initial centers is crucial for the quality of the learned clusters. We propose a new initialization scheme for the $k$-median problem in the general metric space (e.g., discrete space induced by graphs), based on the construction of metric embedding tree structure of the data. We propose a novel and efficient search algorithm, for good initial centers that can be used subsequently for the local search algorithm. The so-called HST initialization method can produce initial centers achieving lower error than those from another popular method $k$-median++, also with higher efficiency when $k$ is not too small. Our HST initialization can also be easily extended to the setting of differential privacy (DP) to generate private initial centers. We show that the error of applying DP local search followed by our private HST initialization improves previous results on the approximation error, and approaches the lower bound within a small factor. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

The so-called HST initialization method can produce initial centers achieving lower error than those from another popular method $k$-median++, also with higher efficiency when $k$ is not too small. Our HST initialization can also be easily extended to the setting of differential privacy (DP) to generate private initial centers. We show that the error of applying DP local search followed by our private HST initialization improves previous results on the approximation error, and approaches the lower bound within a small factor. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

paragraphs: The centers chosen at the start of a clustering algorithm can strongly affect its final quality. This paper develops an initialization method for k-median clustering in general metric spaces, including discrete spaces defined by graphs. Its aim is to provide good starting centers for subsequent local search, rather than treating initialization as a minor preliminary step.

The method constructs a tree representation through metric embedding and uses a new efficient search algorithm to select centers. Called HST initialization, it can produce lower-error initial centers than k-median++. The authors also report greater efficiency when the requested number of clusters is not too small, making that computational advantage explicitly conditional on k.

The initialization can be extended to differential privacy to generate private starting centers. Combined with differentially private local search, the private method improves previous approximation-error results and approaches a lower bound within a small factor. Experiments support the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The contribution connects better starting points with both ordinary clustering quality and the error guarantees available under privacy constraints.
summary.tldr: Tree-based HST initialization improves k-median starting centers and supports stronger approximation guarantees for differentially private clustering.

title: k-Median Clustering via Metric Embedding: Towards Better Initialization with Differential Privacy

abstract: A truly generalizable approach to rigid segmentation and motion estimation is fundamental to 3D understanding of articulated objects and moving scenes. In view of the closely intertwined relationship between segmentation and motion estimates, we present an SE(3) equivariant architecture and a training strategy to tackle this task in an unsupervised manner. Our architecture is composed of two interconnected, lightweight heads. These heads predict segmentation masks using point-level invariant features and estimate motion from SE(3) equivariant features, all without the need for category information. Our training strategy is unified and can be implemented online, which jointly optimizes the predicted segmentation and motion by leveraging the interrelationships among scene flow, segmentation mask, and rigid transformations. We conduct experiments on four datasets to demonstrate the superiority of our method. The results show that our method excels in both model performance and computational efficiency, with only 0.25M parameters and 0.92G FLOPs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work designed for category-agnostic part-level SE(3) equivariance in dynamic point clouds.

paragraphs: Understanding moving point clouds requires identifying rigid parts and estimating how each part moves. These tasks are closely linked: a proposed grouping of points constrains its motion, and motion helps determine which points belong together. This paper combines them in an unsupervised architecture and training strategy that does not require object-category information.

The architecture has two connected, lightweight heads. One predicts segmentation masks from point-level invariant features; the other estimates motion from SE(3)-equivariant features, which respond consistently to rotations and translations. title: Multi-body SE(3) Equivariance for Unsupervised Rigid Segmentation and Motion Estimation

abstract: We present a novel set of rigorous and computationally efficient topology-based complexity notions that exhibit a strong correlation with the generalization gap in modern deep neural networks (DNNs). DNNs show remarkable generalization properties, yet the source of these capabilities remains elusive, defying the established statistical learning theory. Recent studies have revealed that properties of training trajectories can be indicative of generalization. Building on this insight, state-of-the-art methods have leveraged the topology of these trajectories, particularly their fractal dimension, to quantify generalization. Most existing works compute this quantity by assuming continuous- or infinite-time training dynamics, complicating the development of practical estimators capable of accurately predicting generalization without access to test data. In this paper, we respect the discrete-time nature of training trajectories and investigate the underlying topological quantities that can be amenable to topological data analysis tools. This leads to a new family of reliable topological complexity measures that provably bound the generalization error, eliminating the need for restrictive geometric assumptions. These measures are computationally friendly, enabling us to propose simple yet effective algorithms for computing generalization indices. Moreover, our flexible framework can be extended to different domains, tasks, and architectures. Our experimental results demonstrate that our new complexity measures exhibit a strong correlation with generalization error in industry-standard architectures such as transformers and deep graph networks. Our approach consistently outperforms existing topological bounds across a wide range of datasets, models, and optimizers, highlighting the practical relevance and effectiveness of our complexity measures.

Previous topology-based approaches use properties such as fractal dimension, often assuming continuous-time or infinite-time training dynamics. Those assumptions complicate practical estimation from the finite sequence of updates produced by actual training.

The authors instead work directly with discrete-time trajectories. They develop topological complexity measures suited to topological data analysis and prove that these measures bound generalization error without the restrictive geometric assumptions used previously. Computationally efficient procedures turn the theoretical quantities into practical generalization indices.

Experiments find strong correlations between the proposed measures and generalization error across architectures including transformers and deep graph networks.
