paragraphs: Optimizing a system governed by partial differential equations can require repeatedly solving those equations as design parameters change. This makes tasks such as inferring physical properties or designing structures expensive. The paper proposes Amortized Finite Element Analysis, or AmorFEA, which trains a neural network to supply accurate solutions for use during optimization.

The network learns by minimizing the physical potential energy underlying the equations and their finite element formulation. Consequently, training does not require a collection of example solutions generated by costly conventional solvers. The finite element basis still defines the family of possible solutions, connecting the method to the variational structure of traditional finite element analysis.

The central benefit is to spread the work of learning to solve these equations across subsequent optimization steps. The abstract reports faster PDE-constrained optimization than a traditional workflow combining finite element analysis with the adjoint method. Its contribution is therefore both a solver substitute and a training approach that preserves many finite element advantages while avoiding repeated conventional solves.
summary.tldr: AmorFEA learns PDE solutions directly from physical energy objectives to accelerate optimization that would otherwise require repeated finite element solves.

title: Amortized Finite Element Analysis for Fast PDE-Constrained Optimization

abstract: In practical applications of iterative first-order optimization, the learning rate schedule remains notoriously difficult to understand and expensive to tune. We demonstrate the presence of these subtleties even in the innocuous case when the objective is a convex quadratic. We reinterpret an iterative algorithm from the numerical analysis literature as what we call the Chebyshev learning rate schedule for accelerating vanilla gradient descent, and show that the problem of mitigating instability leads to a fractal ordering of step sizes. We provide some experiments to challenge conventional beliefs about stable learning rates in deep learning: the fractal schedule enables training to converge with locally unstable updates which make negative progress on the objective.

paragraphs: Choosing learning rates is difficult even when an optimization problem appears simple. This paper shows that subtle behavior already arises for convex quadratic objectives, where the mathematical setting is comparatively tractable. It studies how a sequence of step sizes can accelerate ordinary gradient descent and how their ordering affects instability.

The authors reinterpret an existing numerical analysis algorithm as a Chebyshev learning rate schedule. Addressing instability leads them to a fractal ordering of its step sizes. The important object is therefore the schedule as a sequence: understanding the effect of an individual step alone does not explain how the complete optimization procedure behaves.

Experiments challenge the belief that successful deep learning requires every update to be locally stable or immediately improve the objective. With the fractal schedule, training can converge despite updates that temporarily make the objective worse. This demonstrates that local setbacks can coexist with overall convergence in the reported experiments. It does not make arbitrary unstable updates reliable; the finding concerns the structured schedules studied in the paper.
summary.tldr: A fractally ordered Chebyshev learning rate schedule accelerates gradient descent and can permit convergence despite temporarily harmful updates.

title: Acceleration via Fractal Learning Rate Schedules

abstract: Correlation clustering is a central topic in unsupervised learning, with many applications in ML and data mining. In correlation clustering, one receives as input a signed graph and the goal is to partition it to minimize the number of disagreements. In this work we propose a massively parallel computation (MPC) algorithm for this problem that is considerably faster than prior work. In particular, our algorithm uses machines with memory sublinear in the number of nodes in the graph and returns a constant approximation while running only for a constant number of rounds. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm is the first that can provably approximate a clustering problem using only a constant number of MPC rounds in the sublinear memory regime. We complement our analysis with an experimental scalability evaluation of our techniques.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering starts with a graph whose edges indicate whether pairs should belong together or apart. The objective is to partition the nodes while minimizing disagreements with those signs. The paper addresses how to approximate this clustering efficiently when computation is distributed across many machines, each with limited memory.

The proposed algorithm operates in the massively parallel computation model. It uses memory per machine that is sublinear in the number of graph nodes, returns a constant-factor approximation, and needs only a constant number of parallel rounds. These guarantees jointly address solution quality, local storage, and the number of coordinated computation stages. The result is considerably faster than prior work in this setting.

The authors describe it as the first known provable approximation for a clustering problem with constant rounds under this sublinear-memory constraint. They also provide an experimental scalability evaluation. The theoretical contribution is a bounded-quality clustering result that requires few parallel rounds even when individual machines cannot hold a linear amount of node-related information.
summary.tldr: A massively parallel correlation-clustering algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation in constant rounds with sublinear memory per machine.

title: Correlation Clustering in Constant Many Parallel Rounds

abstract: Estimating the gradients for binary variables is a task that arises frequently in various domains, such as training discrete latent variable models. What has been commonly used is a REINFORCE based Monte Carlo estimation method that uses either independent samples or pairs of negatively correlated samples. To better utilize more than two samples, we propose ARMS, an Antithetic REINFORCE-based Multi-Sample gradient estimator. ARMS uses a copula to generate any number of mutually antithetic samples. It is unbiased, has low variance, and generalizes both DisARM, which we show to be ARMS with two samples, and the leave-one-out REINFORCE (LOORF) estimator, which is ARMS with uncorrelated samples. We evaluate ARMS on several datasets for training generative models, and our experimental results show that it outperforms competing methods. We also develop a version of ARMS for optimizing the multi-sample variational bound, and show that it outperforms both VIMCO and DisARM. The code is publicly available.

paragraphs: Learning with binary random variables often requires estimating gradients from samples, as in models with discrete latent variables. REINFORCE provides a Monte Carlo approach, but the way samples are related affects the estimator’s variability. Existing approaches commonly use independent samples or negatively correlated pairs, leaving room to use larger sample groups more effectively.

ARMS extends the negatively correlated approach to any number of samples. It uses a copula to construct their joint dependence and produces an unbiased, low-variance gradient estimator. Unbiasedness means that averaging its randomness recovers the target gradient. The framework also connects existing methods: two samples recover DisARM, while uncorrelated samples recover leave-one-out REINFORCE.

The authors evaluate ARMS while training generative models on several datasets and report improvements over competing methods. They also develop a version for a multi-sample variational bound, which outperforms VIMCO and DisARM in their experiments. The contribution combines a broader sampling construction with empirical evidence that coordinated samples improve gradient estimation for these learning tasks.
summary.tldr: ARMS uses mutually antithetic samples to estimate binary-variable gradients without bias and improves generative-model training in reported experiments.

title: ARMS: Antithetic-REINFORCE-Multi-Sample Gradient for Binary Variables

abstract: There are two main attack models considered in the adversarial robustness literature: black-box and white-box. We consider these threat models as two ends of a fine-grained spectrum, indexed by the number of queries the adversary can ask. Using this point of view we investigate how many queries the adversary needs to make to design an attack that is comparable to the best possible attack in the white-box model. We give a lower bound on that number of queries in terms of entropy of decision boundaries of the classifier. Using this result we analyze two classical learning algorithms on two synthetic tasks for which we prove meaningful security guarantees. The obtained bounds suggest that some learning algorithms are inherently more robust against query-bounded adversaries than others.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness is often discussed using two broad access models: black-box and white-box attacks. This paper introduces a more detailed view by considering how many queries an attacker can make. The central question is how much interaction is needed to construct an attack comparable to the strongest attack available with white-box access.

The authors derive a lower bound on the required number of queries in terms of the entropy of a classifier’s decision boundaries. This connects the attacker’s information-gathering requirements to a mathematical property of the classifier. A query limit becomes an explicit part of the robustness analysis, allowing distinctions that a simple black-box versus white-box division can hide.

Using the bound, the authors analyze two classical learning algorithms on two synthetic tasks and prove meaningful security guarantees in those settings. The resulting bounds suggest that some learning algorithms may be inherently more robust to query-bounded attackers than others. The findings establish a way to reason about restricted adversarial access, with the concrete guarantees attached to the analyzed algorithms and tasks.
summary.tldr: A decision-boundary entropy bound links the queries needed for strong adversarial attacks to provable security in two synthetic learning settings.

title: Query Complexity of Adversarial Attacks

abstract: We propose a hierarchical version of dual averaging for zeroth-order online non-convex optimization {–} i.e., learning processes where, at each stage, the optimizer is facing an unknown non-convex loss function and only receives the incurred loss as feedback. The proposed class of policies relies on the construction of an online model that aggregates loss information as it arrives, and it consists of two principal components: (a) a regularizer adapted to the Fisher information metric (as opposed to the metric norm of the ambient space); and (b) a principled exploration of the problem’s state space based on an adapted hierarchical schedule. This construction enables sharper control of the model’s bias and variance, and allows us to derive tight bounds for both the learner’s static and dynamic regret {–} i.e., the regret incurred against the best dynamic policy in hindsight over the horizon of play.

This construction enables sharper control of the model’s bias and variance, and allows us to derive tight bounds for both the learner’s static and dynamic regret {–} i.e., the regret incurred against the best dynamic policy in hindsight over the horizon of play.

paragraphs: The paper studies online optimization with particularly limited feedback. At each stage, the learner faces an unknown nonconvex loss function and observes only the loss incurred by its own choice. It therefore must learn how to act without receiving gradients or a full description of the current loss landscape.

The proposed hierarchical dual-averaging approach builds an online model that accumulates loss information over time. It has two main components: a regularizer adapted to the Fisher information metric and an exploration schedule organized hierarchically across the state space. The regularizer uses an information-based geometry, while the schedule structures how the learner explores possible choices.

Together, these components enable sharper control of the model’s bias and variance. The authors use that control to derive tight bounds for both static and dynamic regret, covering comparison with a fixed hindsight choice and with a changing hindsight policy. The contribution links limited-feedback exploration and model geometry to theoretical guarantees in a setting where nonconvex losses and unavailable gradients make learning difficult.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical dual averaging combines information-based regularization and structured exploration to obtain tight regret bounds from loss-only feedback.

title: Zeroth-Order Non-Convex Learning via Hierarchical Dual Averaging

abstract: General methods have been developed for estimating causal effects from observational data under causal assumptions encoded in the form of a causal graph. Most of this literature assumes that the underlying causal graph is completely specified. However, only observational data is available in most practical settings, which means that one can learn at most a Markov equivalence class (MEC) of the underlying causal graph. In this paper, we study the problem of causal estimation from a MEC represented by a partial ancestral graph (PAG), which is learnable from observational data. We develop a general estimator for any identifiable causal effects in a PAG. The result fills a gap for an end-to-end solution to causal inference from observational data to effects estimation. Specifically, we develop a complete identification algorithm that derives an influence function for any identifiable causal effects from PAGs. We then construct a double/debiased machine learning (DML) estimator that is robust to model misspecification and biases in nuisance function estimation, permitting the use of modern machine learning techniques. Simulation results corroborate with the theory.

We develop a general estimator for any identifiable causal effects in a PAG. The result fills a gap for an end-to-end solution to causal inference from observational data to effects estimation. Specifically, we develop a complete identification algorithm that derives an influence function for any identifiable causal effects from PAGs. We then construct a double/debiased machine learning (DML) estimator that is robust to model misspecification and biases in nuisance function estimation, permitting the use of modern machine learning techniques. Simulation results corroborate with the theory.

paragraphs: Causal estimation often assumes that a complete causal graph is already known. Observational data, however, may identify only a Markov equivalence class: multiple causal structures compatible with the available evidence. This paper studies estimation when that ambiguity is represented by a partial ancestral graph, or PAG.

The authors develop a general procedure for effects that are identifiable from a PAG. Their complete identification algorithm derives an influence function for any such effect. That function then supports construction of a double, or debiased, machine-learning estimator, connecting graphical identification to an actual estimation method.

The estimator is designed to be robust to model misspecification and biases in estimating nuisance functions, the supporting quantities needed to estimate the causal effect. This permits modern machine-learning methods within the estimation process. Simulations support the theoretical results. The contribution fills a step between learning a graph equivalence class and estimating causal effects, while retaining the essential condition that the requested effect must be identifiable from the PAG.
summary.tldr: The paper connects causal identification from partial ancestral graphs to debiased machine-learning estimation for every identifiable effect.

title: Estimating Identifiable Causal Effects on Markov Equivalence Class through Double Machine Learning

abstract: Training convolutional neural networks with a Lipschitz constraint under the $l_{2}$ norm is useful for provable adversarial robustness, interpretable gradients, stable training, etc. While 1-Lipschitz networks can be designed by imposing a 1-Lipschitz constraint on each layer, training such networks requires each layer to be gradient norm preserving (GNP) to prevent gradients from vanishing. However, existing GNP convolutions suffer from slow training, lead to significant reduction in accuracy and provide no guarantees on their approximations. In this work, we propose a GNP convolution layer called \textbf{S}kew \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{C}onvolution (SOC) that uses the following mathematical property: when a matrix is {\it Skew-Symmetric}, its exponential function is an {\it orthogonal} matrix. To use this property, we first construct a convolution filter whose Jacobian is Skew-Symmetric. Then, we use the Taylor series expansion of the Jacobian exponential to construct the SOC layer that is orthogonal. To efficiently implement SOC, we keep a finite number of terms from the Taylor series and provide a provable guarantee on the approximation error. Our experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show that SOC allows us to train provably Lipschitz, large convolutional neural networks significantly faster than prior works while achieving significant improvements for both standard and certified robust accuracies.

The authors also report significant gains in standard accuracy and certified robust accuracy. The contribution combines a norm-preserving mathematical construction with controlled approximation, linking the desired structural guarantee to an implementation that improves the measured training and prediction outcomes.
summary.tldr: SOC uses skew-symmetric matrix exponentials and bounded approximations to train Lipschitz convolutional networks faster with improved reported accuracy.

title: Skew Orthogonal Convolutions

abstract: We provide a detailed analysis of the dynamics ofthe gradient flow in overparameterized two-layerlinear models. A particularly interesting featureof this model is that its nonlinear dynamics can beexactly solved as a consequence of a large num-ber of conservation laws that constrain the systemto follow particular trajectories. More precisely,the gradient flow preserves the difference of theGramian matrices of the input and output weights,and its convergence to equilibrium depends onboth the magnitude of that difference (which isfixed at initialization) and the spectrum of the data.In addition, and generalizing prior work, we proveour results without assuming small, balanced orspectral initialization for the weights. Moreover,we establish interesting mathematical connectionsbetween matrix factorization problems and differ-ential equations of the Riccati type.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how overparameterized two-layer linear models evolve under gradient flow. Although the model is linear, the dynamics of its parameterized layers are nonlinear. The authors show that these dynamics can nevertheless be solved exactly because numerous conservation laws restrict the trajectories that the weights can follow.

A central conserved quantity is the difference between the Gramian matrices of the input and output weights. Its value is fixed at initialization and remains unchanged during gradient flow. Convergence to equilibrium depends both on the magnitude of this difference and on the spectrum of the data, connecting initial weight structure and data structure to the model’s training trajectory.

The analysis does not require small, balanced, or spectral weight initialization, extending results that relied on such assumptions. The paper also establishes connections between matrix factorization and Riccati-type differential equations. These connections provide a mathematical account of the dynamics in the studied model, showing how conserved structure can make an apparently difficult nonlinear evolution exactly tractable.
summary.tldr: Conservation laws make gradient flow in overparameterized two-layer linear models exactly solvable and reveal how initialization and data affect convergence.

title: Understanding the Dynamics of Gradient Flow in Overparameterized Linear models

abstract: This paper presents a method to explain how the information of each input variable is gradually discarded during the forward propagation in a deep neural network (DNN), which provides new perspectives to explain DNNs. We define two types of entropy-based metrics, i.e. (1) the discarding of pixel-wise information used in the forward propagation, and (2) the uncertainty of the input reconstruction, to measure input information contained by a specific layer from two perspectives. Unlike previous attribution metrics, the proposed metrics ensure the fairness of comparisons between different layers of different DNNs. We can use these metrics to analyze the efficiency of information processing in DNNs, which exhibits strong connections to the performance of DNNs. We analyze information discarding in a pixel-wise manner, which is different from the information bottleneck theory measuring feature information w.r.t. the sample distribution. Experiments have shown the effectiveness of our metrics in analyzing classic DNNs and explaining existing deep-learning techniques. The code is available at https://github.com/haotianSustc/deepinfo.

paragraphs: This paper explains deep networks by measuring how information about individual inputs is discarded as computation moves through successive layers. Its focus is the information a layer retains about particular input variables. That provides a perspective on internal processing that can reveal how the treatment of input information changes throughout a network.

The authors define two entropy-based measures. One captures the discarding of pixel-level information used during forward propagation; the other captures uncertainty about reconstructing the input. These offer complementary views of the input information contained in a layer. The proposed metrics also support fair comparisons across layers and across different networks, making comparisons central to their explanatory value.

Using these measures, the paper studies information-processing efficiency and reports strong connections with network performance. Experiments demonstrate their usefulness for analyzing established networks and explaining existing deep-learning techniques. The analysis operates at the level of individual pixels, distinguishing it from information-bottleneck analysis of features relative to a sample distribution. Its contribution is a comparable, input-specific account of information loss, with evidence connecting that account to network behavior.
summary.tldr: Two entropy-based metrics track pixel-level information loss through networks and support fair comparisons across layers and architectures.

title: Quantification and Analysis of Layer-wise and Pixel-wise Information Discarding

abstract: Molecular property prediction is one of the fastest-growing applications of deep learning with critical real-world impacts. Although the 3D molecular graph structure is necessary for models to achieve strong performance on many tasks, it is infeasible to obtain 3D structures at the scale required by many real-world applications. To tackle this issue, we propose to use existing 3D molecular datasets to pre-train a model to reason about the geometry of molecules given only their 2D molecular graphs. Our method, called 3D Infomax, maximizes the mutual information between learned 3D summary vectors and the representations of a graph neural network (GNN). During fine-tuning on molecules with unknown geometry, the GNN is still able to produce implicit 3D information and uses it for downstream tasks. We show that 3D Infomax provides significant improvements for a wide range of properties, including a 22% average MAE reduction on QM9 quantum mechanical properties. Moreover, the learned representations can be effectively transferred between datasets in different molecular spaces.

paragraphs: A molecule’s three-dimensional geometry can be important for predicting its properties, but obtaining that geometry for every molecule is often impractical. This paper asks whether a graph neural network can learn useful geometric information during pretraining and later apply it when only a two-dimensional molecular graph is available.

The proposed method, 3D Infomax, uses existing datasets containing molecular geometry. It trains the graph network by maximizing mutual information between its representations and learned summaries of three-dimensional structure. The aim is to make the graph representation retain information connected to geometry. During subsequent fine-tuning, molecules do not need known three-dimensional structures for the network to use this implicit geometric information.

The authors report significant improvements across a range of molecular properties, including a 22% average reduction in mean absolute error on QM9 quantum mechanical properties. They also find that the representations transfer effectively between datasets occupying different molecular spaces. These findings support using available geometric data as a reusable training resource for property prediction.
summary.tldr: 3D Infomax uses molecular geometry during pretraining to improve property prediction from two-dimensional molecular graphs.

title: 3D Infomax improves GNNs for Molecular Property Prediction

abstract: There has been some recent interest in detecting and addressing memorization of training data by deep neural networks. A formal framework for memorization in generative models, called “data-copying” was proposed by Meehan et. al (2020). We build upon their work to show that their framework may fail to detect certain kinds of blatant memorization. Motivated by this and the theory of non-parametric methods, we provide an alternative definition of data-copying that applies more locally. We provide a method to detect data-copying, and provably show that it works with high probability when enough data is available. We also provide lower bounds that characterize the sample requirement for reliable detection.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to define and detect memorization in generative models. Its starting point is an existing formal notion called data-copying. The authors show that this framework can miss some clear instances of memorization. The issue is therefore partly about what the definition recognizes, before considering how a detector implements it.

They propose an alternative definition that applies more locally, drawing motivation from nonparametric methods. This changes the level at which copying is assessed so that the framework can address shortcomings identified in the earlier definition. The paper then supplies a detection method built around the revised notion, connecting the conceptual change to an operational test.

The authors prove that their detector works with high probability when enough data is available. They also establish lower bounds on the sample requirements for reliable detection. These two results complement each other: one gives a sufficient-data guarantee for the proposed method, while the other characterizes data demands that detection must confront. The contribution combines a revised target for detection with a theoretical account of when reliable detection is possible.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a more local definition of generative data-copying, a detector, and bounds on the data needed for reliable detection.

title: Data-Copying in Generative Models: A Formal Framework

abstract: Bootstrapping from pre-trained language models has been proven to be an efficient approach for building vision-language models (VLM) for tasks such as image captioning or visual question answering. However, outputs of these models rarely align with user’s rationales for specific answers. In order to improve this alignment and reinforce commonsense reasons, we propose a tuning paradigm based on human interactions with machine-generated data. Our ILLUME executes the following loop: Given an image-question-answer prompt, the VLM samples multiple candidate rationales, and a human critic provides feedback via preference selection, used for fine-tuning. This loop increases the training data and gradually carves out the VLM’s rationalization capabilities that are aligned with human intent. Our exhaustive experiments demonstrate that ILLUME is competitive with standard supervised finetuning while using significantly fewer training data and only requiring minimal feedback.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may answer a question about an image without giving the kind of explanation a user expects. This paper focuses on aligning those generated rationales with human intent and commonsense reasoning. It introduces ILLUME, a tuning approach that uses human preferences over explanations produced by the model itself.

The process starts with an image, a question, and an answer. The model generates several possible rationales, and a human critic selects preferred candidates. That feedback is then used for fine-tuning. Repeating the loop expands the training data while progressively shaping the model's ability to provide explanations that people find appropriate.

The experiments show performance competitive with standard supervised fine-tuning while using substantially less training data and requiring only limited feedback. The practical appeal is that people can guide learning by choosing among candidate explanations, making machine-generated material useful for training. The reported achievement concerns the alignment and quality of rationalisation: the interaction loop helps models produce reasons closer to human preferences for the answers they give.
summary.tldr: ILLUME uses human preferences among generated explanations to tune vision-language models with substantially less training data than standard supervised fine-tuning.

title: ILLUME: Rationalizing Vision-Language Models through Human Interactions

abstract: We propose a new class of online learning algorithms, generalized implicit Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (FTRL), that expands the scope of FTRL framework. Generalized implicit FTRL can recover known algorithms, such as FTRL with linearized losses and implicit FTRL, and it allows the design of new update rules, as extensions of aProx and Mirror-Prox to FTRL. Our theory is constructive in the sense that it provides a simple unifying framework to design updates that directly improve the worst-case upper bound on the regret. The key idea is substituting the linearization of the losses with a Fenchel-Young inequality. We show the flexibility of the framework by proving that some known algorithms, like the Mirror-Prox updates, are instantiations of the generalized implicit FTRL. Finally, the new framework allows us to recover the temporal variation bound of implicit OMD, with the same computational complexity.

paragraphs: This paper expands Follow-The-Regularized-Leader, or FTRL, into a broader family of online learning algorithms. Online learning evaluates decisions made over a sequence through regret, which measures their accumulated disadvantage relative to a benchmark. The goal is to provide a common framework that supports both established algorithms and new update rules.

The central change replaces loss linearization with a Fenchel-Young inequality. This produces a constructive theory: the framework guides the design of updates that directly improve a worst-case upper bound on regret. It includes conventional FTRL with linearized losses and implicit FTRL, while allowing extensions of aProx and Mirror-Prox within the same formulation.

The authors show that known Mirror-Prox updates can be understood as particular instances of their framework. They also recover the temporal variation bound of implicit online mirror descent with the same computational complexity. These results make the framework useful both for relating existing methods and for designing updates with improved theoretical regret guarantees.
summary.tldr: Generalized implicit FTRL unifies existing online learning updates and provides a constructive route to improved regret bounds.

title: Generalized Implicit Follow-The-Regularized-Leader

abstract: Open vocabulary models (e.g. CLIP) have shown strong performance on zero-shot classification through their ability generate embeddings for each class based on their (natural language) names. Prior work has focused on improving the accuracy of these models through prompt engineering or by incorporating a small amount of labeled downstream data (via finetuning). However, there has been little focus on improving the richness of the class names themselves, which can pose issues when class labels are coarsely-defined and are uninformative. We propose Classification with Hierarchical Label Sets (or CHiLS), an alternative strategy for zero-shot classification specifically designed for datasets with implicit semantic hierarchies. CHiLS proceeds in three steps: (i) for each class, produce a set of subclasses, using either existing label hierarchies or by querying GPT-3; (ii) perform the standard zero-shot CLIP procedure as though these subclasses were the labels of interest; (iii) map the predicted subclass back to its parent to produce the final prediction. Across numerous datasets with underlying hierarchical structure, CHiLS leads to improved accuracy in situations both with and without ground-truth hierarchical information. CHiLS is simple to implement within existing zero-shot pipelines and requires no additional training cost. Code is available at: https://github.com/acmi-lab/CHILS.

paragraphs: Models such as CLIP can classify images using class names without training on labeled examples for the target task. However, a broad class name may give the model little useful information about what an image could contain. CHiLS addresses this problem by enriching the labels themselves when the classes have an underlying semantic hierarchy.

For each target class, the method creates a collection of more specific subclasses. These can come from an existing hierarchy or be generated by querying GPT-3. It then runs ordinary zero-shot CLIP classification using those subclasses as candidate labels. The predicted subclass is mapped back to its parent, producing an answer in the original set of classes.

Across multiple datasets with hierarchical structure, this procedure improves accuracy both when a ground-truth hierarchy is available and when it is not. It requires no additional model training and fits into existing zero-shot workflows. The finding shows that choosing more informative intermediate labels can improve classification while preserving the broad categories the user actually wants.
summary.tldr: CHiLS improves zero-shot image classification by predicting informative subclasses and mapping them back to the requested parent classes.

title: CHiLS: Zero-Shot Image Classification with Hierarchical Label Sets

abstract: We provide a full characterisation of all of the possible alternating group ($A_n$) equivariant neural networks whose layers are some tensor power of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. In particular, we find a basis of matrices for the learnable, linear, $A_n$–equivariant layer functions between such tensor power spaces in the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. We also describe how our approach generalises to the construction of neural networks that are equivariant to local symmetries.
originalAbstract: We provide a full characterisation of all of the possible alternating group ($A_n$) equivariant neural networks whose layers are some tensor power of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. In particular, we find a basis of matrices for the learnable, linear, $A_n$–equivariant layer functions between such tensor power spaces in the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. We also describe how our approach generalises to the construction of neural networks that are equivariant to local symmetries.

paragraphs: This paper provides a complete characterization of neural networks equivariant to the alternating group, with layers formed from tensor powers of an n-dimensional real vector space. Equivariance requires the network's response to follow the specified symmetry: applying a group transformation to an input must produce the corresponding transformation of the output.

The concrete result is a basis of matrices for learnable linear equivariant maps between those tensor spaces, expressed in the standard basis. A matrix basis identifies independent building blocks that can be combined to express every allowable linear map. This provides an explicit parameterization of the linear layers satisfying the symmetry requirement within the stated architecture family.

The authors also describe how their approach extends to constructing networks with local symmetries. That broadens the construction beyond the initial alternating-group setting. The paper's contribution is structural: it specifies the available symmetry-compatible linear functions completely in its main setting, and explains a route toward applying the same approach when the relevant symmetries are local.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a complete matrix basis for alternating-group-equivariant linear tensor layers and describes an extension to local symmetries.

title: How Jellyfish Characterise Alternating Group Equivariant Neural Networks

abstract: Deep generative models have recently achieved superior performance in 3D molecule generation. Most of them first generate atoms and then add chemical bonds based on the generated atoms in a post-processing manner. However, there might be no corresponding bond solution for the temporally generated atoms as their locations are generated without considering potential bonds. We define this problem as the atom-bond inconsistency problem and claim it is the main reason for current approaches to generating unrealistic 3D molecules. To overcome this problem, we propose a new diffusion model called MolDiff which can generate atoms and bonds simultaneously while still maintaining their consistency by explicitly modeling the dependence between their relationships. We evaluated the generation ability of our proposed model and the quality of the generated molecules using criteria related to both geometry and chemical properties. The empirical studies showed that our model outperforms previous approaches, achieving a three-fold improvement in success rate and generating molecules with significantly better quality.

paragraphs: Many 3D molecule generators first place atoms and then assign chemical bonds afterward. The difficulty is that atom positions generated without considering bonds may admit no compatible bond assignment. This paper calls that failure atom-bond inconsistency and argues that it is a main cause of unrealistic molecules produced by existing approaches.

MolDiff addresses the issue by generating atoms and bonds simultaneously with a diffusion model. It explicitly models their dependence so that the two parts of the molecular representation remain consistent during generation. This brings chemical connectivity into the generative process instead of leaving it entirely to a post-processing stage after atom placement.

The authors evaluate both generation ability and molecular quality using criteria covering geometry and chemical properties. Their empirical study reports a threefold improvement in success rate over previous approaches, together with significantly better molecule quality. The findings support joint atom-and-bond modeling as a way to improve the consistency of generated structures. The claim that inconsistency is the main underlying cause remains the authors' stated explanation.
summary.tldr: MolDiff jointly generates atoms and bonds to address inconsistent 3D molecules, reporting a threefold improvement in generation success rate.

title: MolDiff: Addressing the Atom-Bond Inconsistency Problem in 3D Molecule Diffusion Generation

abstract: Cutting out an object and estimating its opacity mask, known as image matting, is a key task in image and video editing. Due to the highly ill-posed issue, additional inputs, typically user-defined trimaps or scribbles, are usually needed to reduce the uncertainty. Although effective, it is either time consuming or only suitable for experienced users who know where to place the strokes. In this work, we propose a decomposed-uncertainty-guided matting (dugMatting) algorithm, which explores the explicitly decomposed uncertainties to efficiently and effectively improve the results. Basing on the characteristic of these uncertainties, the epistemic uncertainty is reduced in the process of guiding interaction (which introduces prior knowledge), while the aleatoric uncertainty is reduced in modeling data distribution (which introduces statistics for both data and possible noise). The proposed matting framework relieves the requirement for users to determine the interaction areas by using simple and efficient labeling. Extensively quantitative and qualitative results validate that the proposed method significantly improves the original matting algorithms in terms of both efficiency and efficacy.

paragraphs: Image matting estimates an object’s opacity mask so it can be separated from its surroundings. Because the image alone leaves substantial ambiguity, existing methods often ask users to supply trimaps or scribbles. Producing those inputs can take time and may require knowing which parts of the image most need guidance.

dugMatting divides uncertainty into two components and addresses them differently. It reduces epistemic uncertainty through guided interaction that introduces prior knowledge. It addresses aleatoric uncertainty by modeling the data distribution, including statistics associated with possible noise. This explicit separation gives the framework distinct ways to use human input and statistical modeling when improving the opacity estimate.

The interaction framework reduces the burden on users to decide where they should provide information, instead supporting simple labeling guided by the method. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations report significant gains in efficiency and effectiveness over the original matting algorithms. The practical contribution is a more directed interaction process: uncertainty helps determine how additional information should enter the system, making user effort more useful to the matting result.
summary.tldr: dugMatting separates uncertainty sources to guide user input and statistical modeling, improving image matting efficiency and quality.

title: dugMatting: Decomposed-Uncertainty-Guided Matting

abstract: We focus on the task of learning the value function in the reinforcement learning (RL) setting. This task is often solved by updating a pair of online and target networks while ensuring that the parameters of these two networks are equivalent. We propose Lookahead-Replicate (LR), a new value-function approximation algorithm that is agnostic to this parameter-space equivalence. Instead, the LR algorithm is designed to maintain an equivalence between the two networks in the function space. This value-based equivalence is obtained by employing a new target-network update. We show that LR leads to a convergent behavior in learning the value function. We also present empirical results demonstrating that LR-based target-network updates significantly improve deep RL on the Atari benchmark.

Instead, the LR algorithm is designed to maintain an equivalence between the two networks in the function space. This value-based equivalence is obtained by employing a new target-network update. We show that LR leads to a convergent behavior in learning the value function. We also present empirical results demonstrating that LR-based target-network updates significantly improve deep RL on the Atari benchmark.

paragraphs: Learning a value function is a central reinforcement-learning task. A common approach maintains an online network and a target network, coordinating them through their parameters. This paper examines a different basis for that coordination: the values the networks compute, rather than equivalence of their parameter settings.

The proposed Lookahead-Replicate algorithm introduces a target-network update designed to maintain equivalence in function space. In plain terms, the relationship between the networks is expressed through their value predictions. The method is agnostic to whether their parameters are equivalent, shifting the update’s focus toward the quantity that value-function learning is intended to estimate.

The authors show convergent behavior for learning the value function and report that Lookahead-Replicate target updates significantly improve deep reinforcement learning on the Atari benchmark. These contributions provide both a convergence result and an empirical reason to reconsider how target networks are updated. The broader significance is that coordinating neural networks through their outputs can be a useful algorithmic choice, rather than treating parameter correspondence as the defining requirement.
summary.tldr: Lookahead-Replicate coordinates online and target networks through value predictions, showing convergent behavior and improved Atari results.

title: Learning the Target Network in Function Space

abstract: Taming the generation outcome of state of the art Diffusion and Flow-Matching (FM) models without having to re-train a task-specific model unlocks a powerful tool for solving inverse problems, conditional generation, and controlled generation in general. In this work we introduce D-Flow, a simple framework for controlling the generation process by differentiating through the flow, optimizing for the source (noise) point. We motivate this framework by our key observation stating that for Diffusion/FM models trained with Gaussian probability paths, differentiating through the generation process projects gradient on the data manifold, implicitly injecting the prior into the optimization process. We validate our framework on linear and non-linear controlled generation problems including: image and audio inverse problems and conditional molecule generation reaching state of the art performance across all.

paragraphs: D-Flow addresses how to steer an existing diffusion or flow-matching model toward a desired output without retraining a separate model for each task. Its control variable is the initial noise point that starts generation. The method differentiates through the generation process and adjusts that starting point so that the resulting output better satisfies the task’s objective.

The authors motivate this procedure with an observation about models trained using Gaussian probability paths. In that setting, differentiating through generation projects the gradient onto the data manifold, bringing the model’s learned prior into the optimization. This explains why optimizing the initial noise can use the structure learned by the generator while pursuing an external generation requirement.

The framework is tested on both linear and nonlinear controlled-generation problems. These include image and audio inverse problems and conditional molecule generation, with state-of-the-art performance reported across the evaluated problems. The result supports a common control mechanism across these tasks: modify the source noise through the generator’s gradients while using the pretrained generation process to shape the output.
summary.tldr: D-Flow controls pretrained diffusion and flow-matching models by differentiating through generation to optimize their initial noise.

title: D-Flow: Differentiating through Flows for Controlled Generation

abstract: We propose a framework for global-scale canopy height estimation based on satellite data. Our model leverages advanced data preprocessing techniques, resorts to a novel loss function designed to counter geolocation inaccuracies inherent in the ground-truth height measurements, and employs data from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission to effectively filter out erroneous labels in mountainous regions, enhancing the reliability of our predictions in those areas. A comparison between predictions and ground-truth labels yields an MAE/RMSE of 2.43 / 4.73 (meters) overall and 4.45 / 6.72 (meters) for trees taller than five meters, which depicts a substantial improvement compared to existing global-scale products. The resulting height map as well as the underlying framework will facilitate and enhance ecological analyses at a global scale, including, but not limited to, large-scale forest and biomass monitoring.

paragraphs: This paper develops a satellite-based framework for estimating canopy height at global scale. A central challenge is the reliability of the height measurements used as ground-truth labels. Their locations can be inaccurate, and mountainous terrain can introduce erroneous labels. The framework addresses these issues as part of producing more dependable height predictions.

The approach combines advanced preprocessing with a new loss function designed to counter geolocation inaccuracies in the reference measurements. It also uses Shuttle Radar Topography Mission data to filter erroneous labels in mountainous regions. These components make the quality and spatial alignment of training information central to the estimation pipeline.

Against ground-truth labels, the reported overall mean absolute error is 2.43 meters and root mean squared error is 4.73 meters. For trees taller than five meters, those errors are 4.45 and 6.72 meters, respectively. The authors report substantial improvement over existing global-scale products. The resulting map and framework are intended to support global ecological analysis, including large-scale forest and biomass monitoring.
summary.tldr: A satellite-based canopy-height framework addresses location errors and unreliable mountain labels, reporting improved accuracy over existing global-scale products.

title: Estimating Canopy Height at Scale

abstract: Concept guidance has emerged as a cheap and simple way to control the behavior of language models by probing their hidden representations for concept vectors and using them to perturb activations at inference time. While the focus of previous work has largely been on truthfulness, in this paper we extend this framework to a richer set of concepts such as appropriateness, humor, creativity and quality, and explore to what degree current detection and guidance strategies work in these challenging settings. To facilitate evaluation, we develop a novel metric for concept guidance that takes into account both the success of concept elicitation as well as the potential degradation in fluency of the guided model. Our extensive experiments reveal that while some concepts such as truthfulness more easily allow for guidance with current techniques, novel concepts such as appropriateness or humor either remain difficult to elicit, need extensive tuning to work, or even experience confusion. Moreover, we find that probes with optimal detection accuracies do not necessarily make for the optimal guides, contradicting previous observations for truthfulness. Our work warrants a deeper investigation into the interplay between detectability, guidability, and the nature of the concept, and we hope that our rich experimental test-bed for guidance research inspires stronger follow-up approaches.

paragraphs: Concept guidance tries to change a language model’s behavior by adjusting its internal activations during generation. A probe identifies a direction associated with a concept, and that direction becomes a proposed steering signal. This paper tests how well this approach extends beyond truthfulness to appropriateness, humor, creativity, and quality.

The authors introduce an evaluation measure that considers both whether steering brings out the intended concept and whether the resulting text remains fluent. This matters because stronger expression of a desired trait can come with worse language generation. The measure treats those outcomes together rather than judging guidance solely by concept expression.

The experiments find that truthfulness is comparatively amenable to existing guidance techniques, while concepts such as humor and appropriateness can resist steering, require substantial tuning, or become confused. A probe that detects a concept most accurately also need not provide the best steering direction. The findings separate recognizing a trait inside a model from reliably controlling its expression.
summary.tldr: Detecting a concept in a language model’s activations does not necessarily reveal how to steer the model toward it.

title: A Language Model’s Guide Through Latent Space

abstract: Value iteration networks (VINs) enable end-to-end learning for planning tasks by employing a differentiable "planning module" that approximates the value iteration algorithm. However, long-term planning remains a challenge because training very deep VINs is difficult. To address this problem, we embed highway value iteration—a recent algorithm designed to facilitate long-term credit assignment—into the structure of VINs. This improvement augments the "planning module" of the VIN with three additional components: 1) an "aggregate gate," which constructs skip connections to improve information flow across many layers; 2) an "exploration module," crafted to increase the diversity of information and gradient flow in spatial dimensions; 3) a "filter gate" designed to ensure safe exploration. The resulting novel highway VIN can be trained effectively with hundreds of layers using standard backpropagation. In long-term planning tasks requiring hundreds of planning steps, deep highway VINs outperform both traditional VINs and several advanced, very deep NNs.

paragraphs: Value iteration networks incorporate a differentiable planning module into a neural network, allowing planning behavior to be learned end to end. This paper adapts highway value iteration to improve how information and learning signals travel through the network.

The resulting planning module adds three components. An aggregate gate creates skip connections across layers. An exploration module increases the diversity of information and gradient flow across spatial dimensions. A filter gate is designed to keep that exploration safe. Together, these additions address long-term credit assignment: learning how earlier planning computations contribute to later outcomes.

The authors report that highway VINs can be trained with hundreds of layers using standard backpropagation. On tasks requiring hundreds of planning steps, these deep networks outperform traditional VINs and several advanced, very deep neural networks. The findings connect better information flow during training with the ability to learn planning computations over substantially longer horizons in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Highway value iteration networks use gates and exploration components to train hundreds of planning layers effectively for long-horizon tasks.

title: Highway Value Iteration Networks

abstract: AI systems have been shown to produce unfair results for certain subgroups of population, highlighting the need to understand bias on certain sensitive attributes. Current research often falls short, primarily focusing on the subgroups characterized by a single sensitive attribute, while neglecting the nature of intersectional fairness of multiple sensitive attributes. This paper focuses on its one fundamental aspect by discovering diverse high-bias intersectional sensitive attributes. Specifically, we propose a Bias-Guided Generative Network (BGGN). By treating each bias value as a reward, BGGN efficiently generates high-bias intersectional sensitive attributes. Experiments on real-world text and image datasets demonstrate a diverse and efficient discovery of BGGN. To further evaluate the generated unseen but possible unfair intersectional sensitive attributes, we formulate them as prompts and use modern generative AI to produce new text and images. The results of frequently generating biased data provides new insights of discovering potential unfairness in popular modern generative AI systems. Warning: This paper contains examples that are offensive in nature.

paragraphs: Fairness assessments that examine one sensitive attribute at a time can overlook unfairness affecting combinations of attributes. This paper focuses on finding a diverse collection of those intersectional combinations with high measured bias. Its objective is discovery: identifying where a system may behave unfairly across overlapping population subgroups.

The proposed Bias-Guided Generative Network, or BGGN, treats bias values as rewards. This steers generation toward combinations associated with larger bias, rather than relying only on a fixed list of subgroups to examine. Experiments on real-world text and image datasets support the method's ability to discover varied high-bias intersections efficiently.

The authors also investigate generated combinations that are plausible but previously unseen. They turn these combinations into prompts for modern generative systems and examine the resulting text and images. The frequent production of biased outputs provides evidence of potential unfairness in those systems. This extends the discovery process from analyzing existing data to probing possible problematic cases through newly generated content, while retaining the focus on identifying bias rather than demonstrating its removal.
summary.tldr: BGGN uses measured bias as a reward to discover diverse sensitive-attribute intersections and probe potential unfairness in generated text and images.

title: Intersectional Unfairness Discovery

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, have demonstrated impressive zero-shot capabilities for various downstream tasks. Their performance can be further enhanced through few-shot prompt tuning methods. However, current studies evaluate the performance of learned prompts separately on base and new classes. This evaluation lacks practicality for real-world applications since downstream tasks cannot determine whether the data belongs to base or new classes in advance. In this paper, we explore a problem setting called O*pen-world Prompt Tuning (OPT), which involves tuning prompts on base classes and evaluating on a combination of base and new classes. By introducing Decomposed Prompt Tuning framework (DePT), we theoretically demonstrate that OPT can be solved by incorporating out-of-distribution detection into prompt tuning, thereby enhancing the base-to-new discriminability. Based on DePT, we present a novel prompt tuning approach, namely, Decomposed Context Op*timization (DeCoOp), which introduces new-class detectors and sub-classifiers to further enhance the base-class and new-class discriminability. Experimental results on 11 benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of DePT and demonstrate that DeCoOp outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, providing a significant 2% average accuracy improvement.

paragraphs: Prompt tuning can improve a vision-language model using a few examples from selected classes. However, evaluating familiar and new classes separately assumes information that an application may not have: whether an incoming example belongs to a class used during tuning. This paper studies open-world prompt tuning, where evaluation mixes both groups.

The authors introduce a theoretical framework called Decomposed Prompt Tuning. It shows how incorporating out-of-distribution detection can address this setting by improving discrimination between base and new classes. Building on that framework, DeCoOp combines new-class detectors with sub-classifiers. These components address both the distinction between the two groups and the classification distinctions needed within the resulting setting.

Experiments on 11 benchmark datasets support the framework and show DeCoOp outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods, with a reported average accuracy improvement of 2%. The result matters because the evaluation requires the method to handle the mixed class population directly. It therefore tests a capability that separate base-class and new-class evaluations do not capture in the same way.
summary.tldr: DeCoOp combines prompt tuning with new-class detection to improve classification when familiar and unseen classes appear together.

title: DeCoOp: Robust Prompt Tuning with Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: To understand how genetic variants in human genomes manifest in phenotypes - traits like height or diseases like asthma - geneticists have sequenced and measured hundreds of thousands of individuals. Geneticists use this data to build models that predict how a genetic variant impacts phenotype given genomic features of the variant, like DNA accessibility or the presence of nearby DNA-bound proteins. As more data and features become available, one might expect predictive models to improve. Unfortunately, training these models is bottlenecked by the need to solve expensive linear algebra problems because variants in the genome are correlated with nearby variants, requiring inversion of large matrices. Previous methods have therefore been restricted to fitting small models, and fitting simplified summary statistics, rather than the full likelihood of the statistical model. In this paper, we leverage modern fast linear algebra techniques to develop DeepWAS (Deep genome Wide Association Studies), a method to train large and flexible neural network predictive models to optimize likelihood. Surprisingly, we find that larger models only improve performance when using our full likelihood approach; when trained by fitting traditional summary statistics, larger models perform no better than small ones. We find larger models trained on more features make better predictions, potentially improving disease predictions and therapeutic target identification.

However, neighboring variants are correlated, creating expensive matrix calculations during training. This computational bottleneck has restricted earlier approaches to smaller models and simplified summary statistics instead of fitting the full statistical likelihood.

The authors introduce DeepWAS, which uses fast linear algebra to train larger, more flexible neural networks by optimizing likelihood. The approach addresses the computation that previously constrained model fitting. This allows the study to examine whether increased model capacity and additional genomic features improve predictions when the fuller statistical objective becomes tractable.

The results reveal that model size and training objective interact. Larger models improve performance under the proposed full-likelihood approach, but offer no benefit over small models when trained on traditional summary statistics. The authors identify improved disease prediction and therapeutic target identification as potential applications of these advances.
summary.tldr: DeepWAS makes full-likelihood training practical for flexible genetic-effect models, revealing gains from larger models that summary-statistic training did not deliver.

title: Training Flexible Models of Genetic Variant Effects from Functional Annotations using Accelerated Linear Algebra

abstract: The deployment of mixture-of-experts (MoE) large language models (LLMs) presents significant challenges due to their high memory demands. These challenges become even more pronounced in multi-tenant environments, where shared resources must accommodate multiple models, limiting the effectiveness of conventional virtualization techniques. This paper addresses the problem of efficiently serving multiple fine-tuned MoE-LLMs on a single GPU. We propose a serving system that employs similarity-based expert consolidation to reduce the overall memory footprint by sharing similar experts across models. To ensure output quality, we introduce runtime partial reconfiguration, dynamically replacing non-expert layers when processing requests from different models. As a result, our approach achieves competitive output quality while maintaining throughput comparable to serving a single model, and incurs only a negligible increase in time-to-first-token (TTFT). Experiments on a server with a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (80GB) using Mixtral-8x7B models demonstrate an 85% average reduction in turnaround time compared to NVIDIA’s multi-instance GPU (MIG). Furthermore, experiments on Google’s Switch Transformer Base-8 model with up to four variants demonstrate the scalability and resilience of our approach in maintaining output quality compared to other model merging baselines, highlighting its effectiveness.

This paper proposes sharing similar expert components across models to reduce their total memory footprint.

Sharing experts is paired with runtime partial reconfiguration: the system dynamically replaces non-expert layers when requests switch between models. This preserves model-specific processing while allowing consolidated experts to remain shared. Tests with up to four Switch Transformer Base-8 variants also support scalability and output-quality preservation compared with model-merging baselines. The results demonstrate how selective sharing and request-dependent reconfiguration can make multi-model serving more efficient.
summary.tldr: Sharing similar experts and swapping non-expert layers at runtime enables efficient serving of multiple fine-tuned MoE models on one GPU.

title: QoS-Efficient Serving of Multiple Mixture-of-Expert LLMs Using Partial Runtime Reconfiguration

abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture improves Large Language Models (LLMs) with better scaling, but its higher parameter counts and memory demands create challenges for deployment. In this paper, we present MoE-SVD, a new decomposition-based compression framework tailored for MoE LLMs without any extra training. By harnessing the power of Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), MoE-SVD addresses the critical issues of decomposition collapse and matrix redundancy in MoE architectures. Specifically, we first decompose experts into compact low-rank matrices, resulting in accelerated inference and memory optimization. In particular, we propose selective decomposition strategy by measuring sensitivity metrics based on weight singular values and activation statistics to automatically identify decomposable expert layers. Then, we share a single V-matrix across all experts and employ a top-k selection for U-matrices. This low-rank matrix sharing and trimming scheme allows for significant parameter reduction while preserving diversity among experts. Comprehensive experiments on Mixtral, Phi-3.5, DeepSeek, and Qwen2 MoE LLMs show MoE-SVD outperforms other compression methods, achieving a 60% compression ratio and 1.5$\times$ faster inference with minimal performance loss.

title: MoE-SVD: Structured Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Compression via Singular Value Decomposition

abstract: The paradigm of weak-to-strong generalization constitutes the training of a strong AI model on data labeled by a weak AI model, with the goal that the strong model nevertheless outperforms its weak supervisor on the target task of interest. For the setting of real-valued regression with the squared loss, recent work quantitatively characterizes the gain in performance of the strong model over the weak model in terms of the misfit between the strong and weak model. We generalize such a characterization to learning tasks whose loss functions correspond to arbitrary Bregman divergences when the strong class is convex. This extends the misfit-based characterization of performance gain in weak-to-strong generalization to classification tasks, as the cross-entropy loss can be expressed in terms of a Bregman divergence. In most practical scenarios, however, the strong model class may not be convex. We therefore weaken this assumption and study weak-to-strong generalization for convex combinations of $k$ strong models in the strong class, in the concrete setting of classification. This allows us to obtain a similar misfit-based characterization of performance gain, up to an additional error term that vanishes as $k$ gets large. Our theoretical findings are supported by thorough experiments on synthetic as well as real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization trains a stronger model using labels from a weaker model, hoping the student can outperform its supervisor. Previous theory for squared-loss regression relates this performance gain to the mismatch between the two models. This paper extends that relationship to a broader family of learning objectives.

The authors establish a misfit-based characterization for losses corresponding to arbitrary Bregman divergences, assuming the strong model class is convex. Because cross-entropy can be expressed through a Bregman divergence, the result reaches classification as well as regression. The convexity assumption is central to this part of the theory.

To address strong model classes that are not convex, the authors study convex combinations of k strong models in classification. They obtain a similar characterization with an extra error term that vanishes as k grows. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical findings. The work broadens the conditions under which disagreement with a weak supervisor can quantitatively explain a stronger model’s performance gain.
summary.tldr: The paper extends misfit-based weak-to-strong performance theory to Bregman losses and classification, with convexity assumptions or mixtures of strong models.

title: Relating Misfit to Gain in Weak-to-Strong Generalization Beyond the Squared Loss

abstract: We study the statistical-computational trade-offs for learning with exact invariances (or symmetries) using kernel regression. Traditional methods, such as data augmentation, group averaging, canonicalization, and frame-averaging, either fail to provide a polynomial-time solution or are not applicable in the kernel setting. However, with oracle access to the geometric properties of the input space, we propose a polynomial-time algorithm that learns a classifier with exact invariances. Moreover, our approach achieves the same excess population risk (or generalization error) as the original kernel regression problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm to achieve exact (as opposed to approximate) invariances in this setting. In developing our approach, we also resolve a question recently posed by D{ı}az et al. (2025) on efficient computation of invariant bases and kernels with respect to finite groups, even when the group size is prohibitively large. Our proof leverages tools from differential geometry, spectral theory, and optimization. A key result in our development is a new reformulation of the problem of learning under invariances as optimizing an infinite number of linearly constrained convex quadratic programs, which may be of independent interest.

title: Learning with Exact Invariances in Polynomial Time

abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

paragraphs: Methods for controlling language models include prompting, finetuning, and interventions in their internal representations. Comparing them has been difficult without a shared evaluation. AxBench supplies a large-scale benchmark covering two distinct abilities: steering generated text toward a desired concept and detecting whether a concept is present in a model’s representations.

Experiments on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B reveal different winners for the two tasks. Prompting performs best for steering among the existing methods evaluated, followed by finetuning. Representation-based approaches, including difference-in-means, perform best at concept detection. Sparse autoencoders are not competitive on either evaluation, showing that their appeal for interpretability does not translate into leading results on these tests.

The authors also introduce Rank-1 Representation Finetuning, called ReFT-r1, a weakly supervised method that is competitive on both tasks while offering interpretability advantages absent from prompting. They release feature dictionaries at sparse-autoencoder scale for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean. The results make the intended use central: recognizing concepts and controlling outputs call for separate comparisons.
summary.tldr: AxBench finds prompting strongest for steering and representation methods strongest for concept detection, with sparse autoencoders uncompetitive on both evaluated tasks.

title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Event-based object detection has attracted increasing attention for its high temporal resolution, wide dynamic range, and asynchronous address-event representation. Leveraging these advantages, spiking neural networks (SNNs) have emerged as a promising approach, offering low energy consumption and rich spatiotemporal dynamics. To further enhance the performance of event-based object detection, this study proposes a novel hybrid spike vision Transformer (HsVT) model. The HsVT model integrates a spatial feature extraction module to capture local and global features, and a temporal feature extraction module to model time dependencies and long-term patterns in event sequences. This combination enables HsVT to capture spatiotemporal features, improving its capability in handling complex event-based object detection tasks. To support research in this area, we developed the Fall Detection dataset as a benchmark for event-based object detection tasks. The Fall DVS detection dataset protects facial privacy and reduces memory usage thanks to its event-based representation. Experimental results demonstrate that HsVT outperforms existing SNN methods and achieves competitive performance compared to ANN-based models, with fewer parameters and lower energy consumption.

Spiking neural networks are a promising match because they combine rich dynamics over space and time with low energy consumption. The proposed Hybrid Spiking Vision Transformer, HsVT, aims to improve detection using those properties.

HsVT combines two feature-processing modules. The spatial module extracts both local and global information, while the temporal module captures dependencies and longer-term patterns in event sequences. Together, these components represent where relevant information appears and how it develops over time, supporting more complex event-based detection tasks.

The authors also introduce a Fall Detection benchmark whose event-based representation protects facial privacy and reduces memory usage. Experiments show that HsVT outperforms existing spiking-network methods and is competitive with conventional artificial neural network models, while using fewer parameters and less energy. The reported results connect improved spatial and temporal modeling with an efficient approach to event-based detection.
summary.tldr: HsVT combines spatial and temporal processing for event-camera detection, reporting competitive accuracy with fewer parameters and lower energy consumption.

title: Hybrid Spiking Vision Transformer for Object Detection with Event Cameras

abstract: Neural networks often map low-dimensional embeddings to high-dimensional output spaces. Usually, the output layer is linear, which can create a rank bottleneck that limits the functions a model can represent. Such bottlenecks are ubiquitous in link prediction models, such as knowledge graph embeddings (KGEs), as the output space of entities can be orders of magnitude larger than the embedding dimension. We investigate how rank bottlenecks limit model expressivity for fitting the training data. While previous work focused on sufficient bounds on the embedding dimension required for specific KGEs, we show necessary bounds for all KGEs with a linear output layer, which grow with graph size and connectivity. We also consider a non-linear output layer using mixtures to break the bottleneck without significant parameter overhead. Empirically, we show that models using this non-linear layer improve in ranking performance and probabilistic fit for large and dense datasets at a low parameter cost, as predicted by our theory. Our work reveals how linear output layers limit KGEs and motivates non-linear alternatives for scaling to large and dense graphs.
