paragraphs: Link-prediction models often represent entities with compact embeddings while producing scores over a much larger entity space. When the output layer is linear, this creates a rank bottleneck that can restrict which patterns the model can fit. The paper investigates this representational limit for knowledge graph embeddings.

Previous results established embedding dimensions sufficient for particular models. Here, the authors derive necessary dimension bounds covering all knowledge graph embedding models with linear output layers. Those bounds grow with graph size and connectivity. The result identifies a restriction shared across that model class, rather than a weakness of one specific embedding architecture.

The paper also considers a nonlinear output layer built using mixtures to break the bottleneck without substantial parameter overhead. Experiments show improved ranking performance and probabilistic fit on large, dense datasets at low parameter cost, consistent with the theory. Together, the results explain why output-layer structure matters when scaling link prediction and motivate nonlinear alternatives for graphs where linear expressivity becomes restrictive.
summary.tldr: The paper proves dimension requirements for linear-output knowledge graph embeddings and shows that nonlinear mixture outputs can ease their rank bottleneck.

title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-based Link Prediction

abstract: The scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven significant performance gains but created substantial challenges in inference efficiency. While Mixture of Experts (MoEs) architectures address this by decoupling model size from inference cost, training MoEs from scratch is often unstable and compute intensive. Conversion of pre-trained dense models into sparse MoEs has emerged as an alternative solution; however, existing methods typically rely on heuristic neuron clustering or random splitting to partition Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) into experts. In this work, we propose DOT-MoE, a novel framework that formulates the decomposition of dense layers as a Differentiable Optimal Transport (DOT) problem. Instead of static heuristics, we model neuron assignment as a balanced transport problem, utilizing differentiable Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations to enforce strict expert capacity constraints. Furthermore, we utilize Straight-Through Estimators (STE) to jointly learn the discrete neuron-to-expert assignment and the token-to-expert routing policy end-to-end. Extensive experiments across multiple architectures and benchmarks demonstrate that DOT-MoE significantly outperforms structured pruning, heuristic clustering, and random-split baselines, retaining 90% of the original dense model’s performance while reducing active parameters by 50%.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models can keep many parameters while activating only a subset for each input. Converting an existing dense language model offers an alternative to training such a system from scratch. The difficult step is deciding how to divide its feed-forward neurons into experts and how to route tokens among those experts.

DOT-MoE treats neuron assignment as a balanced optimal-transport problem that can be learned during training. Differentiable Sinkhorn–Knopp iterations enforce expert capacity constraints, so the partition respects prescribed sizes. Straight-through estimators allow the discrete assignments and token-routing policy to be optimized together. This connects the construction of experts to the decisions that determine how they will actually be used.

Across multiple architectures and benchmarks, the method outperforms the reported structured-pruning, heuristic-clustering, and random-splitting baselines. The authors report retaining 90% of the original dense model’s performance while reducing active parameters by 50%. This describes a measured performance–computation tradeoff: the reduction concerns parameters used during computation, and the retained performance is below the full dense-model level.
summary.tldr: DOT-MoE jointly learns balanced expert partitions and token routing, retaining 90% of dense-model performance with 50% fewer active parameters.

title: DOT-MoE: Differentiable Optimal Transport for MoEfication

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures are appealing for continual learning because sparse routing should localize updates and reduce interference, yet MoE Transformers still forget substantially even with sparse, well-balanced expert utilization. We attribute this gap to a pre-routing bottleneck: multi-head attention concatenates head-specific signals into a single post-attention router input, forcing routing to act on co-occurring feature compositions rather than separable head channels. We show that this router input simultaneously encodes multiple separately decodable semantic and structural factors with uneven head support, and that different feature compositions induce weakly aligned parameter-gradient directions; as a result, routing maps many distinct compositions to the same route. We quantify this collision effect via a route-wise effective composition number $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and find that higher $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is associated with larger old-task loss increases after continual training. Motivated by these findings, we propose MH-MoE, which performs head-wise routing over sub-representations to increase routing granularity and reduce composition collisions. On TRACE across multiple backbones, MH-MoE consistently improves the retention–accuracy trade-off over LoRA-MoE variants.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts Transformers can still forget earlier tasks even when their experts are used sparsely and evenly. This paper locates a source of interference before expert routing: multi-head attention combines signals from different heads into a single representation, leaving the router to handle mixtures of features.

The authors show that this representation contains multiple separately decodable semantic and structural factors, with different heads supporting them unevenly. Different feature combinations produce weakly aligned gradient directions, yet many combinations receive the same route. A proposed effective composition number measures this mixing within routes. Higher values are associated with larger increases in old-task loss after continual training.

Motivated by that analysis, MH-MoE routes head-level sub-representations separately, giving the routing process finer granularity and reducing composition collisions. Across multiple backbones on TRACE, it consistently improves the balance between retaining earlier capabilities and achieving accuracy compared with LoRA-MoE variants. The results suggest that how features are packaged for routing matters alongside how sparsely or evenly experts are used.
summary.tldr: MH-MoE reduces forgetting by routing attention-head representations separately, addressing feature collisions hidden by balanced expert usage.

title: Multi-Head Attention as a Source of Catastrophic Forgetting in MoE Transformers

abstract: De novo functional protein design aims to generate protein sequences that realize specified biochemical functions without relying on evolutionary templates, enabling broad applications in biotechnology and medicine. Existing approaches adopt either direct function-to-sequence mapping or decoupled structure-sequence generation strategies but often fail to achieve functionality and foldability simultaneously. To address this, we propose CodeFP, a Co-generative protein language model for de novo Functional P**rotein design that simultaneously decodes sequence and structure tokens, thereby enabling superior simultaneous realization of functionality and foldability. CodeFP utilizes functional local structures to enrich functional semantic encodings, overcoming the suboptimal translation of flat encodings into structure tokens, while introducing auxiliary functional supervision to alleviate training ambiguity stemming from the one-to-many structure-to-token mapping. Extensive experiments show that CodeFP consistently achieves average improvements of 6.1% in functional consistency and 3.2% in foldability over the strongest baseline.

paragraphs: Designing a protein for a specified biochemical function requires more than producing an amino-acid sequence: the sequence must also support a suitable folded structure. The paper addresses this joint requirement in de novo design, where generation does not depend on evolutionary templates. Existing direct sequence generation and separated structure–sequence approaches can struggle to satisfy both goals together.

CodeFP tackles the problem by decoding sequence tokens and structure tokens simultaneously. It enriches the representation of the requested function using local structures associated with function, giving the model more structurally informative guidance. It also adds auxiliary supervision about function to reduce training ambiguity caused by the one-to-many mapping from structures to tokens.

The reported experiments show average improvements of 6.1% in functional consistency and 3.2% in foldability over the strongest baseline. These results support the value of coordinating sequence and structure generation rather than handling their requirements separately. The contribution is a model that links functional guidance to structural generation while explicitly training toward both desired function and the ability to fold.
summary.tldr: CodeFP jointly generates protein sequence and structure tokens, improving measured functional consistency and foldability over the strongest baseline.

title: Co-Generative De Novo Functional Protein Design

abstract: Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) demands a sophisticated integration of temporal dynamics, spatial details, and linguistic reasoning to achieve precise pixel-level localization. Existing methods are limited to reasoning over fixed initial inputs and lack the capacity to actively acquire further visual evidence, which is often essential for resolving complex references in long or intricate videos. To address this, we propose $\textbf{VideoSEG-O3}$, the first multi-turn reinforcement learning framework for RVOS that emulates the human $\textit{“coarse-to-fine”}$ cognitive process. It employs a $\textit{multi-turn temporal-spatial chain-of-thought}$ to capture fine-grained details by iteratively pinpointing critical intervals and keyframes. Additionally, to enable the policy to perceive segmentation quality beyond mere text probability of $\texttt{[SEG]}$ during the RL stage, we introduce $\textit{SEG-aware logit calibration}$, which integrates pixel-wise segmentation feedback directly into the token-level logits. Furthermore, we design a $\textit{decoupled thinking trace}$ to hierarchically decompose the reasoning process into temporal, spatial, and linguistic dimensions, and construct $\textbf{VTS-CoT}$, a specialized cold-start dataset featuring comprehensive reasoning trajectories. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VideoSEG-O3 achieves advanced performance across 8 mainstream RVOS benchmarks, particularly excelling in long-horizon and complex reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Reasoning video object segmentation requires interpreting a linguistic reference and identifying the corresponding object at pixel level across a video. Difficult references can depend on both fine visual details and events separated in time. VideoSEG-O3 addresses the limitations of reasoning from fixed initial inputs by allowing the system to seek additional visual evidence over multiple turns.

Its temporal-spatial reasoning process progressively identifies useful time intervals and keyframes, moving from a broad view toward the details needed for segmentation. A separated thinking trace organizes temporal, spatial, and linguistic reasoning. This gives the policy a signal about the quality of its segmentation beyond the text probability assigned to the segmentation token. Experiments across eight mainstream benchmarks report advanced performance, with particular strengths on long-horizon and complex reasoning tasks. The findings support combining active evidence gathering with training feedback that reflects the actual localization outcome.
summary.tldr: VideoSEG-O3 iteratively gathers video evidence and uses segmentation-aware reinforcement learning to improve reasoning-based object localization.

title: VideoSEG-O3: A Multi-turn Reinforcement Learning Framework for Reasoning Video Object Segmentation

abstract: The "reversal curse" exposes a critical asymmetry in autoregressive models, where models trained on facts in one direction often fail to access the corresponding inverse relation. This work studies the phenomenon from a representation-level perspective, characterizing it as a form of chiral asymmetry between subject- and object-oriented latent states. We introduce the Chiral Transformer, a lightweight framework that encourages an involutive adjoint mapping operator $\mathcal{T}$ through contrastive regularization. At inference time, Adjoint-Induced Retrieval (AIR) uses this learned map as a structured readout over model-derived entity representations, rather than as an unconstrained autoregressive generation protocol. Empirical validation on inverse-relation benchmarks shows that this symmetry-aware retrieval setting substantially improves inverse factual access, with AIR reaching 65.07% accuracy on Fact-Inv-300. These findings support a representation-access view of the reversal curse: inverse relations may be difficult not only because of missing data, but also because standard autoregressive readout fails to expose useful latent structure.

paragraphs: The reversal curse occurs when a model learns a fact in one direction but struggles to recover the inverse relation. This paper studies the problem through internal representations, describing an asymmetry between latent states organized around subjects and those organized around objects. That perspective shifts attention toward how stored representations can be accessed during a reverse query.

The proposed Chiral Transformer uses contrastive regularization to encourage a structured mapping between these states. The mapping is intended to be involutive, meaning that applying it twice returns to the starting representation. At inference, Adjoint-Induced Retrieval uses the learned map to read out model-derived entity representations. The evaluated procedure is therefore a structured retrieval setting, rather than unrestricted autoregressive answer generation.

Experiments on inverse-relation benchmarks show substantial improvements in inverse factual access, including 65.07% accuracy on Fact-Inv-300. These findings support the possibility that some inverse relations are difficult to retrieve because ordinary readout fails to expose useful latent structure. They do not establish that missing training data is irrelevant or that unrestricted generation has solved the reversal curse.
summary.tldr: A learned symmetry-aware mapping improves inverse-fact retrieval, supporting a representation-access explanation for part of the reversal curse.

title: Chiral Symmetry Breaking in Transformers: A Group-Equivariant Framework for Addressing the Reversal Curse via Adjoint Manifold Mappings

abstract: While foundation models have revolutionized various domains, their application to time series classification remains rather under-explored, with existing literature predominantly focused on forecasting. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mantis, a transformer-based foundation model pre-trained exclusively on synthetic data via self-supervised contrastive learning. We demonstrate that effective tokenization is critical to unlocking the full potential of transformers, proposing a novel token generator unit. Furthermore, we introduce an enhanced test-time methodology that bridges the performance gap between Mantis and strong specialized approaches by leveraging intermediate-layer representations, self-ensembling, and cross-model embedding fusion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Mantis establishes a new state-of-the-art, outperforming existing foundation models across four diverse dataset collections covering various application domains.

Furthermore, we introduce an enhanced test-time methodology that bridges the performance gap between Mantis and strong specialized approaches by leveraging intermediate-layer representations, self-ensembling, and cross-model embedding fusion. paragraphs: Mantis is a transformer-based foundation model designed for time-series classification, a task the paper identifies as less explored than forecasting. Its pretraining uses exclusively synthetic data and self-supervised contrastive learning. The work examines how that training approach, together with representation design, can support classification across diverse application domains.

A central architectural contribution is a new token generator unit. The paper finds that effective tokenization is critical to realizing the transformer’s potential for this task. It also introduces a test-time methodology that uses representations from intermediate layers, self-ensembling, and fusion of embeddings from different models. These components broaden the information used when making classification decisions.

Experiments across four diverse dataset collections report a new state of the art and improvements over existing foundation models. The enhanced test-time approach also bridges the performance gap with strong specialized methods. The findings connect performance to both the representation learned during synthetic pretraining and the way model representations are combined at evaluation time.
summary.tldr: Mantis combines synthetic contrastive pretraining, tailored tokenization, and enhanced test-time representations for strong time-series classification.

title: Mantis: Lightweight Foundation Model for Time Series Classification

abstract: AI for scientific discovery is entering an agentic era, where protein-engineering systems are expected to prioritize future wet-lab experiments rather than merely fit static measurements. We introduce TadA-Bench, a million-variant wet-lab replay benchmark from 31 TadA directed-evolution rounds for future-round discovery toward agentic protein engineering. TadA-Bench preserves the campaign chronology and defines a fixed-data replay task: given earlier experimental rounds, models rank variants that appear only in later rounds. It provides aligned DNA, RNA, and protein views, and uses Seq2Graph, a graph-based label-unification pipeline, to reconcile noisy enrichment measurements into consistent cross-round activity labels. Random-split controls show strong interpolation, but future-round ranking and finite-budget candidate selection are much weaker. Controlled analyses suggest that evolutionary coverage is more informative than local data density, positioning TadA-Bench as a reproducible wet-lab replay substrate for future-round discovery toward agentic protein engineering; the data and code are released on Hugging Face and GitHub.
originalAbstract: AI for scientific discovery is entering an agentic era, where protein-engineering systems are expected to prioritize future wet-lab experiments rather than merely fit static measurements. We introduce TadA-Bench, a million-variant wet-lab replay benchmark from 31 TadA directed-evolution rounds for future-round discovery toward agentic protein engineering. TadA-Bench preserves the campaign chronology and defines a fixed-data replay task: given earlier experimental rounds, models rank variants that appear only in later rounds. It provides aligned DNA, RNA, and protein views, and uses Seq2Graph, a graph-based label-unification pipeline, to reconcile noisy enrichment measurements into consistent cross-round activity labels. Random-split controls show strong interpolation, but future-round ranking and finite-budget candidate selection are much weaker. Controlled analyses suggest that evolutionary coverage is more informative than local data density, positioning TadA-Bench as a reproducible wet-lab replay substrate for future-round discovery toward agentic protein engineering; the data and code are released on Hugging Face and GitHub.

paragraphs: Protein-engineering models are increasingly expected to prioritize future experiments, which differs from predicting measurements scattered randomly across an existing dataset. TadA-Bench evaluates this prospective ranking problem using a million variants from 31 rounds of TadA directed evolution. It preserves the experimental chronology so earlier rounds provide data for ranking variants appearing only later.

The benchmark is a fixed-data replay of a wet-lab campaign. It offers aligned DNA, RNA, and protein views, while Seq2Graph reconciles noisy enrichment measurements into activity labels that can be compared across rounds. This design makes the historical sequence of discovery part of the evaluation rather than mixing past and future observations.

Random-split controls show strong interpolation, but ranking future-round variants and selecting candidates under finite budgets prove much harder. Controlled analyses suggest that coverage of evolutionary variation is more informative than local data density. The benchmark therefore exposes a gap between fitting available measurements and prioritizing later experimental candidates, providing a reproducible setting for studying the latter capability.
summary.tldr: TadA-Bench preserves experimental chronology to reveal how much harder future protein-variant discovery is than random-split prediction.

title: TadA-Bench: A Million-Variant Benchmark for Future-Round Discovery Toward Agentic Protein Engineering

abstract: 3D visual grounding requires robust cross-modal representation to achieve fine-grained semantic alignment and precise geometric reasoning. However, most methods employ unimodal pre-trained encoders that transfer visual and linguistic knowledge independently, inducing domain shift and poor cross-modal alignment. Meanwhile, spatial modeling with handcrafted priors limits cross-modal geometric representation, struggling to capture complex object relations due to spectral bias. To address these challenges, we propose Text-Aware Feature Tuning (TFT) and Decomposed Spectral Geometry (DSG) to enhance cross-modal semantic representation. Specifically, TFT injects linguistic context into the visual hierarchy to mitigate domain shift and facilitate early cross-modal alignment. DSG employs a learnable Fourier basis and explicitly decomposes pairwise relations into symmetric and antisymmetric spectral components, allowing the model to capture high-frequency geometric details and direction-aware relations for precise spatial reasoning. Extensive experiments on ScanRefer, Nr3D and Sr3D validate the effectiveness of our method, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance with improvements of 2.05% Acc@0.25 for 3DREC and 1.09% mIoU for 3DRES on ScanRefer.

paragraphs: Locating objects in a 3D scene from language requires both semantic matching and precise spatial reasoning. The paper identifies two obstacles: visual and language encoders trained separately can produce poorly aligned representations, while spatial models based on handcrafted assumptions can miss complex geometric relations. DSGCR addresses these obstacles with complementary semantic and geometric components.

Text-Aware Feature Tuning introduces linguistic context into the visual feature hierarchy, encouraging the two modalities to align earlier in processing. Decomposed Spectral Geometry uses a learnable Fourier basis to represent object relationships. It separates pairwise relations into symmetric and antisymmetric components, supporting both fine geometric detail and relations whose meaning depends on direction.

Experiments on ScanRefer, Nr3D, and Sr3D support the method’s effectiveness and report state-of-the-art performance. On ScanRefer, the abstract reports gains of 2.05% in Acc@0.25 for 3D referring expression comprehension and 1.09% in mIoU for referring expression segmentation. The combined approach connects language-guided visual features with a more expressive representation of geometry, addressing both what an object means and how it relates spatially to other objects.
summary.tldr: DSGCR combines early language–vision alignment with spectral representations of geometry to improve object grounding in 3D scenes.

title: DSGCR: Decomposed Spectral Geometry-Aware Cross-Modal Semantic Representation for 3D Visual Grounding

abstract: Securing Contextual Integrity (CI) is critical for privacy-preserving Large Language Model (LLM) agent execution. However, existing agents struggle to balance the agility of direct generation against the prohibitive latency of CI-constrained thinking. To address this, we propose PrivGate, a framework that selectively invokes explicit reasoning based on internal privacy signals. Our approach is grounded in the discovery of a privacy manifold, where models linearly encode privacy sensitivity within their residual streams, even during non-compliant generation. Leveraging this structure, PrivGate employs Latent Gating, a training-free mechanism that requires no fine-tuning of the base LLM and triggers explicit reasoning only when high latent risk is detected, thereby optimizing the efficiency-privacy trade-off by minimizing unnecessary compute. On the contextual PrivacyLens benchmark, PrivGate maintains consistently high performance in out-of-distribution risk identification, validating the generalizability of the discovered manifold. End-to-end evaluations show that PrivGate achieves a 62.6% average relative reduction in privacy leakage with 15.9% token overhead, offering a practical pathway to reconcile rigorous CI requirements with the performance demands of LLM agents.

paragraphs: Privacy-aware language-model agents face a computational trade-off: direct generation is fast, while explicit reasoning about whether information sharing fits its context adds overhead. PrivGate uses signals inside the model to decide when that extra reasoning is warranted. It aims to concentrate privacy-related computation on situations that appear risky.

The framework builds on the finding that privacy sensitivity is linearly represented in the model’s residual stream, including during generation that violates contextual privacy requirements. Its latent gate reads this internal structure and triggers explicit reasoning when detected risk is high. The gating mechanism requires no fine-tuning of the base model, making selective intervention possible without retraining the underlying generator.

On PrivacyLens, PrivGate reports consistently strong identification of risks outside the distribution used to establish the detector. End-to-end evaluations show a 62.6% average relative reduction in privacy leakage with 15.9% token overhead. The results demonstrate a measured improvement in the privacy–efficiency balance: internal risk signals can help target additional reasoning where it is useful, while leakage is reduced rather than reported as eliminated.
summary.tldr: PrivGate uses internal privacy signals to trigger reasoning selectively, reducing average privacy leakage by 62.6% relative with 15.9% token overhead.

title: PrivGate: Steering Contextual Integrity in LLMs via Latent Space Geometry

abstract: Evolutionary model merging provides a powerful framework for the automated, training-free composition of LLMs through parameter-space search. However, existing methods predominantly rely on stochastic, hand-crafted operators that overlook the underlying performance landscape of the coefficient space. We propose Evolutionary Generative Merging (EvoGM), a framework that transcends manual heuristics by employing learnable generative modeling to optimize merging coefficients. Specifically, EvoGM features a dual-generator architecture with cycle-consistent learning to adaptively sample and refine promising merging candidates. By constructing winner-loser pairs from historical search trajectories, our framework effectively captures high-performance parameter distributions and maximizes data efficiency. This generative process is seamlessly integrated into a multi-round evolutionary pipeline, where elite merged models iteratively serve as new expert foundations. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that EvoGM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, exhibiting robust performance on both seen and unseen tasks. Code and data are available at https://github.com/JiangTao97/evogm.

paragraphs: Model merging combines language models through choices made in parameter space. Evolutionary search can automate those choices, but conventional search operators are stochastic and handcrafted. EvoGM aims to learn which merging coefficients tend to produce strong models, using the performance information accumulated during the search itself.

The framework uses two generators with cycle-consistent learning to propose and refine promising coefficient candidates. Historical search trajectories supply winner–loser pairs, allowing the generators to learn from relative candidate quality. This makes earlier evaluations useful training evidence for subsequent search, rather than leaving the selection of new candidates entirely to fixed heuristics.

EvoGM embeds this learned proposal process within multiple evolutionary rounds. Strong merged models become expert foundations for later rounds, so the search can build on its own successes. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, with robust performance on both seen and unseen tasks. The contribution is a learned search mechanism for model composition: the merging process uses trained generators even though the underlying motivation is composition without conventional model retraining.
summary.tldr: EvoGM learns to propose better model-merging coefficients from previous search outcomes and improves performance across seen and unseen tasks.

title: EvoGM: Learning to Merge LLMs via Evolutionary Generative Optimization

abstract: Representation alignment (REPA) has been investigated to accelerate diffusion training, but we observe that regularizing intermediate representations in diffusion Transformers (DiT) may implicitly entangle latents and limit generative capacity. To address this issue, we propose ReGen, a hierarchical multi-prompt representation generation framework that jointly estimates multiple vector fields for both representations and data within a single diffusion model. We further introduce generalized flow matching (GFM) to improve the generalization of conditional flow matching (CFM). We validate ReGen on single-stage waveform diffusion models including neural audio codec and Wave-VAE. ReGen significantly improves waveform generation quality from highly compressed latent representations at 12.5 Hz. We also present ReGenVoice, a latent diffusion model (LDM)-based text-to-speech model that achieves strong speech intelligibility (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) with a small dataset. Moreover, operating the LDM at 6.25 Hz with rich semantic and acoustic latent representation enables efficient training and sampling, requiring only 1 day of training on 4 GPUs and fast inference with an RTF of 0.08. Audio samples are available at https://regenvoice.github.io/demo/

summary.tldr: ReGen jointly models representations and waveforms to improve compressed-latent audio generation and support efficient text-to-speech.

title: ReGen: Hierarchical Multi-Prompt Representation Generation for Efficient Waveform Diffusion Models

abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced the field of embodied manipulation by harnessing broad world knowledge and strong generalization. However, current VLA models still face several key challenges, including limited reasoning capability, lack of status monitoring, and difficulty in self-correction. In this paper, we introduce Sentinel-VLA, a metacognitive VLA model equipped with an active “sentinel” module to monitor real-time execution status. Only when necessary, such as during initial planning or upon detecting an error, the model triggers a dynamic reasoning or formulate error recovery solutions. This on-demand reasoning mechanism ensures robust decision-making while minimizing computational overhead. Notably, all training data (spanning 44 tasks and over 2.6 million transitions) is automatically generated and annotated through our designed pipeline. We also propose the Self-Evolving Continual Learning (SECL) algorithm, which allows Sentinel-VLA to identify its capability boundaries and automatically collect data for expansion, paired with Orthogonal Continual Adapter (OC-Adapter) to constrain parameter updates to an orthogonal space, thereby preventing catastrophic forgetting. Real-world experiments demonstrate that Sentinel-VLA boosts the task success rate by over 30% compared to the SOTA model, PI0. We will open-source all the code, weights, and data generation pipeline.

This sentinel tracks execution status in real time and triggers reasoning when needed, including during initial planning or after detecting an error that requires recovery.

On-demand reasoning is intended to support robust decisions while keeping computational overhead low. An Orthogonal Continual Adapter constrains parameter updates to an orthogonal space to prevent catastrophic forgetting. In real-world experiments, Sentinel-VLA improves task success rate by over 30% compared with PI0. The reported result supports combining execution monitoring and selective reasoning with mechanisms for expanding capabilities while retaining prior learning.
summary.tldr: Sentinel-VLA monitors robot execution, triggers reasoning and recovery when needed, and supports continued learning through automatically collected data.

title: Sentinel-VLA: A Metacognitive VLA Model with Active Status Monitoring for Dynamic Reasoning and Error Recovery

abstract: Accelerating exploration in visual reinforcement learning under sparse rewards remains challenging due to the substantial task-irrelevant variations. Despite advances in intrinsic exploration, many methods either assume access to low-dimensional states or lack task-aware exploration strategies, thereby rendering them fragile in visual domains. To bridge this gap, we present TEB, a Task-aware Exploration approach that tightly couples task-relevant representations with exploration through a predictive Bisimulation metric. Specifically, TEB leverages the metric not only to learn behaviorally grounded task representations but also to measure global intrinsic novelty over the learned latent space. To realize this, we first theoretically mitigate the representation collapse of degenerate bisimulation metrics under sparse rewards by internally introducing a simple but effective predicted reward differential term. Building on this robust metric, we further introduce potential-based global exploration bonuses over anchor states, which measure the relative novelty between observations over the latent space. Extensive experiments on MetaWorld and Maze2D show that TEB achieves superior exploration ability and outperforms recent baselines.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning agents can encounter large changes in appearance that matter little to their task. With sparse rewards, exploration can therefore be distracted by irrelevant variation. TEB ties exploration to a learned representation of behavioral relevance, using a predictive bisimulation metric both to shape that representation and to measure novelty within it.

Sparse rewards can cause degenerate bisimulation metrics to collapse representations, obscuring useful distinctions between states. TEB introduces a predicted reward differential term, with a theoretical account of how it mitigates that collapse. Building on the resulting metric, potential-based exploration bonuses use anchor states to measure relative novelty across the latent space.

Experiments on MetaWorld and Maze2D report stronger exploration and better performance than recent baselines. The central contribution is the coupling between what the agent represents and what it considers worth exploring. Task-relevant distinctions guide the representation, and that same representation guides intrinsic novelty, helping exploration focus on meaningful behavioral differences rather than simply on changing visual observations.
summary.tldr: TEB uses a predictive behavioral metric to learn task-relevant visual representations and guide exploration through latent-space novelty.

title: Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric

abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing enables privacy-preserving, always-on edge perception, but its measurements are often sparse, temporally irregular, and corrupted by high-frequency noise. Existing mmWave pipelines predominantly rely on artificial neural networks (ANNs), which achieve robustness through extensive preprocessing or deep architectures, thereby limiting their efficiency on edge devices. In this work, we study spiking neural networks (SNNs) for mmWave sensing from a mechanism–data alignment perspective. By leveraging the low-pass filtering behavior of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) dynamics, we analyze how their implicit temporal filtering interacts with the frequency structure of mmWave signals. Our analysis shows that when discriminative information resides in low-to-mid frequencies, LIF dynamics can inherently suppress high-frequency noise, clarifying when and why SNNs outperform ANNs. Based on this insight, we derive a principled criterion for configuring the membrane decay factor by matching the effective bandwidth of LIF dynamics to the data’s discriminative spectral content. Experimental results across four widely used mmWave datasets validate the proposed frequency-matching hypothesis, yielding an average test-accuracy improvement of 6.22% and a 3.64$\times$ reduction in theoretical energy consumption relative to ANN baselines, under a unified evaluation protocol.

paragraphs: Millimeter-wave sensing produces measurements that can be sparse, irregularly timed, and contaminated by rapid fluctuations. The paper investigates whether the temporal behavior of spiking neurons can help process these signals efficiently. Its focus is the match between the sensing data's frequency content and the dynamics of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons.

These neurons act as low-pass filters, reducing fast changes while retaining slower variation. The analysis shows why that behavior can help when information needed to distinguish inputs lies in low-to-middle frequencies and noise occupies higher frequencies. From this condition, the authors derive a criterion for choosing the membrane decay factor so the neuron's effective bandwidth matches useful spectral information.

Across four mmWave datasets under a shared evaluation protocol, the method produces a reported average test-accuracy improvement of 6.22% and a 3.64-fold reduction in theoretical energy consumption relative to artificial-neural-network baselines. These results support frequency matching as an explanation and configuration principle for the tested spiking models. The energy comparison concerns theoretical consumption, and the mechanism depends on where discriminative information resides.
summary.tldr: Matching spiking-neuron dynamics to useful mmWave signal frequencies improves tested accuracy and theoretical energy efficiency.

title: Frequency Matching in Spiking Neural Networks for mmWave Sensing

abstract: Cross-resolution person re-identification (CR-ReID) remains challenging in practical surveillance, where camera quality and capture distance lead to substantial resolution gaps between low-resolution (LR) queries and high-resolution (HR) gallery images. Prior approaches commonly rely on super-resolution (SR) or resolution-invariant representation learning, which often increases system complexity and may not directly address the feature mismatch induced by resolution degradation. In this work, we report a new empirical finding from a dedicated analysis in which identity-specific variation is averaged out: the HR–LR feature discrepancy produced by standard ReID backbones exhibits a consistent, resolution-related semantic direction in the embedding space. We further support this observation with statistical analyses based on Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) and Pearson correlation analysis. Motivated by this finding, we propose Vector Panning Feature Alignment (VPFA), a lightweight post-hoc module that learns to pan LR features along the learned resolution direction to obtain pseudo-HR representations. VPFA operates after feature extraction and can be integrated into existing ReID systems with negligible overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple CR-ReID benchmarks show that VPFA achieves state-of-the-art performance while improving efficiency compared to SR-based or jointly trained alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/ashmentlzw/VPFA

paragraphs: Person re-identification becomes harder when a low-resolution query must be matched against high-resolution reference images. Differences in camera quality or capture distance can shift the extracted features. The paper investigates that mismatch directly, seeking an efficient way to align representations produced at different resolutions.

In an analysis that averages out identity-specific variation, the authors find a consistent resolution-related direction in the feature differences produced by standard re-identification backbones. Canonical Correlation Analysis and Pearson correlation analyses support this empirical observation. Motivated by it, Vector Panning Feature Alignment learns to shift low-resolution features along a learned resolution direction, producing pseudo-high-resolution representations.

VPFA operates after feature extraction and can be added to existing systems with negligible overhead. This makes feature alignment a lightweight additional stage in the recognition pipeline. Experiments on multiple cross-resolution benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance and better efficiency than super-resolution-based or jointly trained alternatives. The findings support using the observed directional structure of resolution mismatch to improve matching without reconstructing higher-resolution input images.
summary.tldr: VPFA improves cross-resolution person matching by shifting low-resolution features along an empirically observed resolution-related direction.

title: Resolution as a Direction: Vector-Panning Feature Alignment for Cross-Resolution Re-Identification

abstract: Recent benchmarks reveal that single-cell perturbation response models are often outperformed by simply predicting the dataset mean. Through large-scale in silico simulations, together with analyses of two real-world perturbation datasets, we trace this anomaly to a metric artifact: unweighted error metrics systematically reward mean predictions when perturbation effects are sparse. To address this limitation, we introduce differentially expressed gene (DEG)-aware metrics—weighted mean-squared error (WMSE) and weighted delta $R^{2}$ ($R^{2}_{w}(\Delta)$)—that sensitively measure error in niche, perturbation-specific signals. We further propose explicit negative and positive performance baselines to calibrate these metrics. Under this framework, the mean baseline sinks to null performance, while genuinely informative predictors are correctly rewarded. Finally, we show that using WMSE as a training objective reduces mode collapse and improves predictive performance across multiple model architectures.

paragraphs: Single-cell perturbation models aim to predict how gene expression changes after an intervention. Yet recent benchmarks often rank them below simply predicting the dataset mean. Through large-scale simulations and analysis of two real datasets, this paper traces that surprising outcome to how prediction error is measured when perturbation effects are sparse.

Unweighted metrics systematically reward mean predictions because the relatively few affected genes contribute only a small part of the overall score. The authors introduce metrics aware of differentially expressed genes: weighted mean-squared error and weighted delta R-squared. These metrics emphasize perturbation-specific signals. Explicit negative and positive performance baselines provide reference points for interpreting the resulting scores.

Under this framework, predicting the mean receives null performance, while informative predictions receive appropriate credit. The authors also use weighted mean-squared error as a training objective, reducing mode collapse and improving performance across multiple model architectures. The findings connect evaluation and learning: emphasizing the sparse response signal changes both which models appear useful and which predictions training encourages.
summary.tldr: Gene-aware weighting corrects metrics that favor mean predictions and improves training for sparse single-cell perturbation responses.

title: Needles in the Haystack: Addressing Signal Dilution Improves scRNA-seq Perturbation Response Modeling and Evaluation

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved remarkable success across various vision tasks, yet their deployment is often hindered by prohibitive computational costs. While structured weight pruning and token compression have emerged as promising solutions, they suffer from prolonged retraining and inter-layer dependencies that complicate optimization, respectively. We propose ToaSt, a decoupled framework applying specialized strategies to distinct ViT components. We apply coupled head-wise structured pruning to Multi-Head Self-Attention modules, leveraging attention operation characteristics to enhance robustness. For Feed-Forward Networks (over 60% of FLOPs), we introduce Token Channel Selection (TCS), a training-free method that filters redundant noise channels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across nine diverse models, including DeiT, ViT-MAE, and Swin Transformer, demonstrate that ToaSt achieves superior trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency, consistently outperforming existing baselines. On ViT-MAE-Huge, ToaSt achieves 88.52% accuracy (+1.64%p) with 39.4% FLOPs reduction. ToaSt also transfers effectively to diverse downstream tasks (COCO detection, ADE20K segmentation, CIFAR-100 classification), achieving 52.2 versus 51.9 mAP on COCO. Code: https://github.com/SHANNonLab-HUFS/ToaSt.
originalAbstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved remarkable success across various vision tasks, yet their deployment is often hindered by prohibitive computational costs. While structured weight pruning and token compression have emerged as promising solutions, they suffer from prolonged retraining and inter-layer dependencies that complicate optimization, respectively. We propose ToaSt, a decoupled framework applying specialized strategies to distinct ViT components. We apply coupled head-wise structured pruning to Multi-Head Self-Attention modules, leveraging attention operation characteristics to enhance robustness. For Feed-Forward Networks (over 60% of FLOPs), we introduce Token Channel Selection (TCS), a training-free method that filters redundant noise channels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across nine diverse models, including DeiT, ViT-MAE, and Swin Transformer, demonstrate that ToaSt achieves superior trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency, consistently outperforming existing baselines. On ViT-MAE-Huge, ToaSt achieves 88.52% accuracy (+1.64%p) with 39.4% FLOPs reduction. ToaSt also transfers effectively to diverse downstream tasks (COCO detection, ADE20K segmentation, CIFAR-100 classification), achieving 52.2 versus 51.9 mAP on COCO. Code: https://github.com/SHANNonLab-HUFS/ToaSt.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can be expensive to deploy, and different parts of the model present different compression challenges. Structured weight pruning may require lengthy retraining, while token compression introduces dependencies between layers that complicate optimization. ToaSt addresses these issues with separate strategies for attention modules and feed-forward networks.

For multi-head self-attention, ToaSt uses coupled head-wise structured pruning designed around the attention operation. For feed-forward networks, which account for more than 60% of floating-point operations in the paper’s framing, it introduces Token Channel Selection. This component filters redundant noise channels during inference without training, targeting a major source of computation.

Evaluations across nine models, including DeiT, ViT-MAE, and Swin Transformer, show better accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs than the tested baselines. On ViT-MAE-Huge, ToaSt reaches 88.52% accuracy, an increase of 1.64 percentage points, while reducing floating-point operations by 39.4%. It also transfers to detection, segmentation, and classification tasks, including COCO detection performance of 52.2 versus 51.9 mAP. The findings support tailoring compression to each component’s computational role.
summary.tldr: ToaSt combines attention pruning with training-free feed-forward channel selection to improve Vision Transformer accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs.

title: ToaSt: Token Channel Selection and Structured Pruning for Efficient ViT

abstract: Reasoning post-training with GRPO is typically built on static uniformity: uniform prompt sampling and a fixed number of rollouts per prompt. For heterogeneous, heavy-tailed reasoning data, this wastes compute on already-solved patterns while under-training the long tail of hard problems. We cast GRPO post-training as two independent GDRO games (not coupled) over dynamic difficulty groups defined by an online train-time pass@$n$ statistic (computed from the rollouts used for GRPO updates): a data adversary that reshapes prompt sampling and a compute adversary that redistributes rollouts. Prompt-GDRO applies multiplicative-weights reweighting over bins (with an EMA-debiased difficulty score) to upweight persistently hard groups without frequency bias. Rollout-GDRO allocates rollouts across bins under a fixed mean budget via a shadow-price controller, improving gradient information efficiency on high-uncertainty groups while preserving the mean train-time rollout budget. Our approach is principled and theory-driven: we provide no-regret guarantees for the Prompt-GDRO game (via an entropy-regularized GDRO surrogate) and a variance-proxy analysis that yields a square-root optimal compute allocation for Rollout-GDRO. On DAPO 14.1k with Qwen3-Base (1.7B/4B/8B), each controller improves pass@8 by 9–13% over GRPO; targeted Qwen3-4B reruns reproduce the Prompt-GDRO gap under a second seed, show second-seed Rollout-GDRO gains on four of five comparable benchmarks, and show low sensitivity to several key hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Reasoning reinforcement learning often samples prompts uniformly and generates the same number of attempted answers for each. This can spend computation on already-mastered patterns while neglecting difficult ones. The paper groups prompts by difficulty measured online from the same answer attempts used for GRPO updates, then studies two independent allocation controllers.

Prompt-GDRO changes how often difficulty groups are sampled, using multiplicative reweighting and a corrected moving difficulty estimate to emphasize persistently hard groups without frequency bias. Rollout-GDRO changes how many answer attempts each group receives while maintaining a fixed mean budget. Its controller directs computation toward groups where additional attempts provide more useful gradient information.

The theory supplies no-regret guarantees for the prompt-sampling surrogate and a variance-based analysis supporting square-root compute allocation. On DAPO 14.1k with three Qwen3-Base sizes, each controller improves pass@8 by 9–13% over GRPO. Targeted second-seed tests reproduce the prompt-controller gap and show rollout-controller gains on four of five comparable benchmarks. The findings support both allocation strategies separately, rather than establishing a coupled controller.
summary.tldr: Two independent controllers improve reasoning training by adapting prompt sampling or redistributing answer attempts across dynamically measured difficulty groups.

title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization-Driven RL for LLM Reasoning

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit puzzling failures in multi-object visual tasks, such as hallucinating non-existent elements or failing to identify the most similar objects among distractions. While these errors mirror human cognitive constraints, such as the "Binding Problem”, the internal mechanisms driving them in artificial systems remain poorly understood. Here, we propose a mechanistic insight by analyzing the representational geometry of open-weight VLMs (Qwen, InternVL, Gemma), comparing methodologies to distill "concept vectors” - latent directions encoding visual concepts. We validate our concept vectors via steering interventions that reliably manipulate model behavior in both simplified and naturalistic vision tasks (e.g., forcing the model to perceive a red flower as blue). We observe that the geometric overlap between these vectors strongly correlates with specific error patterns, offering a grounded quantitative framework to understand how internal representations shape model behavior and drive visual failures.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can struggle with scenes containing multiple objects, sometimes reporting absent elements or confusing which objects are most similar. This paper investigates these failures through the geometry of internal representations. It studies open-weight models from the Qwen, InternVL, and Gemma families to connect visual errors with how concepts are encoded.

The authors compare ways of extracting concept vectors: directions in the model's internal space associated with visual concepts. They test these vectors by intervening on model processing and observing changes in behavior. The interventions reliably steer responses in simplified and naturalistic tasks, including making a model perceive a red flower as blue.

The study finds that geometric overlap between concept vectors strongly correlates with particular error patterns. This supplies a quantitative connection between internal representation structure and visible failures. The steering experiments establish that the extracted directions can influence behavior, while the overlap analysis links their geometry to mistakes. Together, these results provide a mechanistic perspective on how overlapping visual representations may contribute to multi-object confusion.
summary.tldr: Steerable visual concept vectors reveal a strong correlation between representational overlap and specific vision-language model errors.

title: The Geometry of Representational Failures in Vision Language Models

abstract: Recently, the spiking neural networks (SNNs) have shown great promise in enhancing AI task performance by utilizing the brain-inspired and energy-efficient computational paradigm via the binary (0/1) spikes. Modern SNNs, especially those based on transformers, often require FPGA accelerators or neuromorphic chips to enable spike-driven computations. However, this domain-specific hardware is not always accessible on commodity edge devices like NVIDIA Jetsons, which may degrade SNNs’ energy efficiency due to massive computational waste on inactive "0" spikes and finally undermine the usage boundary. This limitation raises an interesting question: is it possible to make SNNs edge-friendly and tame the computations mostly on active "1" spikes? We present the answer yes and propose Spik4lite, which serves as a lightweight plug-and-play module to significantly improve SNN’s performance between model accuracy and computational efficiency. The key is to refactor SNN’s channel-wise neuromorphic sparsity by zeroing out low-efficiency channels while proactively compensating for the eliminated spikes. Different from prior methods mainly focusing on optimizing the theoretical synaptic operations, our design philosophy can evolve the SNNs into a physically compact manner, thus inherently saving more computational and energy costs. Extensive experiments based on real edge devices show that Spik4lite can be integrated into existing SNN baselines to further improve their accuracy-and-efficiency performance, guaranteeing the model accuracy while saving the computational and energy costs.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through binary spikes, offering a route to energy-efficient computation. However, commodity edge devices may still spend substantial work processing inactive zero spikes. Without specialized hardware, a network’s sparse activity therefore does not necessarily translate into reduced computation or energy use.

Spik4lite is a lightweight module that reorganizes this sparsity across channels. It removes low-efficiency channels while compensating for the spikes that are eliminated. The intended result is a physically more compact network, so efficiency comes from reducing actual computational structure as well as exploiting sparse activity. This targets the gap between theoretical savings in synaptic operations and savings on accessible devices.

Experiments on real edge hardware show that Spik4lite can be integrated into existing spiking-network baselines to improve their accuracy–efficiency trade-off. The authors report preserving accuracy while reducing computational and energy costs. These findings support a practical route for deploying spiking models on commodity devices, where the representation of sparsity must match how the hardware executes the network.
summary.tldr: Spik4lite makes spiking networks physically more compact to reduce real edge-device computation and energy use while preserving accuracy.

title: Spik4lite: Refactoring Neuromorphic Sparsity for Efficient Spiking Neural Networks on Commodity Edge Devices

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems typically rely on a single retriever and a single set of hyperparameters, despite facing highly heterogeneous queries that range from simple factoid questions to complex multi-hop reasoning. We propose a method that automatically selects a small, diverse subset of retrievers (a portfolio) from a large pool of candidates, to cover different regions of the target query distribution. We formalize this setting via an expected best-of-$k$ objective over the query distribution and show that it admits an efficient portfolio construction algorithm with near-optimal guarantees. Across multiple QA benchmarks, our learned portfolios and router pipeline consistently outperform single-retriever and naive multi-retriever baselines on both retrieval metrics and answer quality. In addition, compared to inference-time hyperparameter tuning approaches, fixed portfolios enable parallel retrieval and LLM calls, achieving comparable (and sometimes better) accuracy with substantially lower latency and token cost.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation systems often use one retriever with fixed settings for every query. Yet a short factual question and a question requiring several reasoning steps can benefit from different retrieval choices. This paper selects a small, diverse portfolio from a larger pool of retrievers to cover different parts of the target query distribution.

The selection problem is formalized through an expected best-of-k objective: the portfolio should contain useful retrieval options across the queries it is expected to face. The authors derive an efficient construction algorithm with near-optimal guarantees for that objective. A router pipeline then works with the learned portfolio, connecting the selection procedure to an adaptive question-answering system.

Across multiple question-answering benchmarks, the approach improves retrieval metrics and answer quality over single-retriever and naive multi-retriever baselines. Fixed portfolios also allow retrieval and language-model calls to run in parallel. Compared with tuning retrieval hyperparameters during inference, this yields comparable, and sometimes better, accuracy with substantially lower latency and token cost. The contribution links principled portfolio selection to practical deployment efficiency.
summary.tldr: Selecting and routing among small retriever portfolios improves tested RAG quality while reducing latency and token cost relative to inference-time tuning.

title: Retriever Portfolios: A Principled Approach to Adaptive RAG

abstract: In many applications of LLMs, natural language responses often have an underlying structure such as representing discrete labels, numerical values, or graphs. Yet, existing decoding and uncertainty estimation methods operate only in language space and largely disregard structural information. We address this by modeling LLM outputs directly in a task-dependent latent structure. By equipping this structure with a dissimilarity measure, we can compute Bayes-optimal responses. These are not selected from sampled generations but are newly synthesized by combining individual responses in the latent space. Across different tasks, Bayes-optimal responses consistently outperform standard decoding methods like beam search. Moreover, quantifying uncertainty via the induced Bayesian risk captures variations in terms of the latent structure and improves alignment with output quality and correctness. Our decision-theoretic framework is applicable to any problem that admits a latent response structure and enables reliable task-aware LLM predictions.

paragraphs: A language-model response often represents something more structured than text, such as a label, number, or graph. Conventional decoding and uncertainty methods can overlook that structure by operating entirely on language. This paper models responses in a task-dependent latent structure so that answer selection and uncertainty reflect the underlying task.

The framework equips that structure with a measure of dissimilarity and computes a Bayes-optimal response. It can synthesize a new answer by combining individual responses in the latent space, rather than being restricted to selecting one sampled generation. This matters when the useful information spread across several responses can be combined into a better structured answer.

Across the evaluated tasks, these synthesized responses consistently outperform standard decoding methods such as beam search. Uncertainty measured through the associated Bayesian risk also aligns better with quality and correctness because it captures variation in task structure. The framework applies to problems that admit a latent response structure, making that representation the basis for both generation and confidence assessment.
summary.tldr: Modeling answers in task-specific structures enables better synthesized responses and uncertainty estimates more aligned with correctness.

title: Task-Awareness Improves LLM Generations and Uncertainty

abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) strategies have emerged as a lightweight approach to boost reasoning in large language models, but their applicability to vision-language models (VLMs) remains unclear. We present a systematic study of TTC for visual reasoning across seven open-source VLMs and six benchmarks, revisiting two paradigms: (i) feature-based scoring of chain-of-thought (CoT) traces and (ii) confidence-based aggregation via majority voting (MV). In the single-model setting, feature cues (e.g., length, pivot words) fail to improve accuracy, while MV yields only modest, CoT-dependent gains. To explain this limitation, we theoretically show that the voting method’s effectiveness depends on prediction diversity: when outputs are highly correlated, the benefit of voting vanishes. In contrast, multi-model ensembles introduce stronger diversity through architectural differences, training data, and scale, making them both more realistic and more promising for TTC. However, MV treats all models equally, leaving it vulnerable to correlated errors from weaker models. To address this, we propose Entropy-based TTC, which selects the most confident prediction based on predictive entropy. Our method reduces to MV in the single-model case but, in ensembles, leverages confidence disparities to prioritize stronger models. We prove that our method theoretically outperforms MV under mild dependence assumptions, and empirically show that it consistently surpasses both MV and the best individual model across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks. This demonstrates that smaller models can enhance, rather than hinder, larger ones when combined appropriately, unlocking ensemble gains not achievable with existing TTC strategies.

paragraphs: Generating more answers at inference time helps only if the additional predictions contribute useful information. summary.tldr: Diverse vision-language ensembles benefit from entropy-based prediction selection, outperforming majority voting and the best individual model in the reported evaluations.

title: Diversity Matters: Revisiting Test-Time Compute in Vision-Language Models

abstract: Muon updates matrix parameters via the matrix sign of the gradient and has shown strong empirical gains, yet its dynamics and scaling behavior remain unclear in theory. We study Muon in a linear associative memory model with softmax retrieval and a hierarchical frequency spectrum over query–answer pairs, with and without label noise. In this setting, we show that Gradient Descent (GD) learns frequency components at highly imbalanced rates, leading to slow convergence bottlenecked by low-frequency components. In contrast, the Muon optimizer mitigates this imbalance, leading to faster and more uniform progress. Specifically, in the noiseless case, Muon achieves an exponential speedup over GD; in the noisy case with a power-law frequency spectrum, we derive Muon’s scaling law and demonstrate its superior scaling efficiency over GD. Furthermore, we show that Muon can be interpreted as an implicit matrix preconditioner arising from adaptive task alignment and block-symmetric gradient structure. In contrast, the preconditioner with coordinate-wise sign operator could match Muon under oracle access to unknown task representations, which is infeasible for SignGD in practice. Experiments on synthetic long-tail classification and LLaMA-style pre-training corroborate the theory.

This paper studies why that operation can help in a linear associative-memory model with softmax retrieval, where query-answer pairs occur at different frequencies. In this setting, ordinary gradient descent learns frequency components unevenly, allowing rare components to become a bottleneck.

The analysis shows that Muon reduces this imbalance and makes learning progress more uniform. Without label noise, the authors establish an exponential speedup over gradient descent in the studied model. summary.tldr: In a structured associative-memory model, Muon balances learning across frequency components and achieves stronger convergence and scaling than gradient descent.

title: Muon in Associative Memory Learning: Training Dynamics and Scaling Laws

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of distributed clients while protecting privacy. To enhance generalization capability in FL, prototype-based FL is in the spotlight, since shared global prototypes offer semantic anchors for aligning client-specific local prototypes. However, existing methods update global prototypes at the prototype-level via averaging local prototypes or refining global anchors, which often leads to semantic drift across clients and subsequently yields a misaligned global signal. To alleviate this issue, we introduce hyper-prototypes, defined by a set of learnable global class-wise prototypes to preserve underlying semantic knowledge across clients. The hyper-prototypes are optimized via gradient matching to align with class-relevant characteristics distilled directly from clients’ real samples, rather than prototype-level descriptors. We further propose FedHPro, a Federated Hyper-Prototype Learning framework, to leverage hyper-prototypes to promote inter-class separability via mutual-contrastive learning with client-specific margin, while encouraging intra-class uniformity through a consistency penalty. Comprehensive experiments under diverse heterogeneous scenarios confirm that 1) hyper-prototypes produce a more semantically consistent global signal, and 2) FedHPro achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Prototype-based federated learning shares class representations that help clients align their locally learned features. However, averaging local prototypes or refining global anchors can allow their meanings to drift across clients. FedHPro addresses this problem by learning global class representatives, called hyper-prototypes, that aim to preserve more consistent semantic information.

The key change concerns how these representatives are optimized. Gradient matching connects the hyper-prototypes to class-relevant characteristics distilled directly from clients’ real examples, rather than relying only on prototype-level summaries. FedHPro then uses mutual-contrastive learning with client-specific margins to separate different classes, alongside a consistency penalty that encourages representations within each class to agree.

Experiments cover several forms of data heterogeneity across clients. The authors report that hyper-prototypes provide a more semantically consistent global signal and that FedHPro achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets. The findings support improving the source of shared class information, as well as the objectives that use it, when aligning clients whose local data differ.
summary.tldr: FedHPro uses gradient matching to learn shared class prototypes that provide more consistent guidance across heterogeneous federated clients.

title: FedHPro: Federated Hyper-Prototype Learning via Gradient Matching

abstract: Computational identification of lipid-binding proteins is critical for both fundamental research and therapeutic development. Existing models are typically trained in a fully supervised manner, treating unlabeled samples as negatives. However, missing evidence does not imply non-binding, leading to systematic false negatives. Pocket-level lipid-binding prediction also remains underexplored compared to residue- or sequence-level approaches. To bridge these gaps, we present LipoPU, a pocket-centric predictor that formulates lipid-binding learning under a ranking-based positive-unlabeled objective, and supports both binary lipid-binding detection and multi-label lipid category prediction. LipoPU learns an attention-based pocket representation that is robust to ambiguous pocket definitions while providing residue-level interpretability. Experiments show consistent gains over supervised baselines and prior pocket-level work, and a structural case study recovers a literature-supported allosteric lipid-binding pocket while highlighting biologically informative residues.

paragraphs: Predicting where lipids bind to proteins is useful for biological research and therapeutic development. A central training problem is that an unrecorded interaction does not necessarily mean binding cannot occur. Models that label all unobserved cases as negatives therefore introduce systematic false negatives. LipoPU addresses this ambiguity while focusing on protein pockets, a less explored level than sequences or individual residues.

The method uses a ranking-based positive-unlabeled learning objective, distinguishing confirmed binding examples from cases with unknown status. It supports both deciding whether a pocket binds lipids and predicting multiple lipid categories. An attention-based pocket representation is designed to handle ambiguity in pocket definitions while exposing which residues contribute to the prediction.

Experiments report consistent improvements over supervised baselines and previous pocket-level methods. A structural case study also recovers an allosteric lipid-binding pocket supported by the literature and highlights biologically informative residues. These findings connect the treatment of uncertain labels with useful pocket-level predictions, while the residue-level interpretation helps explain what information the model uses.
summary.tldr: LipoPU predicts lipid-binding pockets using positive-unlabeled learning, avoiding the assumption that every unrecorded interaction is a negative example.

title: LipoPU: Pocket-level Prediction of Lipid-Protein Interactions via Positive-Unlabeled Learning

abstract: During conversational interactions, humans subconsciously engage in concurrent thinking while listening to a speaker. Although this internal cognitive processing may not always manifest as explicit linguistic structures, it is instrumental in formulating high-quality responses. Inspired by this cognitive phenomenon, we propose a novel Full-duplex LAtent and Internal Reasoning method named FLAIR that conducts latent thinking simultaneously with speech perception. Unlike conventional "thinking" mechanisms in NLP, which require post-hoc generation, our approach aligns seamlessly with spoken dialogue systems: during the user’s speaking phase, it recursively feeds the latent embedding output from the previous step into the next step, enabling continuous reasoning that strictly adheres to causality without introducing additional latency. To enable this latent reasoning, we design an Evidence Lower Bound-based objective that supports efficient supervised finetuning via teacher forcing, circumventing the need for explicit reasoning annotations. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this think-while-listening design, which achieves competitive results on a range of speech benchmarks. Furthermore, FLAIR robustly handles conversational dynamics and attains competitive performance on full-duplex interaction metrics.

title: The Silent Thought: Modeling Internal Cognition in Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Models via Latent Reasoning

abstract: Model distillation enables efficient emulation of frontier large language models (LLMs), creating a need for robust mechanisms to detect when a third-party student model has trained on a teacher model’s outputs. However, existing fingerprinting techniques that could be used to detect such distillation rely on heuristic perturbations that impose a steep trade-off between generation quality and fingerprinting strength, often requiring significant degradation of utility to ensure the fingerprint is effectively internalized by the student. We introduce antidistillation fingerprinting (ADFP), a principled approach that aligns the fingerprinting objective with the student’s learning dynamics. Building upon the gradient-based framework of antidistillation sampling, ADFP utilizes a proxy model to identify and sample tokens that directly maximize the expected detectability of the fingerprint in the student after fine-tuning, rather than relying on the incidental absorption of the un-targeted biases of a more naive watermark. Experiments on GSM8K, OASST1, and MBPP demonstrate that ADFP achieves a significant Pareto improvement over state-of-the-art baselines, yielding stronger detection confidence with minimal impact on utility across mathematical reasoning, dialogue, and code generation, even when the student model’s architecture is unknown.

paragraphs: When a student language model learns from a teacher model’s outputs, the teacher’s owner may want to detect that training relationship. Existing fingerprinting approaches alter generated text to leave recognizable traces, but stronger traces can come at a substantial cost to the usefulness of the teacher’s responses.

Antidistillation fingerprinting selects those alterations with the student’s learning process in mind. It builds on a gradient-based sampling framework and uses a proxy model to identify tokens expected to make the fingerprint more detectable after student fine-tuning. The central change is to optimize for what training will leave inside the student, rather than simply introduce biases and hope they survive.

Experiments on GSM8K, OASST1, and MBPP cover mathematical reasoning, dialogue, and code generation. The authors report a better trade-off between detection confidence and utility than leading baselines, including when the student architecture is unknown. The findings suggest that modeling fingerprint absorption can improve attribution without imposing the same degree of output degradation.
summary.tldr: Antidistillation fingerprinting chooses teacher outputs to make subsequent student training more detectable while minimally affecting usefulness.

title: Antidistillation Fingerprinting

abstract: Policy mirror descent (PMD) provides a principled framework for reinforcement learning (RL) by iteratively solving KL-regularized policy improvement subproblems. While this approach has been adopted in training advanced LLMs such as Kimi K1.5/K2, the ideal closed-form PMD updates require reliable partition function estimation, a significant challenge when working with limited rollouts in the vast action spaces of LLMs. We investigate a practical algorithm, termed PMD-mean, that approximates the log-partition term with the mean reward under the sampling policy and performs regression in log-policy space. Specifically, we characterize the population solution of PMD-mean and demonstrate that it implicitly optimizes mirror descent subproblems with an adaptive mixed KL–$\chi^2$ regularizer. This additional $\chi^2$ regularization constrains large probability changes, producing more conservative updates when expected rewards are low and enhancing robustness against finite-sample estimation errors. Experiments on math reasoning tasks show that PMD-mean improves stability and remains competitive in the stale-rollout settings while enabling higher throughput through larger rollout batches. These findings deepen our understanding of PMD-mean and illuminate pathways toward principled improvements in RL algorithms for LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/horizon-llm/OpenKimi.
