paragraphs: Policy mirror descent improves a reinforcement-learning policy through updates constrained by how far they move from a reference policy. Its ideal update requires estimating a partition function, which is difficult with limited sampled responses and a language model's enormous action space. This paper studies what happens when that difficult quantity is approximated.

The analyzed algorithm, PMD-mean, replaces the log-partition term with the sampling policy's mean reward and fits updates in log-probability space. The authors characterize its population solution and show that this substitution introduces an adaptive mixture of KL and chi-squared regularization. The additional term restrains large probability changes, yielding more conservative updates when expected rewards are low and greater robustness to finite-sample estimation errors.

Math-reasoning experiments show improved stability and competitive performance when training uses stale rollouts, meaning samples generated by an earlier policy. Larger rollout batches also support higher throughput. The central insight is that a practical approximation changes the update's regularization in a structured way, helping explain its observed training behavior.
summary.tldr: PMD-mean's partition-function approximation implicitly adds adaptive regularization that helps explain its conservative, stable policy updates.

title: Approximation of Log-Partition Function in Policy Mirror Descent Induces Implicit Regularization for LLM Post-Training

abstract: The SWE-Bench Verified leaderboard is approaching saturation, with the top system achieving 78.80%. However, we reveal that this performance is inflated: our re-evaluation demonstrates that one in five “solved” patches from the top-30 agents are semantically incorrect, passing only because weak test suites fail to expose their errors. We present SWE-ABS, an adversarial framework that strengthens test suites through a two-stage pipeline: (1) coverage-driven augmentation utilizing program slicing to target untested code regions, and (2) mutation-driven adversarial testing that synthesizes plausible-but-incorrect patches to expose semantic blind spots. On SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances), SWE-ABS strengthens 50.2% of instances (a $25.1\times$ improvement over prior work) and rejects 19.78% of previously passing patches. Consequently, the top agent’s score decreases from 78.80% to 62.20%, causing significant leaderboard reshuffling (e.g., the top-ranked agent drops to 5th place).

paragraphs: A software patch can pass a benchmark's tests while still implementing the wrong behavior. This paper finds that roughly one in five previously solved patches from the top 30 agents on SWE-Bench Verified is semantically incorrect. Weak test suites allow these errors to remain undetected, inflating the apparent rate of successful repairs.

SWE-ABS strengthens those suites in two stages. Coverage-driven augmentation uses program slicing to target untested code regions. Mutation-driven adversarial testing then synthesizes plausible but incorrect patches to expose gaps in the tests' ability to distinguish correct behavior. Together, these stages address both missing execution coverage and semantic blind spots.

Across the benchmark's 500 instances, SWE-ABS strengthens 50.2% of instances, a 25.1-fold improvement over prior work, and rejects 19.78% of previously passing patches. The top agent's score falls from 78.80% to 62.20%, and that agent moves to fifth place. These changes show that stronger tests can materially alter both measured success and comparative rankings in the evaluated benchmark.
summary.tldr: SWE-ABS strengthens software-repair tests and rejects nearly one fifth of previously passing patches, substantially changing benchmark scores and rankings.

title: SWE-ABS: Adversarial Benchmark Strengthening Exposes Inflated Success Rates on Test-based Benchmark

abstract: We propose Parameterized Diffusion Policy (PDP), a framework that learns a diffusion policy parameterized in a smooth continuous space. By structuring a latent manifold such that distances between latents’ values reflect the semantic similarity of physical trajectories, we transform diffusion from a mechanism of stochastic diversity into a precise tool for behavior steering. Our approach also enables smooth interpolation between known strategies and efficient generalization to novel constraints without the need to update policy weights. We demonstrate that PDP significantly improves adaptation performance on complex multimodal benchmarks in both simulation and real-robot hardware compared to regular diffusion policy, particularly in scenarios requiring the discovery of novel behaviors.
originalAbstract: We propose Parameterized Diffusion Policy (PDP), a framework that learns a diffusion policy parameterized in a smooth continuous space. By structuring a latent manifold such that distances between latents’ values reflect the semantic similarity of physical trajectories, we transform diffusion from a mechanism of stochastic diversity into a precise tool for behavior steering. Our approach also enables smooth interpolation between known strategies and efficient generalization to novel constraints without the need to update policy weights. We demonstrate that PDP significantly improves adaptation performance on complex multimodal benchmarks in both simulation and real-robot hardware compared to regular diffusion policy, particularly in scenarios requiring the discovery of novel behaviors.

paragraphs: Parameterized Diffusion Policy, or PDP, aims to make the variety of behaviors produced by a diffusion policy easier to steer. The framework learns a smooth, continuous space of policy parameters in which distances reflect the semantic similarity of physical trajectories. This gives the parameter space behavioral meaning: proximity corresponds to similarity in the resulting motion.

The structured space supports smooth interpolation between known strategies and adaptation to new constraints without changing the policy's weights. The key idea is to make behavior selection accessible through this continuous representation. A policy can therefore use its learned range of trajectories as a basis for controlled adaptation, including combinations or variations beyond the strategies already known.

Experiments on complex benchmarks with multiple behavior modes, in simulation and on real robots, report significantly better adaptation than regular diffusion policy. Improvements are especially pronounced in scenarios requiring discovery of novel behaviors. The findings support organizing a diffusion policy's behavioral variation into a meaningful parameter space as a practical mechanism for steering and adaptation.
summary.tldr: PDP organizes diffusion-policy behaviors in a smooth parameter space, enabling steering and adaptation without updating policy weights.

abstract: In this paper, we present an information-theoretic approach to learning a Mahalanobis distance function. We formulate the problem as that of minimizing the differential relative entropy between two multivariate Gaussians under constraints on the distance function. We express this problem as a particular Bregman optimization problem—that of minimizing the LogDet divergence subject to linear constraints. Our resulting algorithm has several advantages over existing methods. First, our method can handle a wide variety of constraints and can optionally incorporate a prior on the distance function. Second, it is fast and scalable. Unlike most existing methods, no eigenvalue computations or semi-definite programming are required. We also present an online version and derive regret bounds for the resulting algorithm. Finally, we evaluate our method on a recent error reporting system for software called Clarify, in the context of metric learning for nearest neighbor classification, as well as on standard data sets.

Our resulting algorithm has several advantages over existing methods. First, our method can handle a wide variety of constraints and can optionally incorporate a prior on the distance function. Second, it is fast and scalable. Unlike most existing methods, no eigenvalue computations or semi-definite programming are required. We also present an online version and derive regret bounds for the resulting algorithm. Finally, we evaluate our method on a recent error reporting system for software called Clarify, in the context of metric learning for nearest neighbor classification, as well as on standard data sets.

paragraphs: A learned distance function determines which examples count as similar, affecting methods such as nearest-neighbor classification. This paper develops an information-theoretic approach to learning a Mahalanobis distance. It seeks a distance that satisfies specified constraints while minimizing a measure of difference between two multivariate Gaussian distributions.

The authors express the problem as minimizing LogDet divergence under linear constraints, placing it within Bregman optimization. The formulation accommodates a broad range of constraints and can optionally include prior information about the distance function. The resulting algorithm avoids eigenvalue computations and semidefinite programming, supporting the paper’s claim of a fast, scalable method.

An online version extends the approach to sequential learning, and the authors derive regret bounds for that algorithm. They evaluate metric learning for nearest-neighbor classification on standard datasets and in Clarify, a software error-reporting system. The contribution combines a flexible way to express distance requirements with computational advantages and an online formulation. The abstract reports these evaluations without specifying a comparative accuracy outcome.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic metric learning fits constrained Mahalanobis distances efficiently, supports optional priors, and has an online version with regret bounds.

title: Information-theoretic metric learning

abstract: One of the most common problems in machine learning and statistics consists of estimating the mean response X.beta from a vector of observations y assuming y=X.beta+epsilon where X is known, beta is a vector of parameters of interest and epsilon a vector of stochastic errors. We are particularly interested here in the case where the dimension K of beta is much higher than the dimension of y. We propose some flexible Bayesian models which can yield sparse estimates of beta. We show that as K tends to infinity, these models are closely related to a class of Levy processes. Simulations demonstrate that our models outperform significantly a range of popular alternatives.

We are particularly interested here in the case where the dimension K of beta is much higher than the dimension of y. We propose some flexible Bayesian models which can yield sparse estimates of beta. We show that as K tends to infinity, these models are closely related to a class of Levy processes. Simulations demonstrate that our models outperform significantly a range of popular alternatives.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear regression when the number of unknown coefficients greatly exceeds the number of observations. The observations are modeled as a known design matrix multiplied by a coefficient vector, plus random error. The estimation target is the mean response represented by that matrix-vector product, with particular attention to sparse coefficient estimates.

The authors propose flexible Bayesian models that can yield such sparse estimates. Sparsity means that the fitted representation can rely on a limited subset of the available coefficients, even though the parameter vector is large. This directly addresses the structure of the problem under study: many possible contributions must be considered from a much smaller observation vector.

The paper also examines what happens as the number of coefficients tends to infinity, establishing a close relationship between the proposed models and a class of Lévy processes. Simulations show significant improvements over a range of popular alternatives. The contribution thus combines a flexible sparse-regression construction, an infinite-dimensional mathematical connection, and empirical evidence from simulated problems.
summary.tldr: Flexible Bayesian regression models produce sparse estimates, connect to Lévy processes in an infinite-dimensional limit, and outperform alternatives in simulations.

title: Sparse Bayesian nonparametric regression

abstract: Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are important tools for modeling sequence data. However, they are restricted to discrete latent states, and are largely restricted to Gaussian and discrete observations. And,learning algorithms for HMMs have predominantly relied on local search heuristics, with the exception of spectral methods such as those described below. We propose a non parametric HMM that extends traditional HMMs to structured and non-Gaussian continuous distributions. Furthermore, we derive a local-minimum-free kernel spectral algorithm for learning these HMMs. We apply our method to robot vision data, slot car inertial sensor data and audio event classification data, and show that in these applications, embedded HMMs exceed the previous state-of-the-art performance.

However, they are restricted to discrete latent states, and are largely restricted to Gaussian and discrete observations. We propose a non parametric HMM that extends traditional HMMs to structured and non-Gaussian continuous distributions. paragraphs: Hidden Markov models describe sequence data through hidden states and observations. The paper identifies restrictions in conventional models, including discrete latent states and observation models largely confined to Gaussian or discrete distributions. It also highlights that most HMM learning algorithms rely on local search, which motivates a different approach to fitting the model.

The authors propose a nonparametric HMM based on Hilbert-space embeddings that extends the framework to structured and non-Gaussian continuous distributions. They derive a kernel spectral learning algorithm that is free of local minima. The contribution therefore changes both what distributions the model can represent and how the model is learned.

Evaluation uses robot vision, slot-car inertial sensors, and audio event classification. The embedded HMMs exceed the previous state-of-the-art performance in these applications. These results support the usefulness of the representation and learning method across several sequence-data settings. The reported performance advantage applies to those applications, while the local-minimum-free property is a separate characteristic of the proposed learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric embedded HMM supports richer distributions and a local-minimum-free kernel spectral learner, outperforming prior methods in three reported applications.

title: Hilbert Space Embeddings of Hidden Markov Models
